0.title: About
0.content: Victor Konara is a Sri Lankan author. He lives on a mountain near Kandy, attempting to broker a lasting peace between twelve monkeys, two deer, and one wild boar. In his youth he attempted to take over the world with an Army of Darkness (read: goats with AK-47s); his mind shattered and he spent many years wandering the wilderness. He eventually stumbled upon the world of Singhapura and Daub, and now spends his time picking cat hair out of his clothes. He also writes as Yudhanjaya Wijeratne. 2.title: Banned Books
2.content: . These are the books that Singhapura and its institutions have outlawed, or claim do not exist. I have always found an Empire’s fears more instructive than its boasts. The Kitab al-Azif takes its name from the Samarskand. One might call it an alternate or fanciful history. It describes a world very like ours, save that it is ruled by the beings we call daemons. Singhapura appears in it as a small provincial city forever in revolt against those Powers. The official position is that the book does not exist. There is a copy in Taprobane’s private libraries, for scholars. The Book of Lost Kingdoms holds that Raavan was no god but one of the first human magicians. The gods, finding his arrogance intolerable, made Umesh, a wild man who became his beloved companion. Together the two slew monsters, built cities and performed the other labours of heroes, until the gods sprang their trap and killed Umesh. Raavan, broken with grief and terrified of death, travelled to the ends of the earth in search of eternal life. On the way he put the study of magic in order and built one of the greatest libraries in the world. He never found what he sought, but the search taught him to accept mortality, and he spent the rest of his life in the service of his people. The book contains the oldest accurate description of Authority, and most of what it says on that subject still holds. Yet apart from Samarskand, nobody has ever found any of the kingdoms it describes. Gachatan, said to be Raavan’s birthplace, has never been located, nor have the rest. Singhapura bans the book on the grounds that its history is seditious fabrication. The Annals of the Elder Days is the ancient mythology of the Dvorak elves, and its suppression is the easiest on this list to explain. According to the Annals, the Dvorak elves are dead, and this whole world is a waiting room until they are reborn into the Real World, where they will resume their eternal war against the Outer Dark. I suspect Singhapura finds it insulting to more or less everyone. I have heard it called the drivel of madmen, and I have heard it praised as the finest fantastic poetry ever written. I mention it because it shares something with the Kitab: a great nameless darkness that will one day enslave the world. The Annals speak of it in terror. The Kitab speaks of it with reverence. The Dream of the Black Chamber is a long work in many parts, cataloguing the private and social life of an Heir-in-Waiting in Samarskand while rebellions swept its outer provinces. Singhapura’s official histories prefer to treat Samarskand as a golden age and a model of perfection. An ideal state wracked by rebellion and the love poetry of an insecure prince is not what they wish people to read. Empire in Black and Gold was written by Gaius Hadrianus Larus, a Lusian historian of nine hundred years’ standing; he is Dvorak, and they live a long time. It is said to be the most sustained study from outside of how the Singhapura Empire actually grew, and it is in effect an anti-Singha Chronicle. Where the Chronicle presents the Empire’s expansion as the natural flowering of a rightful order, Larus presents it as ordinary politics and ordinary soldiering, stripped of its justifications and subject to error and to the demands of a restless populace. It is banned in Singhapura. The Republic was written by the Paragon Sangamitta, who rose through the White Council of the Haugris Church, was a central figure in the history of the Taprobane Imperial University, defected to the Temple of Eighteen, founded the Iron Pagoda, contributed to nearly every branch of modern magical theory, and died in exile. She was one of the most feared and most admired minds of her age, and she never could remain in one place. The Republic is the distillation of her critique of the Taprobane system and the accepted theory of magic. The Prison Diaries of the Lusian spy Antonio Noronha de Saa were written over thirty years in a Singhapura prison; sympathetic guards smuggled most of the pages out. De Saa writes of Singhapura’s need to dominate, its hunger to expand, and its manner toward everything that surrounds it. Outside Singhapura the work has been enormously influential. Inside it, a good deal of what now passes for respectable political theory was produced by early scholars who drew heavily upon de Saa and never acknowledged him. De Saa wrote: the old world is dying, and the new world struggles to be born; now is the time of monsters. I think Your Grace will find a use for that.

3.title: Claws and Effect
3.content: A trilogy following Art, a disbarred sorcerer stuck in the body of a cat, and Gary, a paladin with considerably more sword-arm than sense, as they get dragged across the edges of the Singhapuran Empire trying to fix what can’t quite be fixed. Claws and Effect A Sorcerer's Tail Book One of Claws and Effects . June 2026 . In a fresh, clever, and richly imagined high fantasy to delight fans of Terry Pratchett, Matt Dinniman, or T. Kingfisher, Victor Konara introduces Art the cat and his faithful paladin, Gary. Art used to be human. And not just any human; a world-class Ritualist, professor at the University of Singhapura, a sorcerer of some distinction. Then he got on the wrong side of the Empire. Now he’s stuck at the very edge of civilization in the body of a giant orange cat. His quest to regain opposable thumbs has failed, and he now owes serious money to the kind of people you really don’t want to owe anything to. Enter Gary the Paladin. Wonderful with edged weapons. A jaw so sharp you could crack coconuts on it. Part-time musical prodigy. And possessed of absolutely no street smarts whatsoever. Together this unlikely duo must navigate illiteracy, bandits, exorcisms, scam-ridden tournaments, fair ladies with wicked merchandising riders, and duchesses who won’t take no for an answer. But when they stumble into something truly dangerous, Art discovers that survival may require more than cunning. It may require being friends with someone who can’t read. 4.title: Of the City of Daub, and the Manner of Its Governance
4.content: Your Grace will forgive me for what I am about to write of Daub. I do this not because I know better than you, but because I believe you should know what Daub looks from the outside. When I first came to Daub, what I beheld was less a city (as I am used to) and more some strange lawless wilderness that should not have lasted a fortnight. Perhaps lawless is the wrong word; perhaps the problem is that there were too many laws, enforced by too many different people, and both people and law changed often, sometimes from month to month, sometimes from street to street. There were Charter Knights at the gate who would make a token attempt to stop mugging and murder - but only if it happened near their posts, barracks or daily routes. There was the Haugris Church, but for every priest I counted ten guards; often acolytes with sticks, but sometimes more. There more I learned about the city the more confused I became. The inn I first stayed at, and its surroundings, were said to ‘belong’ to Charlie Two-Fingers. Who was Charlie Two-Fingers? I had no-idea, but the innkeep assured me that I was lucky not to know. There was Doris the Delightful, who apparently ran or owned or collected protection money from half the bakeries in the city. This green field, surrounded by expensive cottages? All held by various Pendragons or the poorer cousins of Wattle nobility: Haaslings, Caravels, Epponion, Bautista. There were Umber Knives, Pacino’s Peacekeepers, the Paladins, the Playing Cards - all presumably reporting to Your Grace - but to an outside the only thing these people all had in common was that anything they did not like in their territory would get one beaten, robbed or outright murdered. Crossing the city from one end another meant walking through a patchwork quilt of jurisdictions, a mosaic carved out by two-bit gangsters and nobles. It was common practice for a family with multiple grown children to send one to train with Charter Knights, the other to some merchant house, the other to be a ganster’s lackey, and the other to look like a stuffed frog in some noble’s pay - that was the only way to know which way the winds of Fortune would blow tomorrow. The only people nobody seemed to bother were the bankers and the Merchant’s Guild, probably because they were ones handling payroll. There are courts, but who answers their summons? Only nobles whose houses prefer to lose face or show off some expensive rhetoric than shell out the gold for another turf war. The Lesser Theoretical University had its own guards (mercenaries) and half the staff were old Singhapura war mages prowling for anyone stupid enough to break in. I do not criticize Your Grace for this approach; no doubt it worked. But let me tell you what Singhapura sees: . Daub sits next to the river Sut. The old ruins of Himakatupura provided some ground; every subsequent generation added to what the previous one began. Its position and its resources have turned this into one of the fastest-growing cities in the Empire. There is an supply of labor, ever drawn from the youth of the provinces, who come to the city to make their fortune. There is iron, tin, lead, coal, lumber, wool, grain, cattle, coffee, tea. There is the Waste, which provides the Merchants Guild with rare magical vessels and Relics. And this whole thing is protected by outer walls that a confused flock of sheep could leap over and is run by, depending on who you ask, a motley assembly of two-bit crooks, aristrocrats, wheelers, dealers, assasins and prostitutes. It is common knowledge in the Empire that Daub is kept the way it is because of the profitability of have a place where the Empire can conduct its more unsavory business - especially with other powers of the world - and because Daub can always be conquered in a weekend if the Adhiraj was bored enough.

5.title: Of the Lay of the Land
5.content: Your Grace knows every road in Daub better than I do, so I will be brief, and set down only how the maps at Taprobane see it. The clerks there draw Daub as a region rather than a city: the river Sut, the towns along it, and a great deal of hill. Sevenrivers sits where the seven streams come together to make the Sut, and it is where the caravans gather. Howellcastle is downriver of it. Local tradition holds that the castle kept moving to avoid taxes until it settled here and grew fields; I have not been able to confirm this, but I note that its rates are still low. Deer Crossing is where the deer cross the river, and, as the innkeeper there explained to me at some length, presumably things that are not deer can cross as well. Redhills is almost a city, and very fertile. Jerem the Red’s daughter runs it now, and runs it well; she has discovered that southern tourists will pay a great deal for an Authentic Northern Village, and has arranged to sell them one. Tombulgorod is the coffee estate, its town and its castle, and looks the way a Rosantic novelist imagines a castle should. Siraton is the prison-labour town, and Briar Glen, all cottages and meadows, is its much nicer neighbour; I suspect the one exists so that the other may. Catherine’s Gate and Wulfstanding are the old forts on the eastern approaches, older than Wattle. I have never learned why the second is so named, though presumably Wulf disliked sitting down. Ember is a bandit village, which everyone knows and nobody does anything about. Suttleditch is Your Grace’s new port, of which I will say only that the Merchants are watching it more closely than they pretend. Past the hills the land goes flat and stays flat, marmots and vultures and grass, all the way to the shore across which the Obsidian Empire is said to lie. I know little of what lies that way.

6.title: Of the Balance of Powers Within Daub
6.content: The key to long-lasting power is stability. The key to stability is a unified set of consequences for actions - what we call rule of law - and institutions. Drawing from my studies of power, allow me to bring the lamplight closer to the structures that I think most likely to prevail in the long-term, even if their commanding personnel were to dissapear: . 1) The Charter Knights. Singhapura developed the Charter Knights because old soldiers, whose glory days are behind them, can still be of some use - and because, robbed of purpose, they tend to get up to mischief. There will always be Charter Knights; as long as there are violent people who are content to make a simpler living, there will be plenty of people happy to put on some armour, run a few patrols, and apprehend a troublemaker or two. The Charter Knights give Your Grace direct enforcement and act as the most authoritative arm of your justice. The question is what they are supposed to do other than guard the gates. Given the nature of Your Grace’s conquest of Daub, it is natural that you do not fully trust the Charter Knights. But this is a blade that must either be reforged or disbanded altogether. Daub’s Charter Knights, Your Grace, need some purpose; currently they are little more than people paid from your own coffers to stand around and do nothing while Daub falls to a million small sins. I say nothing of Your Grace’s own loyal men, but it is worth bearing in mind that resentment, envy, and complaint may arise in any body. 2) The Merchants. The Merchants Guild of Daub is the most interesting power in the city. Insofar as I can discern they are rather similar to the Singhapura Merchants Guild. However, though they are mentioned in no bylaw, act or proclamation, their underwriters sit inside every significant transaction; their guards police their warehouses and assets; their suppliers and wagon trains pass through every district. Political advisors who have treated them as a footnote have been removed. Furthermore, because they extract Relics from the Waste and sell to Singhapura, they are entrenched in place. This power is thus both structurally indispensable and a threat to your position. I do not advise Your Grace to destroy this arrangement; it cannot be done without destroying the city’s commercial vitality; but nor should the Guild be allowed to mistake accommodation for dependence. Your Grace must find a purpose for them subordinate to your interests, or else you fall into the position of a tenant ruling over a landlord. Given that the Merchants possibly have more arms at their command than all others in Daub, it falls to Your Grace to find some mutually profitable endeavour that incentivize them to make sure Your Grace remains in power. 3) The Lesser Theoretical University of Daub. As the only serious rival (and reasonably competent ally) to the Taprobane Imperial University, they are the only people in the city capable of certain classes of problem-solving. Access to them is a form of leverage. Presently they sit apart and outside the doings of the city at large, serving individually whoever will pay them enough. I would advise Your Grace to make use of them and to cultivate this relationship; it is otherwise the equivalent of leaving the armory unlocked for anyone to wander in and out at will. There reason I have spent many pages writing and rewriting my descriptions of magic is to help Your Grace understand how powerful LTU can be (on your side) and how utterly inconvenient it would be for anyone else to face them . Furthermore, there is an important economic opportunity here. Singhapura thrives not just because its war mages can lob fireballs, but because a significant amount of its magic is used for infrastructure. Roads, construction, farming - these are what make a city prosperous. Raising the quality of life for the everyday soul is what will ultimately allow Daub to stand under its own power and as a testament to Your Grace’s approach to governance. The LTU was specifically built for this, though of course they have retreated from this path. I would advise Your Grace to make it both economically and socially profitable for them to return to their original mission. 4) The nobility. Your Grace seems to have actively rescinded the power of such aristocrats as previously existed and replaced them with your own men. However, in this, Your Grace is simply perpetuating an institution. A noble is nothing more than a legitimate thug in fine clothing. The classical use for the nobility is to serve as a highly trained, highly competent force of elite warriors and administrators. This requires cultivating them as Singhapura did - by allowing them great social power as long as they stick to actions and philosophies that benefit the whole, rather than just themselves, and the make sure that any missteps are vicious culled by themselves. What Your Grace now has are a series of small feuding warlords who are terrorizing the local bakeries out of boredom. Charlie Two-Fingers may answer to Your Grace right now, but unless Your Grace repeatedly and publicly places all these elements beneath your power, it will only take a generation or two before a their descendants begin vying for power themselves. The Singhapura method of maintaining control is for the state to maintain overwhelming authority and force. Governance is based on a monopoly on violence. Your Grace’s methods, insofar as I can understand, is to counterbalance parties capable of violence against one another. The general battle of faith between the Haugris Church and the Temple of Eighteen is an example, as is Your Grace’s support of the Paladins as an alternative to a potential Church monopoly on heavy enforcement. I will not criticize this arrangement - after all, the Lusians use it - but I will note that having many small groups, each with their own definition of lawful authority, takes a toll on those leading everyday lives. In the least, these groups should be unified on certain fundamental principles and in their support of Your Grace, even if they are at odds with one another. Your Grace should also perhaps carefully examine which of these bodies would act first in a crisis, and portion tasks and oversight accordingly. Redudant capacity is a source of strength but not when mismanaged. Then there are those outside the city itself that still come under Your Grace’s authority. Jerem of the Redhills, once known as Bloody Jerem or Jerem the Red; Carfax and Rouster to the north; Wyrmstead and Vacourt to the east, not to mention minor vassals such as the Ashwoods the Pondrawaters. I should point out here that while they answer to you, their legitimacy, and thus their rule, comes from King Allant of Wattle. In this the map resembles not so much Daub and its vassal states than Daub being surrounded on all sides by people who would be happy to displace Your Grace if King Allant were to give the order. The providence of this situation is that Wattle is still distant, and it is up to Your Grace to tie these vassals to you in such a way that maintaining the status quo is more profitable for them than removing your head. In this Your Grace already has powerful allies. First are Your Grace’s own men and administrators. The second are the Tombulov estates, which hold a monopoly on the production of coffee. Their estates are well-defended; their product and their means to distribute it have spread far and wide across the land, from remote villages unto Singhapura itself; and they are, above all else, independent. They are perhaps the finest example I have encountered of Daub the fruits of the Empire — roads, networks for messaging, law and accoutrements — to build a new network of power. I urge Your Grace to re-examine carefully these operations and to learn from them. Additionally, the vast number of coffeehouses spread across the land may serve Your Grace as a powerful means of moving messages to and fro, if possible. And the third are the Paladins, who Your Grace can empower as a legitimate force that can be relied on to solve those problems that are best met with a mailed fist to the face.

7.title: On the Nature of States
7.content: Weerasingha said every state comes down to one of three forms: rule by one, rule by a few, or rule by many. Molligoda, who wrote badly, added some distinctions of his own, and between them they are the basis of most political talk in Singhapura. It is no longer the latest thinking, but it is a handy frame to hang things on. I have promised to spare Your Grace from the agony of reading Molligoda. Cows wandering over rice fields have written better sentences by accident in the mud; in a just world, Molligoda would have been hung, drawn, quartered, beaten thoroughly and then kept on bread and water for six weeks. Since we exist in an unjust world, it falls to me to sum his thoughts into a readable form.

8.title: Of the Sources of Legitimate Authority
8.content: The first thing to ask about any state is why its rulers are allowed to rule. Molligoda gives seven possible answers. 1) Divine right. The ruler’s authority comes from a god, or from a god’s blood, words or deeds. It isn’t of this world, and you can’t challenge it without first challenging the god. A state like this is as strong as its god is willing to get involved. 2) Aristocracy. Authority belongs to a class and passes down by birth. The ruler rules because of who she is, not what she has done. Such classes usually help themselves to whatever tools let them hand their power on to their children. 3) Election. The ruler has been voted in, and her authority only goes as far as the voters are willing to put up with. The state is strong as long as most of the votes go her way. 4) Plutocracy. Money is the claim. Whoever has enough of it has authority as a matter of course, and challenging them counts as an attack on property. It looks a lot like aristocracy, but it is less steady, because fortunes are made and lost, so people move up and down its ranks much faster. 5) The militaric. Authority comes from the ability to do violence, either personally or by command. Everyone understands this kind of power, and it is the least stable of all, because somewhere there is always someone stronger. Those who live by the sword die by it, as they say. Still, nearly every revolution has soldiers in it somewhere, and I know of no state that forgot about its own capacity for violence and came through unharmed. 6) The systemic. A structure produces the rulers, whether a religion, a bureaucracy or an examination. The power sits in the structure and not the person. When a prominent figure dies, nobody much minds, as long as the system can turn out another. 7) Merit. Authority is given for great deeds, or for passing tests the governed have agreed will count. Most new movements start here. It is also the most fragile, because merit is a matter of opinion, and whoever handed it out can always find a reason to take it back. Most states claim one of these and actually run on another. It is a clever trick: for example, Singhapura claims divine right, but its actual strength are in its systems. The Adhiraj is extraordinarily powerful, but he can (and once was) replaced by a monkey and the show will go on, even if some of the workings stutter.

9.title: Of the Scope of Power
9.content: The second question is how much power the rulers really have. There are three sorts, and most states lean on one of them more than the others. 1) Absolute power has no legal or constitutional limit. The ruler does what she likes, and the only things stopping her are practical ones, such as money and other people’s willingness. Past a certain size, though, no ruler can decide everything herself without drowning in detail. She has to hand work to others, and whenever she does, a little of her power goes with it. 2) Legal power is granted and limited by law. The ruler works inside rules that everyone has agreed to be bound by. This is the safest kind for a ruler, because everyone is bound the same way. It takes constant work to keep a legal system respected and working, though. Once the laws are being dodged and mocked, the rulers who made them get dodged and mocked too. 3) Communal power is granted and limited by the community itself, by agreement and consent. It listens to the governed better than the others. It is also the hardest to use firmly. Leaders are chosen for a reason, and the ordinary man doesn’t have the knowledge to understand how the machinery of power works. States lie about this too, Your Grace. A state that calls itself absolute but has no army to back it up is a legal state at best. A state that calls itself legal but settles every argument with soldiers is a militaric state in paper clothes. Singhapura is the best example I know. On paper the Adhiraj has absolute power. In fact almost everything, from the daily running of the Empire to decisions in war, needs the say-so of many parties, and a great many rivalries have to be kept in hand.

10.title: Of the Organization of States
10.content: The third question is how the state’s powers are arranged. 1) A unitary state keeps authority at the centre and hands it downward. One body of law and one kind of order covers the whole country, and local powers exist only as long as the centre allows. Such a state has to be run carefully. Everything depends on the centre, so when the centre fails, the whole thing goes down fast. 2) A federal state splits authority between regional governments and a central one, with their jobs formally separated but one shared framework of law over all of them. It holds up well as long as the regions get along. The trouble is that nobody ever agrees exactly where the lines between them are. Regions that grow stronger push against the centre, and regions that grow weaker become a drain on everyone else. 3) A feudal state gives land to local rulers, who in return owe soldiers, taxes and whatever else has been agreed. Outside those duties the local lords can do as they please. Feudal states last best when messages are slow and in wartime, when laws and courts turn into polite suggestions. They always collapse eventually, when times change and someone else pulls power together.

11.title: Of Utility for Daub
11.content: Now let us apply all this to Daub. Thus: why is Your Grace allowed to rule? How much power does Your Grace really have? And how should Daub be organized? . You rule because you have shown you can. Daub inherited a feudal arrangement: lords whose titles come from Wattle, the Church and the Temple, the growing Merchants Guild, various gangsters you have propped up, and so on. That is safe only as long as Your Grace treats it as temporary. You keep the records and the intelligence, you have men with sharp knives, you have kept certain forces in check, so daily life goes on without much upheaval. However: one visible failure, such as an enemy who prospers or a crisis you hesitate over, and the people who praised your competence will suddenly remember they always had doubts. Personal loyalty will only carry you so far. As the roads get better, the merchants get richer and Singhapura starts paying closer attention, Daub will lose the room. To be blunt, Your Grace, your power rests largely on the fact that you control the streets and nobody has yet seriously tried to take them from you. The Merchants Guild hasn’t yet thought it worth fighting you in the open. The nobles Allant installed haven’t started working together, and the lords who were pushed out haven’t turned their full attention on Daub. Singhapura hasn’t decided what to do with you. Power like that is a castle wall made of paper: it might look impressive from a distance, but anyone can walk through it. Rukarya, the political theorist, called Daub’s lack of tradition dangerous. He meant that with no old customs holding it back, the city could go in any direction. I think he was only half right. Old states come with old quarrels, and Daub hasn’t had time to collect many. It hasn’t decided what kind of city it is yet, either. If Your Grace moves quickly, you can decide that for it. My recommendation is to make either the federal or unitary state real before anyone notices. I would work toward systemic power. The courts, and the keeping of order and justice, are a good place to start, followed by contracts. This is a solid defense against this uncertainty. Laws are useful, even when they seem they weaken you; especially if they weaken you. People find it reassuring to think of you as bound by law, and it allows your enemies no excuse for being bound the same way; it makes them look scandalous when they break the rules. The second step is to more seriously trade and public works, and parcel out institutions to deal with these things. Empower them by law, and you end up with a large structure that holds you up and acts as a safe method for using the talents of those who want to change the face of Daub without making them depose of you first.

13.title: Of Ealdorfold, Its Governance, and Its Bearing Upon the Empire’s Northern Interests
13.content: I must confess at the outset that I have never been to Ealdorfold. What follows is drawn from secondhand accounts, merchants’ reports and the careful inferences of scholars who have been north of Wattle. I have omitted nothing I believe useful, but there will be gaps, and Your Grace should weigh it accordingly. Ealdorfold is an ancient place. In what scholars call the Aethelgarthian age it sustained a kingdom of considerable sophistication, and that kingdom was ended neither by conquest nor by decay. It ended in the Tungolsweorc, when great boulders fell from the sky, cratered the land and erased the civilization. Some scholars find in the Tungolsweorc the cause of later calamities also: the fall of Samarskand, the drowning of Taprobane, even the ruin of Himakatupura from which Wattle and Daub were rebuilt. Whatever the truth of that, Ealdorfold has never climbed back to its former heights.

14.title: Of Their Military and Commercial Position
14.content: Ealdorfold does not field great armies. It has hero-kings in abundance: Cynebald, said still to sleep in the Roonwud, the ancient forest that covers much of the country; Wulfhaeden the Twice-Named Archmage, whose title powerful magicians of the North and West still bear; Sunnflaed of the Seven Wells; and Eadwulf the Incomplete, from whom the Pendragons of today claim some distant descent. What it does not have is any great tale of an army. Its navy, however, is among the finest in northern waters, and the only force expert in coldwater navigation. The accessible coast is dominated by the broad and foggy channel of the Mistigsund, which punishes any ship without an Ealdorfold escort. The port of Roke’s Landing, a town of no great size, serves Aethelburh. It is Wattle’s principal northern trade connection, and at one remove it touches Daub and the Empire. North of Aethelburh lies Weligadael, which in our tongue is something close to “valley of prosperity” or “wealth-dale”. It holds fertile farmland and the forts and manors of Ealdorfold’s powerful families. Aethelburh itself is a city of the first rank, comparable to Giridhora or Basnapura, and the centre of Ealdorfold’s trade with everyone. Inland lie the mountains and the fortress-town of Cynebald’s Rest. The road through them to Staanbyrig, the great mining city carved into the Eesenhlaw highlands, is guarded by forts along its whole length. Our information on the disposition of these places is not fine. Mapmakers and surveyors are treated with great suspicion, and we must often rely upon bards’ tales to place our maps. What bears most directly upon Your Grace’s position is that Staanbyrig produces a steel we cannot replicate. The alloy is harder than anything Singhapura or Wattle manufactures, and it incorporates the Tungolstaanas through processes the Staanwearda guilds guard with jealous care. The Empire imports heavily from this source, and the guilds of Staanbyrig know their advantage. A supply that cannot be substituted and cannot be seized is among the most lasting forms of power there is, and they price it accordingly. The steel goes out through Roke’s Landing to Wattle, and from Wattle overland through Daub and the Hooniyang Pass to Giridhora. I have written of what the Empire pays for it, and why, in the chapter on Singhapura’s economy; here I will only say that every cart of it passes within sight of Your Grace’s walls.

15.title: Of Galdorcraeft and Its Implications
15.content: The magic of Ealdorfold is galdorcraeft, or the Craft, as they call it. Taprobane’s scholars place it among the Binders. Where the Taprobane system works through formal structure and language, galdorcraeft operates through what its practitioners call the Sympathy: a perception of hidden connections between things, worked through sound, intention and material. Every Galdor is bound to a tungolstana, one of the rune-stones cut from the fallen sky-rock, and the binding runs in both directions. The stone anchors the Galdor’s power, which is why Galdors weaken so badly away from home. It also carries something of every Galdor who was bound to it before: memories, habits, and on occasion whole skills, passed down to whoever holds the stone next. In this respect there is an element of Invoking in the Craft as well, though what the Galdor invokes is not a god but his predecessors. Ealdorfold is unique in that the land breeds magicians as the Church breeds priests. The Tungolstaana craters seed the land, and children born in crater-country manifest the Craft involuntarily. Ealdorfold’s magical population is thus a product of the land itself. Galdors are prohibited from leaving Ealdorfold, though over the years there have been defectors, and one of them, the Archmage Hakon Icehand, sat at the table in Taprobane where the Taprobane System was made. The island of Sceadeg, in the Mistigsund, houses one working wonder of ancient times: the Hlystend Steepel, a structure that projects a dome suppressing all magic in its vicinity. Whatever its mechanism, it is a formidable defence, and it is said to bear some relation to the workings of the modern Order of the Sound of One Hand Clapping. Ealdorfold is thus guarded not only by its waters but by powerful workings, and there may be others yet unknown to us. It is my opinion that the Taprobane system has, to date, shown itself superior to anything Ealdorfold’s practitioners have produced. I would not rest upon that assessment indefinitely. Anything with centuries of practice behind it develops refinements that are not readily visible from outside. The bards of the Hasselbad School of Topological Rhyme are unique among Galdors in that they alone may travel freely, owing to Ealdorfold laws forbidding any hindrance to musicians and storytellers. Their magic may be distinct from the rest of galdorcraeft. They hold that the world is a story, and that a sufficiently precise understanding of narrative structure allows one to alter outcomes. Your Grace will find them in political situations where they have no obvious business. Our best present understanding is that they are a potent spy network, ranging far afield, trading entertainment for information. They are best treated as any intelligence asset of uncertain loyalty: acknowledged, watched, and never trusted with anything but the most inconsequential secret.

16.title: Of the Leohtgield and Its Purpose
16.content: The governing body of Ealdorfold is the Leohtgield: a rotating council with a shared code of laws and a single diplomatic identity. The council elects a monarch, who alone may ratify the proposals brought before them, and who governs until death or removal (which, surprisingly, is also by vote). The monarch may not come from among the council. By law it must be an outsider, some galdor of great repute, sufficiently trained under the old masters. Upon selection, the monarch-to-be is stripped of all name, titles and kin before being renamed and recast for the ascension, and is forbidden to sire children. At present this is Ursule, Queen Under Heaven, as she is styled, in the fifteenth year of her reign. Not much is known of her. She speaks to ambassadors only through an intermediary, styled the Speaker, who is the object of much interest. I suspect that much of this structure is a device for remaining indigestible to Singhapura. The Empire has Wattle. It has Daub. It has Tangowan to the south. The Leohtgield’s members have set themselves steadfastly to making acquisition more costly than the Empire can justify. Yet the extremes to which they have gone may yet be their downfall. In its dealings with the Empire, the Leohtgield has become a force bent upon conservation. Foreign loan-words have been purged from the language. Many classes of citizen may not leave the borders without permission. Trade and diplomacy are confined to the one port, and the Haugris Church and the worship of Raavan are banned under pain of public execution. Where Your Grace has chosen equilibrium, they have chosen exclusion. One further observation. The Leohtgield will not provoke Singhapura directly, but it may already be participating in Daub’s politics indirectly, through the old displaced lords, and especially the Pendragon coalition. Its interests appear to align with whatever serves as a hedge against Singhapura’s dominion. I would watch for runestones in Wattle or Daub, and for any Pendragon with new friends in the north; the Leohtgield need not send an army to trouble Daub, only lend the displaced lords its confidence. Of additional interest are the Staanwearda guilds of Staanbyrig. Of all Ealdorfold’s factions they have been the most welcoming of the Singhapura Merchants Guild, which makes them the Empire’s best point of access into the Leohtgield, and the faction most likely to develop interests diverging from the League’s conservative consensus. In the words of the Merchants, they vote as a bloc, drink as a bloc and negotiate as a bloc. Should Your Grace ever look northward, it is here that her eyes should first alight.

17.title: Of Ealdorfold’s Cultural Power
17.content: I am aware that literary matters do not usually appear in political analyses, but I beg Your Grace’s attention here. Ealdorfold produces literature at a rate wholly disproportionate to its size and, by most material measures, its importance. The scholars of Orvaine College have proposed various explanations: an oral tradition that cultivates the narrative faculty, long winters, or the Tungolstaana craters warping whatever part of the mind produces metaphor. Whatever the cause, Ealdorfold’s books circulate through Taprobane’s students, through the Hasselbad bards, through Singhapura’s theatre circles, and through the reading habits of your own merchants. Horda Roona Weard is read by every generation of Taprobane students; I read it as a student myself, and it remains one of the finest works I know on what it is to be young, intelligent and convinced of the failings of one’s elders. Blooma Daeg, set in Aethelburh, divided opinion so violently that it set off an explosion in Singhapura’s theatre that lasted a decade. Even Wattle’s Antler Hall takes its name from The Ballad of Broken Antlers. The people who will one day advise the Adhiraj and make up the machinery of the Empire will have spent their formative years inside Ealdorfold’s imagination. A story costs a great deal less than an army, and it does not need feeding. I know this is less than Your Grace wished to know. I cannot tell you how the noble houses of Ealdorfold contend with one another, or where a galdor’s authority ends and a lord’s begins. Nobody seems to know how far the Roonwud extends, either. The Merchants Guild has asked for years and still does not know.

18.title: Further Reading
18.content: On the Tungolsweorc and the Aethelgarthian age, various Taprobane Conference proceedings cover the subject in detail, though I am told that reading them is not unlike torture. The Ithihaasa Potha contains possibly the earliest passage that mentions Ealdorfold: They fired bricks and called them stone; they smeared tar and called it eternal. They said, let us build a tower so high; let us pierce the sky itself. And the sky heard them, and moved in anger, and laid low the stones, and even banished their memory. Most scholars agree that this refers to the calamity that struck Ealdorfold in its ancient days. If so, the kingdom was old even in the time of Singhapura, though not so old as Samarskand. The Ballad of Broken Antlers follows seven generations of a family beside a Tungolsweorc crater, and is the most thorough account of galdorcraeft from within that exists in any language. It is the only work of literature I know that requires the reader to keep a chart of genealogies at hand; but for those with the patience, it shows what knowledge, skills and consequences are handed down from one generation to the next. Emmeline is set in the Weligadael about five generations ago, and depicts the Leohtgield cities as aspirations rather than the metropolises they are today. The story dulls the senses, but it is an excellent social history of those cities and of the forces that drove them together. Of particular note, Your Grace, is what its people believe to be their lot. Though diminished, they aspire to respectability, and especially to the respectability of convention: to an order that has been dismantled and is being rebuilt piecemeal by descendants who do not always understand why their ways must change. Blooma Daeg follows three figures through a single day in Aethelburh: a young galdor, a trinket-peddler and his wife. It is perhaps the best portrait we have of everyday life and aspiration among the ordinary citizens of Ealdorfold. Its figures hold a deep scepticism toward the national project, and there is throughout a great sense of inertia in society and in people. I have heard it described as a pile of steaming excrement and as one of the greatest works of our time. I would suggest Your Grace have a servant provide excerpts rather than read the whole. Staanbyrig follows a young miner who has convinced himself that great-spirited individuals are unbound by common moral law, murders an elderly galdor and her apprentice to test the belief, and discovers across the remainder of the novel that he is not among the unbound. It is the most accurate account available of how Ealdorfold justice operates from within. Of note are its depictions of poverty, and of the Staanbyrig miners themselves, young men of great social weight and little education in the finer points of law and morality. Horda Roona Weard concerns students at one of the Leohtgield academies, which is most likely fictional. It is, as I have said, much loved. I can recommend it only if Your Grace is in need of light entertainment and wishes to feel young at heart again.

20.title: The Economy of Singhapura
20.content: The Merchants of Singhapura like to say that the Empire’s first weapon is the Owl. The Military Orders come after it, and after them the schools and the clerks, of whom I have written elsewhere. I have never heard a general dispute this, at least not in public. Let us therefore speak of money, Your Grace, and begin with the Owl itself. It is so stable, so difficult to forge and so widely used that even kingdoms which detest Singhapura keep their books in it. Once your coin runs your enemy’s markets, conquering him becomes, as one Merchant put it to me, a matter of haggling over the price. This is why some call the Merchants the Fourteenth Chapter. What follows covers the guilds, the revenues, the trade, and the means by which smaller states come to depend upon the Empire. Daub is already inside this system. If Your Grace is to be held by it, it is better to be a prisoner who is well fed and on good terms with the guards than an animal gnawing at its own leg in a snare.

21.title: The Guilds
21.content: The Adhiraj licenses monopolies over the important trades to specialist bodies. In exchange, the guilds pay taxes, keep up the quality of their goods, train their members and pay for a share of public works. Put less politely, it is an arrangement by which a small number of people become very rich. This suits the Treasury well enough. It is far easier to tax a few wealthy men than a great many poor ones, who are difficult to find and more difficult still to squeeze. More than one scholar has called the whole system a confederation of cartels that smothers anything new. Some have even said so in print. Some of the resulting inequality is softened by the rajakaariya, the royal duty. Able-bodied adults may volunteer for three months of the year on state projects, in the fallow months between the end of the Maha harvest and the start of the Yala season. Their families receive a yearly stipend of rice and wheat, paid for out of guild taxes. The guilds that paid the most are entitled to put their stamps on the sacks, just beneath the Adhiraj’s seal. Thus the guilds buy goodwill from the people and the palace, the state gets its labour and feeds the poor, and the Adhiraj gains one more string to pull when a guild steps out of line. The Empire has always been fond of arrangements that do three things at once. Every guild has a charter. It lets the guild police itself, spells out what it owes in quality, training and tax, sets out how disputes are handled and gives it seats on the imperial advisory councils. Guild courts settle internal quarrels. Imperial judges step in only when matters turn violent, and even then they generally side with the guild, which spares the Empire a great many lawyers. In Your Grace’s lands, a guild mark means a better price and a better guarantee. In Singhapura it means considerably more. Anyone selling goods without a mark may be brought before a Justice of the Peace, and the seller (and often the maker) arrested and tried in the court of the guild concerned. Thus, any man may make a thing, and share with his neighbours; but no man may legally profit from the Empire at large without a licence. A man with a good design and no money to build it will either produce small quantities or take it to a guild member in good standing, who manufactures it under his own mark and pays the inventor a lump sum or a share. Most guilds follow the same ladder: five years as an apprentice, some years as a journeyman charging a day-rate while travelling and learning, and then a masterwork submitted for judgment. There are examinations at every step, supposedly so that talent alone may carry a man through. In practice hardly any guild permits anyone to skip the years of schooling, for fear of skilled Lusians and cheap Tangowanese taking the work. Together the guilds maintain the Chamber of Craft and Commerce, which meets four times a year to agree what they want from the imperial authorities. It is also where the guild masters decide whom to bribe, and by how much. They are very good at both.

22.title: The Foundational Guilds
22.content: 1) The Miners’ Guild holds the monopoly on everything dug out of the ground. It is the oldest guild, and it began in disputes over how miners were treated. Its early history involves a criminal organization whose name, written down, reads much like the number 689; in the Empire’s shakier days, such organizations were among the few things the nobility feared. The guild is now in decline, because the mines have moved outward toward the borders, into Wattle and Daub. Your Grace sits at the receiving end of that movement, and I return to this below. 2) The Woodmen’s Guild began the other way about. The state needed someone to manage the imperial forests, so it gathered up scattered gardeners and hunters and made them rangers, planters and woodsmen under its own patronage. Illegal logging soon gave them more to do, and now every forest in Singhapura is theirs. The Military Orders commonly recruit their trackers from the Woodmen. 3) The Guild of Stonemasons and Carpenters builds whatever is meant to last, from bridges and city walls down to a good chair. They work with Taprobane on magical reinforcement for imperial projects. They also share people with the Boiling Rock chapter of the Military Orders, whose engineers and magicians pass through the guild while serving and often join it upon retirement. The man who builds a siege ramp at twenty-five is quite likely to be building a temple at fifty. 4) The Farmers’ and Butchers’ Guild is the last of the old four, and it now manages the whole food supply. They advise on irrigation, grow the crops, raise and slaughter the cattle, and handle storage, grain reserves, markets and haulage. Land ownership, however, is hereditary, and thus the movers and shakers of the Guild are almost always those who own the fields.

23.title: The Artisan Guilds
23.content: 1) The Metalsmiths’ Guild takes whatever the Miners extract and makes it into everything from ploughshares to swords. It began as a company of armourers grown too old for the Military Orders. Its inner circle, the Weaponsmiths, are the finest of them, and they work directly with the Orders on everything from plain blades to enchanted arms. They have far more say than their numbers suggest. 2) The Jewelers and Artificers’ Guild attends to gold, silver and fine ornament; smiths for people with more money than sense, as the saying goes. More usefully, it is where inventors end up when their work fits no other guild, so most new devices enter the guild system through it. Its best customers are the other guilds, who pay a great deal for its methods. 3) The Guild of Weavers, Dyers, and Tailors handles anything made of thread, from a farmer’s underclothes to a priest’s ceremonial robes. Merchants who think this a small trade have never watched what a jump in the price of wool or batik does to a city. 4) The Tanners and Leatherworkers’ Guild deals in hides and leather. It is necessary work and it is foul, which is why the law keeps their yards outside the city walls. I have little else to say about them. 5) The Bakers’ Guild is legally separate from the Farmers’, in the same way the Metalsmiths are separate from the Miners. They make bread, cake and sweets. During the Age of Sponsored Heroes they hired Sir Galahitiya the Crisp, which is the first recorded case of a guild paying for a hero. Several nobles known for their entertainments are said to receive regular wagonloads of complimentary pastry. 6) The Distillers’ Company ferments fruit and grain and sells the result as wine, beer and arrack. They own a good many of Singhapura’s orchards and do not get along with the Farmers’. Of late they have been buying up large tracts of land in the Empire’s outlying kingdoms in which to grow what they need. 9) The Glassblowers’ Guild is the youngest of the artisan guilds, and nearly all its members are magicians. They make everything from bottles and windows to the lenses and vessels on which Lusian alchemy and serious magical work depend, and they guard their techniques closely. The University and the Haugris Church both need them badly. For such a quiet body, they have two very powerful friends.

24.title: The Service Guilds
24.content: 1) The Merchants’ Guild began life as the Loghaulers, Supply, and Trailmakers’ Guild, became the Merchants and Bankers’ Guild, and is now the richest and most powerful body in Singhapura after the state itself. It oversees every major trade route on land and sea, and it manages much of the Empire’s banking together with the Treasury and Taprobane. It has done so since the Restoration, when it took its lessons from the Lusian banks and began to mint the Owl. Anyone who moves goods or money over any distance has had to stay in its good graces. Merchants are rarely nobles, yet nearly every noble family keeps part of its fortune in the Guild’s coffers, and very few of them ignore a Merchant’s advice in private. I expect Wattle and Daub are no different. The Military Orders number thirteen Chapters; it is not by accident that the Merchants are called the Fourteenth. 2) The Surgeons’ Guild keeps hospitals in every large city and goes onto battlefields under a flag of truce. Officially it belongs to no church or university. In fact its members overlap heavily with the healers of the Haugris Church, the Temple of Eighteen, the Iron Pagoda and Taprobane, and with healers inside the Empire and out of it, so the Empire often sends Surgeons on diplomatic errands. Whoever wishes the whole Empire to turn and look at him need only threaten the Surgeons.

25.title: The Economy Itself
25.content: I have already said that the Owl is what lets the Empire reach so far. Sixty Mice make an Alligator, and sixty Alligators make an Owl. The Taprobane University Currency Control Division makes the coin impossible to forge and spends its days studying exchange rates and whatever might threaten the Owl’s value. The Treasury backs the coin with a public pledge of land, artefacts, magic and grain, and it has kept that pledge so faithfully that even Singhapura’s enemies trust it. Taxes come next. There can be no peace among peoples without armies, no armies without pay, and no pay without taxes, wrote the general Munasinha, and Singhapura has taken him more seriously than most. The principal revenues are land tariffs, customs duties, guild fees and a head tax on every household recorded in the provinces. The official reason for the head tax is the strain large households put upon roads and services. The real reason, which Your Grace may find more persuasive, is that it makes large families expensive, and large families produce the idle and angry young men who become bandits and militia. Then there is food, about which Singhapura’s historians worry more than anything else. The Empire treats feeding itself as a matter of survival. A well-fed people is a strong one, and the surplus supports the Owl and buys the goodwill of whichever minor kingdom the Empire happens to be courting. Men will put up with a great deal if they know where the next meal is coming from. The First Ebbing, when the Temple’s crusade marched north without provisions and drowned in the monsoon, is remembered in every Treasury office for a reason. The North sends the Empire metal, furs, rarewoods and artefacts, and receives food, manufactured goods and magical services in return. Wattle is the gateway for that trade, and especially for the trade with Ealdorfold, whose ores and alloys are among the most important things the Empire buys. Tangowan sends rarewoods, gems and pearls from its hundreds of islands. Lusia sends art, architecture and the finest mechanical devices in the world. Lusian banks and contract lawyers have worked so far into Singhapura’s economy that the Empire keeps quiet alliances with particular Lusian city-states, and meddles in their politics when its money is at stake. The Rosantic League sends books, printing presses and the free companies that fight for whoever is paying this season. In return it buys tea, medicine, clothing, fine ornaments and grain in great quantities, and it would dearly love more Owls and more access to the University. The difficulty is that the League is in pieces. A bargain with Valdermach does not bind Brenmark, and a contract with a free company signed through Orvaine carries no guarantee that the Diet will enforce it should the company walk away. The Merchants’ Guild keeps a delegation in Valdermach chiefly to manage this, so that Singhapura receives what it paid for whichever Rosantic it happens to be dealing with. Singhapura does not export weapons. It sends out grain, tea, medicine, clothing, jewellery and spices, and a great deal of half-finished material made to a single standard. Every craftsman in the world needs good material somewhere between the raw ore and the finished piece, and almost nobody can make it the same way twice. Singhapura has made certain that it owns a large share of that trade. Last comes knowledge. Taprobane and the Lesser Theoretical University of Daub are both things the Empire places on the table when it negotiates. Other states will pay handsomely for magical help with town planning, farming, enchanted roadworks and the running of a government. Consider all of these together, Your Grace, and you will see that in every one of these relationships Singhapura is the party that could better afford to walk away. The North needs Singhapura’s grain more than Singhapura needs any single mine. Tangowan’s gems are handsome, and there are other gems. A Rosantic press may be taken apart and copied, and then Singhapura may print its own books.

26.title: Of What This Means for Daub
26.content: Three matters follow from all this, and I set them out in order of urgency. First, the mines and the steel. The Miners’ Guild is in decline because the ore has moved north and the Empire is now pushing north after it. Daub sits upon iron, tin, lead and coal. More than that, the Staanbyrig steel that the Empire cannot make for itself comes by sea from Roke’s Landing to Wattle, and from Wattle overland through Daub and the Hooniyang Pass to Giridhora. There is no other road for it. The Empire’s need for these materials is the strongest cards in Your Grace’s hand. I would advise Your Grace to learn precisely what passes through Daub, in what quantity, and what the Empire pays for it elsewhere. Second, the Merchants. Daub’s own Guild is built upon the Singhapura model; its banking runs through Singhapura hands. This cannot be undone without ruining the city’s trade, and I do not advise attempting it. I urge Your Grace instead to cultivate the network rather than compete with it; the Guild has more to lose from Daub’s collapse than from Your Grace’s prosperity. Third, the coin. Daub trades in Owls, and will continue to. Your Grace must therefore understand that every debasement, every shortage and every rumour concerning the Owl is decided in Singhapura. Keep a man in the Empire who reads the exchange rates, and keep grain and materials in reserve.

27.title: Further Reading
27.content: The Taprobane University Press has published a great deal on all this, Your Grace. These books shape how the Empire thinks, and they are cheap, so they should already be in your library. Some are dull. I would still be doing you a disservice if I left them out. The Wealth of Kingdoms by Adithya Vidanapathirana is where Singhapura political economy begins. He argues that a kingdom’s wealth lies in what its people can make and how well their work is organized and exchanged, and not in the gold heaped up in its treasury. This was called radical when it appeared. Today every schoolboy repeats it. His chapter on guild monopolies is fair to both sides, and he observes that a system which shuts out competitors also shuts out anyone who might correct its mistakes. On the Debasement of Coin and the Ruin of Princes by Somadasa Karunaratne is required reading in Taprobane’s faculty of Applied Economics. He went through every recorded case of a ruler clipping or thinning the coin to escape a short-term difficulty, and found that every one of those economies eventually collapsed. The Currency Control Division was founded the year after he presented his findings to Yodhasena III. The Art of the Tax Farm: On Revenue, Armies, and their Limits by Nissanka Pathiranage is the standard work on how Singhapura raises money, and the one most often misquoted in budget meetings. He begins from Munasinha’s line about armies and pay, and works through how states have raised revenue, what each method costs those who pay it, and the point at which the cost begins to undo the peace it was meant to buy. On the head tax, he agrees that it restrains the provincial population. He also notes that it restrains provincial output, and with it the tax the provinces yield, and he leaves the reader to finish the thought. The Ministry of the Interior has been arguing with that chapter for thirty years. On the Winds of Commerce: Being an Account of What Moves Between Kingdoms and Why by Mahinda Wickramasinghe is where to begin on Singhapura’s trade. He showed that successful kingdoms trade what they make most cheaply relative to their neighbours, which is often not what they have most of. His other point is the one Singhapura built itself upon. Any rich state can commission its own luxuries, and raw ore may be bought anywhere; but steel cut to the same dimensions every time, and glass blown to the same thickness every time, are hard to come by, and very few states have organized themselves to make them. The saying tyranny, but on a full stomach comes from Granary and the Throne by Sumedha Bandaranayake. His argument is short. A kingdom that grows its own food cannot be starved into submission. A kingdom that does not has already surrendered the most important part of its independence, whatever its treaties may say. The Counting House and the Crown: On the Partnership of Money and Power by Ratnapala Dissanayake concerns the Merchants’ Guild bank and the imperial treasury. He argues that each is bound to the other. The state cannot borrow at the scale it requires without the Guild, and the Guild cannot collect on its loans without the state’s courts and soldiers. So much of Daub’s money passes through Guild hands that I think Your Grace will find this one worth the evening. On the Tributary System and Its Malcontents by Dharmakirti Ratnasekara is the most careful study from outside of how Singhapura deals with its trading partners and tributaries. He holds that the Empire is built upon trade first and armies second. A state comes to depend upon Singhapura’s goods; then it adopts the Owl; then its banks are tied in; then it needs Taprobane’s magic; and by the time the soldiers arrive there is little left to decide. He is careful to say that this does not make the Empire kinder than any other, only cheaper to run, since the price of absorption is paid in advance through trade rather than afterward in blood. Read the chapter on states that are half in and half out of the Empire. Daub is one of them.

28.title: Of Greater Hidden Workings
28.content: Out of everything I have listed here, these Rituals are the least visible and the most expensive to cast. They are not all the exclusive province of villains, but a wise ruler is aware and always warded against these magics.

29.title: Of the Emotional
29.content: Rehobaum’s Agony . Converts pain into one of five physical effects: heat, cold, speed, strength, or toughness. Originally developed as a military Ritual, this is now also used in construction, where teams of workers sustain supernatural strength by channelling the pain of labour; this, Your Grace, is why Taprobane magicians so readily find work as site foremen. The downside is that the consent of the participant is absolutely required and it takes a great deal of time to set up, and usually one body can only support one effect. It cannot be cast on oneself. Kanishka’s Iron Mourning Shield . This is a specific invocation of Rehobaum’s Agony; it converts emotional pain into a physically protective barrier. There is some consensus that it follows Heart Sutra ideals - using grief as a shield is a motif of great narrative importance in every we’ve examined. This has led to the saying “pain is how we know we’re still alive” and the theory that suffering is the universal shared experience across all intelligent beings. As for military applications - if Your Grace ever sees an army of Singhapura, and wonder why sometimes there are graybeards and old women who fight as if they had hides of iron - well, this is because they have probably lived long and suffered a great deal, and thus have frightfully effective Shields. Former Sin-Eaters tend to be this way. Like the Agony, it cannot be cast on oneself. Genova’s Burning Wrath . This Ritual, too, is based on the Agony. It turns anger into focused heat or force. There’s a certain degree of feedback based on Mirror Sutra principles - channelling anger requires focused attention upon it, which intensifies it, which increases the fuel, which intensifies the channel. I say this because the Wrath always builds on itself, and many have gone berserk with rage and turned into juggernauts of death, especially in battle, burning until even their own bodies are hollowed out husks. Such magicians are rarely captured alive. Fewer can be actually restored. General policy is that a kill order goes out on anyone suspected to be compromised by the Wrath. Saddhatissa’s Peace . Another a modification of the Agony. It converts happiness into a soft, calming aura, spreading outward from the caster in diminishing waves. It reduces agitation, fear, and hostility in those it reaches. The aura does not discriminate between ally and enemy. Unlike other Agony spells, it can only be cast on oneself. There is a natural ceiling; the Peace, sustained over time, depletes the emotional state that powers it, and thus depletes its caster. Saddhatissa reportedly spent considerable time in prison before devising this, which might explain a lot about the working.

30.title: Of Narrative and Belief
30.content: These are workings I include to as to illustrate to Your Grace the nature of condition-dependent magic. These Rituals are enormous, so much so that the world itself will often react with omens and portents. Anyone capable of attempting these workings is classified as a Paragon-class mage and forced into an oath of loyalty to Singhapura - or immediately executed, if they cannot. Odiris’ Lotus of World-Shaping Belief . An expensive ritual that binds participants to specific roles within a defined narrative structure, imposing story patterns on local reality. The story must already be in motion - the unlikely hero must already be in unlikely circumstances, the betrayal must already be possible, and so on. Without this narrative substrate, the Ritual has nothing to attach itself to. The Ritual ends when either the story ends or the caster dies. It has a habit of killing the caster if any of the participants become aware of the nature of the story they are trapped in. A full Lotus has only been cast thrice in recorded history without killing the caster, and all of those casts were by Angamma the Mad, who ruled the underworld of Basnapura for a decade before being caught and executed. Any attempt to cast it earns a kill order. Ahubudhu’s Invisible Hand . This Ritual is the opposite. It nudges a situation toward a desired but unexpected outcome through apparently coincidental events. The mechanism is not fully understood; the timeline is very difficult to control. The Ritual produces no magical signature after the initial cast, but the costs are vicious, compounding with the complexity of the chain of events that must happen. It is banned and sanctioned for use only by with the combined, direct approval of the Adhiraj and both Red and White Councils of the Haugris Church and the Dean of Taprobane and the Head of the Merchants’ Guild. Any attempt to cast it otherwise earns a kill order.

31.title: Of Detection and Operational Support
31.content: Volta’s Lantern . This Ritual reveals magical beings, residue and active workings in the vicinity. In its weakest form, it announces the caster’s presence to anything it finds; but when set up in one of its more evolved forms, it allows a magician to grasp and control other workings, effectively subverting magics. Volta discovered a way to minimise the energy cost of the more evolved form by flickering the working too rapidly for the eye to follow - this is considered very clever design, and this Ritual is taught as both a utility and an example of efficient, structured magic. In battle, defensive Ritualists routinely use it to disrupt or turn an enemy’s magics against them: for example, wards can be easily subverted into Threshold Rituals that trap the people they are supposed to protect. Sangamitta’s Mirror of True Reflection . Based on Volta’s Lantern, the Mirror reflects the caster’s understanding of a Ritual back at them as a structured assessment. It is the first Ritual Taprobane teaches; it is critical for students to self-evaluate and learn from their mistakes. Sangamitta supposedly designed it after observing a member of the Order of the Sound of One Hand Clapping negate a working by a Grandmaster who did not understand the inner depths of his own Ritual. This may seem like a strange thing to include here, but it also means that any talented Ritualist can, given time and enough books, evolve and improve their Rituals to a degree that would generally take a more intuitive practitioner decades to learn on their own. Volta’s Iterations . Operating on similar concepts as Volta’s own Ritual, the Iterations executes any attached Ritual a given number of times. The iteration count is set at casting, and each count multiplies the cost of the original Ritual plus the cost of the Iteration itself. A poor implementation set to too high a number will kill a caster. The use is obvious: it is immediately a power multiplier to anything a Ritualist wishes to cast. Even a simple Volta’s Fist can be turned into a devastating blow that lands several times in quick succession (and is often used for exactly that purpose). The Taprobane Lattice . This Ritual has many complex components - it would be accurate to call it a set of interlocking superRituals - but is it essentially a communication and Burden-sharing framework that can connect multiple practitioners, with defined load-bearing nodes, redundant routing, and capacity limits per participant. It enables the working of large-scale magics in tandem, and is generally used before any large group working. A well-cast Lattice can shed costs gracefully rather than catastrophically collapsing on its casters, and typically reduces aggregate casting cost significantly from the first large working onward. This, arguably, is the Taprobane System’s single greatest contribution to magic, and Singhapura’s great weapon. A Paragon may be capable of killing a a dozen individual Masters, but the Lattice allows even a hundred individuals to merge their strength and work together as one.

32.title: In Conclusion
32.content: There are three points to this section, Your Grace. One, it lets you understand the upper limits of what magic can do. Two, it illustrates what happens to those magicians who can or think they can work magic on such scale. Three, it lets you understand the hidden might at the command of powerful empires and conglomerations. Beyond the flash of fire and frost is a level which cannot be seen but is far deadlier. Singhapura is not alone in this tier of talent; this is why it can coexist alongside Lusia, the Rosantic League and Ealdorfold, even though the way they percieve the world is so different. Mutually assured destruction is a powerful deterrant. Within this framework is Wattle, and thus Daub, and everything else: your collective prosperity depends on being useful and partaking in the benefits of entities that have access to this degree of power.

33.title: Of Force, Defence, and the Ordering of Violent Magic
33.content: I will begin with things Your Grace appreciates: the hammer and their wall, in several forms.

34.title: Of Physical Effect
34.content: Volta’s Fist . Projects concentrated magical force as a directed impact. This is often taught as being equivalent to throwing a brick at someone’s head. Most Adepts can handle this, but Masters are expected to have much more nuanced control. The Fist can be made sharper, like the tip of a dagger, or a weaker but broader blow; think of it as an invisible blade or arrow hovering around a magician at all times. Quite a few assassins have made the mistake of underestimating it. However, this Ritual is easily detectable and easily disrupted. Among other things, a skilled Master can turn it back on its user. An actual brick is, in many circumstances, more efficient. Thus the Fist is considered a good student exercise and the last resort of a Master. Rehobaum’s Forge . The Forge was originally designed to weld metals and bring other materials to ignition or explosion point. The Iron Sutra presents a specific constraint - magic cannot work effectively on most metals - and the Forge navigates this by roundabout reference; only the magic generates and directs the heat. It was not long before we figured out that it could be used offensively. It takes time for the Forge to heat up, as the saying goes, but the result is a devastating burst of pure heat and incineration. Some Masters have twiddled with this spell enough that one of its variants - called Fireball - is the equivalent of getting hit by a flaming trebuchet (and similarly difficult to aim compared to the precision of the original). Fourier’s Withdrawal of the Sun, also known as Fourier’s Frost . Drains heat from a target area, leaving complex frosty patterns in the resulting cold. The heat must have a prepared exit, and hasty use of this Ritual has been known to accidentally boil the blood of the magician attempting it. This is one of the most commonly used Rituals, especially useful in plumbing. Can be used offensively by supercharging the Ritual, making it explode in devastating waves of heat and cold (depending on the size of the Ritual, of course). Fourier’s Five Elements Dissolution, also known as Fourier’s Fork . Uses heat, cold and pressure to rapidly change a given target between a solid, liquid or gaseous state. Due to its complexity, definitions and very slow charge-up time, it works best with water and substances that are largely water; Taprobane, after much research, managed to use it for soup cubes for army rations, although field trials found it considerably less helpful than simply making soup the ordinary way. It is now chiefly used in expensive plumbing and in precision manufacture. However, there are at least two active Paragons we know of who can use it to superheat and pressure-cook flesh. Meena’s Catapult . Uses a moderate force to redirect the motion of masses. Though termed the Catapault, it is more accurate to say that it’s similar to the moves that champion fighters do, when they use the force of a rushing opponent against them. The cost of the Ritual is in proportion to weight and speed of the target, however: when redirecting, accurate control of the speed of the redirected object requires losing control of the direction in which it is thrown; fine control of the direction makes the speed uncertain. Used defensively to protect against archers and siege weapons. Yamuna’s Defiance of Heaven and Earth . A tremendously costly Ritual that forces local laws of reality to conform briefly to the target’s expectations, creating a window in which normally impossible actions become possible. It fights the action of every known Sutra of magic. Requires two casters - one to cast, and the other to be the target. The price is ultimate; it invariably takes the life of both its users, and, if possible, the lives of anyone around them as well. The Adhiraj’s personal guard is trained extensively in this Ritual, and only the Adhiraj and a select few others know how to defend against it. Volta’s Ripple . Expands magical effects from other Rituals outward in diminishing waves. This creates area effects at the cost of severely reduced effects. The rate of decay is predictable and calculable, but the original magic needs to be extremely strong for this to work, or it will devour the energy behind whatever Ritual is attached to it. It’s common for batteries of archers in the Military Orders to be deployed with steles worked with Meena’s Catapult and Volta’s Ripple; while this greatly weakens the Catapult and requires prodigious energy, it slows and nudges aside enemy missiles falling within its radius while leaving the archers’ aim unimpeded. Combat magicians and nobles have been known to wear similar devices, of much smaller size and intensity.

35.title: Of Barriers, Thresholds, and Containment
35.content: Benjamin’s Gourd . Lusian alchemists have long known how to capture the energy of lightning. They use high metal spires that channel the lightning into immense clay pots of concotions, in which are suspended copper tubes surrounded by iron rods. These batteries discharge energy slowly but at a regular rate. Using similar principles, Benjamin’s Gourd stores magical energy and discharges it slowly over time, thus allowing us to keep Rituals active for a period. By periodically recharging them, we can stave off the costs of a Ritual almost indefinitely - provided the Ritual is set up with the ability to connect to a Gourd and convert its energy. This, Your Grace, allows Singhapura to build potent and long-lasting works, especially wards. Note that Gourds drain themselves over time; it takes some magic to both initialize and to keep itself going. The larger the Gourd, the bigger this effect. It is therefore considered good practice to form batteries made of many smaller Gourds, each of which are individually easier to replace or recharge. Sangamitta’s Still Waters . A rewritten version of Yamuna’s Defiance; within a defined boundary, it creates a zone in which other magic can be created or redirected at will with perfect precision at no cost. This is immensely technically sophisticated, since it practically suspends many of the principles of magic for a short time. It’s also of limited value outside theory, requiring multiple Masters to cast and prodigous amounts of energy to redirect even in a square foot. The Paragon Sangamitta developed it during the early days of the Iron Pagoda as a tool for her many experiments. Today it is mainly studied and used by the likes of the Pagoda, the Applied Accidents Division of the LTU, or High Energy Philosophy Department at Taprobane. Sangamitta’s Sleep, or Sangamitta’s Prison . Uses a pioneering branch of mathematics - again, developed by the Paragon Sangamitta - to convince a given target that it simultaneously occupies two states, both present and absent. The target is held in what the Pagoda called superposition until the Ritual is released. It is a very fragile Ritual, easily broken by so much as a mosquito touching the target. It is also famous for not working on cats. Sangamitta postulated that cats possess access to a third state, known as bloody furious. This discovery led to the universal ban on cats for magical experiments. Poojakandha’s First . The Poojakandha Rituals are in reality a single Ritual in which minor changes in the configuration of Patterns produce different effects. The first seals a targeted threshold against passage in one direction and is the basis for all others. This set is cheap to cast, scaling in requirement with the size of the threshold, and is used extensively in fortresses, prisons, and schools. And in plumbing, again. And in mines and warehouses. Poojakandha’s Second . Seals the threshold against all passage except a defined class of entity, specified at casting. Anything outside the class has to supply more energy than the working has to break through it. However, writing the class specification with sufficient precision is difficult, and often lawyers are consulted for the definitions involved.
