Many Threshold Ritualists have gone on to second careers as criminal lawyers after retirement. Famously, such a Ritual, designed to keep out male visitors to an Imperial Princess, failed when her lover, who thought of themselves as female, simply walked in and eloped with her. This led to a certain revision of laws (and slowly, attitudes) on gender . Poojakandha’s Third . Does not seal the door at all. Instead, it decouples the threshold’s actual location from its apparent one and puts the real passage elsewhere. Redirection is cheaper than denial, so the ongoing cost of the Ritual is lower than any of the seal formulations. Often used as a security measure by the rich and the powerful to thwart assasins. However, while it is easy to cast and maintain, Water Sutra workings will route anyone who finds the illusion unconvincing towards unintended destinations. In my time at Taprobane there was a locked door that, having been poorly configured, would deposit curious students into the sealed section of the library, the armory, or into a toilet bowl in the women’s dormitory. Poojakandha’s Fourth . Seals the threshold conditionally - the door remains sealed until a specified condition is met, at which point it opens freely. Well-specified conditional seals can run unattended for centuries. Poorly specified ones are a nightmare. This is especially a problem that compounds over generations, as the world changes, language evolves, and people’s understanding of what words mean shifts over time. This makes for some interesting challenges in inheritance law and storage. Many doors in the Waste, for example, can be solved by riddling; the general consensus is that these are the effect of such ancient seals malfunctioning. Poojakandha’s Fifth . Seals the threshold in both directions and returns external force at double magnitude to its source. The caster pays the difference between what is received and what is reflected. A sustained assault by multiple parties is not manageable on a single practitioner’s budget. When the working runs out of energy, it typically destroys whatever it was cast upon. Some Chapters of the Military Orders use this spell on shields which can then double as incendiary explosions when thrown.

36.title: In Conclusion
36.content: I have, of course, omitted the vast number of workings in favor of the basic ingredients. I do not expect Your Grace to learn every Ritual and every variant; only to impress on you what is well-known. You will agree that several of these workings allow us to turn even ordinary Charter Knights into absurdly lethal weapons - with proper training and resources, of course. There are improvements that are easy to make and there are improvements that, given Daub’s resources, should only be limited to a handful of people. Perhaps this also will help explain why getting into a battle of any sort with Singhapura forces is a terrible idea: if one knight can become an unholy terror, imagine tens of thousands of heavy infantry empowered by hundreds of mages, and you will perhaps better understand why it is necessary to stay in the good books of the Empire.

38.doc: Gods of the Empire and the North
38.title: Gods of the Empire and the North
38.content: Certain philosophers hold that the gods are so far above us that a ruler may leave them out of her calculations. I disagree. Belief is older than any state, harder to predict than any enemy, and it does not send a herald ahead of it. What follows concerns the gods whose followers Your Grace governs or must deal with. I begin with the two great institutions, then the older gods of the household and the road, and end with the Light, which is the newest and the least understood.

39.doc: Gods of the Empire and the North
39.title: Of the Church and the Temple
39.content: Great Raavan comes first. The whole religious order of Singhapura rests upon him, and the Haugris Church holds his remains as the Divine Corpus. The Church teaches that Raavan is dead, that his death scattered his magic across the world, and that the Church is the rightful keeper of what he left behind. I have one piece of advice here, and I give it as strongly as I can: whatever Your Grace believes or does in private, do not speak heresy against the Church in public. It is one of the great powers of Singhapura, and it has made peace and war in about equal measure. Its favour will serve you. Its indifference will do you no harm. Its anger is slow, and it is very long. The Temple of Eighteen is the second power. By most counts only a tenth of Singhapura still worships there, but the Temple’s houses stand all across the provinces, and especially at the edges of the Empire. Its adherents spend years training themselves to act according to the nature of one of the Eighteen Litanies, until they resemble that deity closely enough for the Litany to take hold of them. The Temple keeps its secrets. Much of modern magic comes from its writings and sutras, so it plainly understands how the world works; yet for three centuries it has withdrawn, step by step, from politics. Some Litanies are known by name. The most powerful are hidden. On paper, the Temples choose a High Priest together to sit at the Emperor’s court. Your Grace should treat this as a polite fiction. No Temple has authority over another. There is no hierarchy, only custom, obligation and shared practice. It has survived its disgrace after the First Ebbing and its ruin after the Withering of Himakatupura on exactly that basis, which is more than can be said for several dynasties.

40.doc: Gods of the Empire and the North
40.title: Of the Baara and the Older Gods
40.content: Outside the Church and the Temple there are older gods. Many people make baara, which means bargains or vows, with quieter deities, some of them older than any church. These gods have no priests and no institutions, though some have shrines. The person making the vow promises to do certain things, or to live in a certain way, and in exchange asks the god to intervene in some matter. When a man does something that his politics, his faith, his character and his friendships cannot explain, it is worth discovering whether he has made a baara. Ginisundara Devi is commonly worshipped as a minor goddess of the hearth and home, but she is in truth a goddess of fire in every form, and after Raavan she may be the most widely worshipped god there is. Household shrines to her, with a clay lamp and a small offering, are found all over the Empire and especially in the provinces, and women generally keep them. She is said to appear in person to women who are cold and in trouble. Mahasona’s name means mass grave. In the older accounts he was one of Great Raavan’s generals; the Mahason Chronicle has him ruling the leaderless Yakshas after Raavan’s death. He is now the god of graveyards, slaughter, revenge and punishment. Gravediggers and soldiers smear ash upon their hands in his name, and mothers use him to frighten unruly children. Nobody worships him officially. Half the army does. Great Yama is worshipped as a protector in Nagenapura, and in the rest of Singhapura as a god of wisdom and survival. Some accounts make him a guard, others an advisor to Raavan, and a few make him Raavan’s teacher, or his predecessor. Soldiers and travellers leave him offerings before a dangerous journey. Metera Samsina, called Goyamma in the south and sometimes Miyara Devi, is the Mother Who Reaps. She presides over harvests and floods, easy births and deaths, the turning seasons, and the lives of ordinary people, whom she is said to love above all others. She appears as a young girl or an old woman, and stands by at births and deaths. People leave her milk-rice, honey and salt on birthdays and when someone in the house is sick. Your Grace will find very few who omit this, even among those who never speak her name. Yakadha Hadhawatha, also called Ironheart, is said to have been an Adhiraj whom history has since forgotten. He spent an age pursuing Raavan’s power and let all else decay. The ambitious pray to him, and especially those who want power badly enough to alarm their families. Galwadu is the Stone-Maker, or Stone-Hand. I believe he came from Ealdorfold, where a similar god called Lapidon rules the deep places under the earth. In Singhapura he is the god of building and of endurance, and so miners, masons, builders, engineers and a good many soldiers pray to him. His sign is carved upon bridges and into the foundations of buildings, and these are treated as shrines. Because the Stonemasons have made him part of the Empire’s building trade, he has more of an organization behind him than most gods. Ratnamaris rules the oceans, the tides and fortune, and the merchants and sailors of Basnapura are his principal worshippers. On land he appears as a greedy merchant hung with gold and jewels. At sea he is a monster, or a thundercloud. He makes and breaks fortunes, and he is said to prefer the greedy to the generous. Guild merchants across the Empire wear charms bearing his face. I have seen them in Daub.

41.doc: Gods of the Empire and the North
41.title: Of the Light
41.content: The Light is the god everyone can see at present, and the one we understand least. We do not know where it came from. The Paladins draw their power from it, and part of the arrangement appears to work like a contract. The Paladins keep poor records, but we do know that a Paladin who ceases to behave like one loses the Light, and that some who behave like Paladins are blessed by it. Whether this happens young or old, nobody has established. Your Grace knows the recent events, so I will not repeat them. I will add one thing. A Paladin so blessed is compelled to take on quests for some idea of the good, and the Light holds him to it. A Paladin without cunning may find himself bound to an impossible quest, and sent to his death by it.

42.doc: Gods of the Empire and the North
42.title: Of What This Means for Daub
42.content: Daub holds the Church, the Temple, the Paladins and every household shrine described above within a single set of walls. On most of them I can advise. Keep the Church’s goodwill and the Temple’s confidence at once, as Singhapura has done for six centuries by favouring neither in public. When a man in Daub behaves inexplicably, ask whether he has made a baara before you ask who has paid him. On the Light I cannot advise, and I would distrust anyone who claims he can. Your Grace has raised the Paladins as a counterweight to the Church, and it is a sound choice; but nobody, not the Church, not Taprobane, not the Paladins themselves, knows what the Light wants, or why it chose them, or what it will do when a Paladin’s quest and his Duchess’s orders point in different directions. I have spent a good many pages in this treatise telling Your Grace how things work. This is the one power in Daub about which I must simply say that I do not know. Further Reading . The Thirty-Seven Stations of Raavan by the Paragon Priyadharshana is the most serious attempt to reconcile the Church’s account of Raavan’s death with the considerable evidence pointing elsewhere. As a Paragon of the University, Priyadharshana was well protected, and could safely examine every occasion on which the Church changed its mind or rewrote its own doctrine. The Old Gods: Being a Survey the Baara Tradition by Kumara Dharmawardena is the best single book on the gods that came before Singhapura’s churches and remain after them. Dharmawardena spent thirty years in the field documenting the cults. The book shows how shrine-keeping, soldiers’ brotherhoods, merchant networks and private vows quietly do the work of laws and courts in a great many places. The Light and Its Obligations by Renaud de Chastelain is a Rosantic work of theology on the Paladin compact. De Chastelain holds that the Light and the Paladins are bound by a contract obliging both sides. It is a very Rosantic way to see it, since they have long treated their gods somewhat as lawyers treat clients. The Litanies Exposed by Aldhelm Truthseeker (an obvious alias) attempts to identify and describe the Temple’s secret Litanies from the outside alone. It is full of notes on how practitioners behave, studies of the language of the surviving sutras, and accounts from those who saw Temple workings at close range. Whether he identified them correctly is disputed. Curiously, an Aldhelm is recorded as having been executed for heresy in Wattle; then again in several Rosantic cities; and again in Singhapura.

43.title: The History of Singhapura
43.content: “There are two ways to think about our history. On one hand, it’s a terribly inconvenient load of shit that I have to live up to. On the other hand, we do need to give the children enough stuff to keep them in schools, so we might as well use it.” - Devakumara II, Adhiraj of Singhapura . A ruler who wishes to deal with Singhapura must understand how it came to be what it is, since states are shaped as much by their founding circumstances as by their present intentions. What follows is that official account abbreviated from the Singha Chronicle, corrected and annotated where correction is warranted. In this I may be deemed heretical by some, but I remind Your Grace of the value of truth, and beg protection in advance for the words I must write to convey it.

44.title: The Founding
44.content: The Singha Chronicle opens with the founding of Singhapura, thus: Kaaryagamunu I received a prophetic vision of a lion standing at the mouth of the Diamond River, with the rusting arms and armor of fallen empires at its feet. Having resurrected the ancient Samarskand arts of engineering, magic, and law, he presented himself to the seven cities of the region and demonstrated his mastery through seven miracles. He was declared the first Singha Adhiraj - the Lion Emperor - and the cities merged into Singhapura. I present to Your Grace a more likely version from the Himakatu Chronicles, which records the deranged dreams of the Empress Kudakaali II. Waking from one such, she explains to her infant son his legacy, thus: . Kaaryagamunu was the chieftain, or the son of a chieftain, of seven villages - not cities - at the mouth of the Diamond River. The river delta was good agricultural land, which made for a reasonable population and great surplus. Whence came the name? The obvious choice would have been Rathnapura, the City of Jewels, after the river’s original name, but there was already a Rathnapura to the north, well-established. There was a Ridheepura, a Swarnapura, even a Madapura, which translates as City of Mud and suggests that cities of those times had largely exhausted their enthusiasm for names. Kaaryagamunu looked around for the most unlikely name available. Singhapura meant City of the Lion. Nobody had seen a lion in a thousand years, so the name was unclaimed, and the iconography could be invented from scratch. He pointed to his cat, instructed the artists to make improvements, and the Lion of Singhapura was thereby established. To embellish her account, let me explain his miracles. One scholar, Janashakthi Dhaarya, who had studied the histories carefully at the Taprobane Imperial University, observed that three of the seven miracles involved predicting the annual flooding of the Diamond River, which occurs every year without exception, and another consisted of possessing a working abacus and seven bricks. He was found drowned in the Diamond River with his feet weighted by exactly seven bricks. To dull the ache of reading histories (which I know Your Grace is unimpressed by), allow me to change to a more present style.

45.title: The Age of Expansion and the Kaaryagamunu Dynasty
45.content: Years 115 to 125 from the founding. Kaaryagamunu III raises a proper army, suppresses the Muthukumara rebellion - the Diamond Prince, a name which suggests his supporters had not entirely abandoned the poetic ambitions of the original founders - and begins expanding the borders in earnest. Tributary towns fold into Singhapura with regularity. Rathnapura, which was indeed rich in gemstones, is first to submit. Second is Balalgoda, whose name translates as a heap of cats, which requires some explanation. The early governors of Balalgoda had, some years prior, instituted a program to address a severe rat problem in the granaries. This program solved the rat problem and produced a cat problem of comparable severity. Kaaryagamunu III, surveying this situation upon his arrival, interpreted it as evidence of divine favour and formalized the arrangement into a guild - establishing thereby the origins of guilds in Singhapura, which would in time become one of the most consequential features of the empire’s political economy. This is an apt reminder, your Grace, that even the strangest and most inconsequential actions of rulers cast long shadows. Kaaryagamunu III, dying, is awarded the title Singha Adhiraj by his people. This is the first occurrence of this title in any text. A hundred thousand cats are said to have attended his tomb for weeks. The Singha Chronicle records this as miraculous. It is at least consistent with everything that preceded it. Years 130 to 150. Singhapura is now a modest but functional kingdom extending from the mouth of the Rathna to the Balalpura Plains. It has a standing army instead of reservists and has begun building proper roads.

46.title: The First Ebbing
46.content: Year 155. Religion, as an instrument of state policy, is discovered. This is to say, religions had always existed, but it was at this point that a government was first unwise enough to formalize its patronage. The records make light of how the Temple of Eighteen rose to such prominence, but a key promise seems to have been expansion. The Temple of Eighteen, thus newly, sets out northward toward the Raavanskandha Mountains with a mandate to expand the borders, conquer the wilderness, and carry its Litanies to the uttermost reaches of the world. It fails. The failure owed nothing to magic and everything to the calendar, for no one had accounted for the monsoon season. The entire vanguard was mired in mud; thousands of pilgrims and would-be soldier-saints died stranded on uncharted borders. From this we may derive some supporting evidence for the idea that the Temple of Eighteen was, at that point, relatively new to the South. The failure was sufficient to drag down the Kaaryagamunu dynasty and a considerable portion of the treasury with it. Your Grace will observe here a principle that recurs throughout this history: divine mandate is not an edible food source, and no degree of theological confidence has ever prevented rain.

47.title: The Singhavikrama Era and the Ascension of the Church
47.content: Year 165. Singhavikrama I, having inherited the wreckage, spends his early reign suppressing the disputes the First Ebbing had ignited. Singhapura becomes simultaneously a laughingstock and an unintended adversary to the small kingdoms on its borders, which begin calling it Balalpura - the Empire of Cats. Years 170 to 180. The Haugris Church, spreading southward from Raavanskandha, makes its first recorded contact with Singhapura. It is useful here to understand what each party brought to the arrangement. Singhapura brought a wounded empire still grimly claiming the mantle of Samarskand, in need of legitimacy, allies, and better magic. The Church brought a mountain - the most magically significant mountain in the known world, and three relics of Great Raavan, and some degree of familiarity with the border kingdoms; it was, however, painfully aware that religions need armies and soldiers as much as prayers and ritual. The relics required some diplomatic delicacy: if one totalled all the relics of Raavan claimed at the time, one arrived at twenty eyes, thirty-four teeth, and no fewer than six hands. This is most likely the origin of the artistic convention depicting Raavan with ten heads, early Singhapura being, above all else, practical. But the mountain was real and defensible; the foreign relations were real; and the Church had impressive magic that it was willing to share. The Temple of Eighteen was disgraced and stripped of patronage. Udanuwara and Giridhora joined Singhapura at the Church’s insistence. The empire thereby acquired a continuous line from the Rathna River to the Raavanskandha Mountains - the river to the grave, as the saying goes. If Your Grace ever wants to know how a church ends up running a country, start with this deal. Year 190. Singhavikrama II, seized by a mid-life crisis of exceptional completeness, abdicates, abandons his wife, his children, and his court, shaves his head, and retires to the wilderness to become a guru. His sermons, preserved today in the Taprobane Museum, prove uniformly banal, and he vanished from the record. Naagadattha I, his successor, is approximately twelve years old. His mother, Queen Visanthari, appoints the High Priest of the Haugris Church as a temporary Vizier. The Church’s reach and power grow rapidly. Your Grace may want to remember this one.

48.title: The Valigame Interregnum
48.content: Year 255. Naagadattha I dies - of a surfeit of honey-cakes, or of poison, or of poisoned honey-cakes, the sources declining to commit to a position. The Royal Council enters deadlock. The Church desired a priest-king. The Army desired a general. The Merchants desired a reduction in taxes. The Law of the First Foot stipulated that should no heir be determined within thirty days, and that the first living soul to enter the Throne Room at sunrise on the thirty-first day should be named Regent. The Council locked the doors, intending thereby to admit the High Priest of the Church before any other candidate. However, a grey langur, entering through an open skylight in search of breakfast, arrived first. Regent Valigame, the Tailed One, governed for five years. It was, as recorded in the Singha Chronicle, a period of remarkable civil tranquility, attributable in large part to the Regent’s constitutional inability to declare war, raise taxes, or conduct any kind of foreign policy. Its contributions to diplomacy consisted primarily of throwing fruit at visiting dignitaries. The same High Priest who had arranged the original succession eventually interpreted a screech as a formal act of abdication. The Law of the First Foot was repealed, and to this day it is considered treason to leave skylights open overnight in government buildings.

49.title: The Age of Kudakaali
49.content: Years 300 to 325. Under Kudakaali, the First Empress, the empire reaches its greatest territorial extent. By now the army is a serious one: six Arbiters each commanding a legion of four thousand, each legion subdivided into specialist Chapters of heavy infantry, cavalry, engineers, and archers, permitting the kind of coordinated expansion that transforms the empire into what later cartographers would describe as a bloated cuttlefish. Moving North and using Udanuwara and Giridhora as a base, Kudakaali extends the empire to the foot of the Himakatu mountains. The name, if Your Grace be so interested, means “Bones of Snow”. Across these mountains is the Hooniyang Pass, a treacherous entry to the lands beyond; having conquered the bandits who live there, the empire reshapes the pass to accommodate the passage of armies, and thus Kudakaali breaks through to the North. Here she establishes the site of a new city: Himakatupura. Your Grace will recognize the name, for Wattle and Daub are descendants of this ancient City. Kudakaali sends envoys to all the kingdoms and peoples of the North, including to far Ealdorfold. Himakatupura quickly becomes a highly profitable trading point and is regarded as the key to the North. Moving east, Kudakaali encounters a dragon who names herself the Northeast Monsoon, who prophesies that a great threat will swallow the empire’s borders if left unchecked. Kudakaali thanks the dragon and immediately commences building more cities: Basnapura in the west, Nagenapura in the east, and towns around their periphery. She leaves her successors an injunction: move Singhapura to the center of the empire, and let the old city be the tip of the south. With three centuries of hindsight, this looks like the worst misunderstanding in Singhapura’s history. Kudakaali took the prophecy to mean a foreign invasion. The dragon most likely meant what actually happened, which Your Grace will read about shortly.

50.title: The Yodhasena Era
50.content: Years 330 to 365. Yodhasena I executes his mother’s design. Singhapura is rebuilt precisely halfway between its old site and Himakatupura, set against the foothills of the Raavanskandha Mountains, where the Haugris Church’s fastness provides a steady supply of both magic and labor. The old city becomes Ruhunapura. Four cities - four shields - disposed around the heart-city at the centre. Kudakaali’s Great Design is complete. Northern and eastern trade begins refilling the much-depleted treasury; the Western city of Basnapura, built as a large port, takes some years to complete, but soon becomes an centre for trade from all over the world. Year 380. A volcano destroys Taprobane, a major trading partner on the other side of the Diamond River. Scholars, merchants, and hydromancers flee to Basnapura. Singhapura receives them. Year 400, approximately. The Taprobane Imperial University is established. The immediate problem Yodhasena II was attempting to solve was practical: what was to be done with a growing accumulation of highly intelligent, occasionally dangerous, perpetually expensive scholars and magicians? It is well known that Yodhasena had a love of puzzles, and spent much of his time challenging his tutors to provide him with such diversions. His solution, therefore, was also intended as a diversion: to place them all in one institution, provide good libraries and adequate plumbing, and assign them a puzzle of sufficient complexity to occupy their attention indefinitely. The puzzle he posed was whether there existed a unified theory and systematic application of magic. He then returned to his other concerns, entirely unaware that he had initiated the most important piece of scholarship in the empire’s history, and ruled for some forty years from the arrangement before results arrived. This is recorded by posterity as visionary patronage.

51.title: The Second Ebbing
51.content: Years 462 to 480. Kudakaali II, initially a promising ruler, sets about undoing as much of her predecessors’ work as she can. Perhaps she was burdened with too great a name. She resurrects the patronage of the Temple of Eighteen, to which the Haugris Church reacts with great ire. In an attempt to remove herself from their reach, she moves the royal court to Ruhunapura and tries to move the Taprobane Imperial University as well, which refuses. Frustrated, she removes herself to the new city Himakatupura, where she sets in motion events whose consequences will alter the geography of the known world. The period as a whole is called the Second Ebbing. Several legions disappear without adequate explanation. In Udanuwara, the practice of mahagewal revives - independent walled communities answering only to themselves or the Church. Various Rosantic and Lusian armed orders, coming in through the West, flourish in proportion to the breakdown of central authority - the Paladins, the White Lotus, the Crimson Typhoon; they even influence local lords, who fashion themselves into such organizations as the Lions of the South and the Redistributionists. The Withering of Himakatupura . Years 480 to 500. These events are the heart of the Himakatu Chronicle. Kudakaali II, after years of one terrible decision after another, believes herself beset by enemies and ill-wishers on all sides. She commissions a torture facility for her enemies and engages the mad architect Girika for its creation. Girika creates a design of such ambition and vile magic that it is called the Hell Garden; even the blueprints, a copy of which exists today in the Taprobane museum, are considered infohazards of the highest order. Girika also commissions Pandukha, a magician of equal derangement, to open a gateway to the daemon realm using the foul energies released, so that at the end of torture, corpses may be disposed of by tossing them into the portal. This is to be the facility’s culminating feature. A word on this, Your Grace. These incidents happened long before anyone designed the Rituals that now let us knock politely at the door of to the daemon realm. Pandukha and Girika attempted entry by force; torturing hundreds - some say thousands - of innocents to channel the energies of death itself into weakening the barrier between worlds. This is the first properly documented contact between Singhapura and the daemon world. Your Grace will no doubt readily imagine what responses one is moved to when blood-soaked strangers attempt to dump corpses in your palace. Thousands of daemons poured through the tear between worlds. Using magic that none of our systems has managed to describe since, they split the city, stretched the fabric of the world, and produced a desert in which the portal itself - now an abyss sufficient to swallow a city entire - continues to rotate, irradiating everything within hundreds of miles and warping reality across a radius that our best instruments have still not fully measured. This is the Great Northern Waste, Your Grace. This is how it was born. The Singha Chronicle counts these events as the Empire’s great shame. Kudakaali II died in the first days of its creation, torn limb from limb. It is said that Girika, for his sins, was nailed to a tree at the center of the Waste, forced to endure and suffer for all eternity. Not everyone disgraced themselves. Manavarma and Gajabahu, the two generals whose statues stand at the gates of Udanuwara today, conducted a fighting retreat that preserved the empire, holding back the daemonic forces with nearly a hundred thousand soldiers. It is said, too, that every adherent of the Temple of Eighteen who had flocked to Kudakaali’s patronage gave their lives to channel their Litanies, and thus daemonic magic was met with the diefic, and a great battle was fought for thirty-nine days, at the end of which the daemons, having slain nearly all who stood, retreated. Naagadattha III, who inherited this situation, devoted his reign to recovery expeditions, the suppression of rebellions born of the resulting chaos, and to the composition of theatrical works cursing, in roughly equal proportion, Himakatupura, the daemon realm, the Waste itself, and the clerk Sangabo, who had the misfortune of delivering the weekly situation reports. Sangabo’s offense, so far as can be established, was merely competence: he was the man who was tasked with keeping the Emperor from letting his frustrations turn to excess. Reminding an Emperor now and then that burning one’s own towns is bad form is not, in and of itself, a crime. Naagadattha III died attempting to firebomb the ruins of Himakatupura, leaving behind an exhausted state and a body of dramatic work that historians of literature rather admire. His most celebrated play, The Mule Who Wore a Turban, is still performed, and the actor playing Sangabo is, by custom, struck with a rotten papaya upon his first entrance. I have played Sangabo twice in amateur productions, and, having been pelted thus, am wholly in sympathy with Sangabo and his duties. Himakatupura is deconsecrated and abandoned. The empire contracts. All daemonic-inquiry magic is permanently prohibited. The Great Northern Waste is left. The Temple, once again, is reduced; and once again the Haugris Church fills the gaps, attempting to hold together the crumbling remains. It is in this period that the Church begins to develop its own armed forces.

52.title: The Mirrored States Period
52.content: Years 525 to 570. With every royal dynasty exhausted and all political capital spent, the empire divides. The twins Halapahara and Balapahara establish the Sunset and Sunrise Singhapura Empires - Balapahara in the east with the patronage of the Temple of Eighteen, Halapahara in the west with the backing of Lusia, which enters Singhapura’s history in its characteristic fashion, bearing money, mercenaries, and promissory notes in exchange for future revenues. The war that follows is distinguished less by its military engagements than by its administrative comedies. Halapahara decrees the Standard Foot to be henceforth based upon his own foot, which was famously small, thereby giving merchants more land to sell overnight and producing uncontrollable inflation. Balapahara, not to be surpassed, removes Tuesdays from the calendar, on the grounds that he was born on a Tuesday and desired it consecrated as a holy day. Halapahara responds by declaring every day to be Tuesday. For six months, residents of the border territories were unable to determine what day it was, and the postal service collapses entirely. The fort-town of Galkumbura dates from this period. The name means “fields of stones”, in the paddy-field sense, and it is the most honest description of a settlement’s farming prospects in any Singhapura record. Naturally, foreign influence and mercenary orders grow, and the Church’s own Sequence of Acts take increasingly harder stances against such matters, retaliating in word and deed while supplying what food, healing and administration it can. Read the Mirrored States next to the Withering of Himakatupura, Your Grace, and you will have two quite different ways for a state to wreck itself. The ruins of Himakatupura, by now completely unprotected, are settled by Normons and begin, by slow degrees, to become the cities of Wattle and Daub. So Daub was built on the leftovers of one disaster, and nobody stopped it because everyone was busy with another.

53.title: The Restoration
53.content: Years 600 to 720. The war ends through exhaustion and the reorientation of commercial interest. In the east, Temple of Eighteen adherents broker a de-escalation among parties too tired to continue fighting. In the west, Lusian capital, having by this point acquired a controlling interest in the Sunset Empire, concludes that peace serves the investment better than prolongation and acts accordingly. The Taprobane Imperial University, which has spent the intervening period defending Singhapura and aiding the Church in its administration, begins and completes the training of a new class of civil servants picked from among such nobles as still remain loyal, and, having tested them rigorously, deems one fit to be the Emperor anew. Singhapura is restored through the combined efforts of the Church, Lusian gold, and the collective exhaustion of every party to the conflict. Your Grace, I advise you to pay careful heed to the consequences of this failure of state. The power of the Church grew, so much so that the Sequence of Letters became the only reliable method of messaging and the Sequence of Acts became the most reliable hand of order across the empire. The power of the University grew, such that the training of those who perform functions of the state - law, courts, order, engineering - was rendered unto their hands for ever more. In this time also came the rise of the Guilds; having taken their lessons from the Lusians, the Guilds rose to protect and control their trades, and the flow of private capital became indispensable to the maintenance of the cities and their provinces. Thus a new nobility was born, one more powerful than the old. The Singhapura Merchants Guild, made in imitation of Lusian Banks, begins to monopolize not only trade, but begins to mint its own currency, the Owl. The Paladins, too, rose in this occasion, becoming a force answerable only to their own codes and oaths. When things fall apart, people run to whatever still works, and once they have made it strong they do not leave. Whatever a state hands over in a crisis, it rarely gets back. That is why the laws of Singhapura cannot be changed today without the consent of every one of these parties, and why the Adhiraj sometimes has to lean on a very small number of people who are loyal to him alone.

54.title: The Dawn of Magic
54.content: Years 641 to 700. At the Taprobane Imperial University, the Paragon Vidyaadhara invites the northern Archmage Hakon Icehand, an exile from Ealdorfold, and the Lusian Grandmaster Alessia the Cartographer, to collaborate upon Yodhasena’s question, which still drives the intellect of the University. Over the succeeding thirty years, joined eventually by Grandmasters Rossum, Tharupaalaka, and Naagakanthi, they produce the Taprobane System - a formalized grammar of magic, the closest approximation to a Samarskand resurgence the world had seen to date. This is what remade the Empire. Until then magic had belonged to madmen and saints. Now it could be written down and taught to anyone patient enough, and new uses turned up every year. Singhapura rebuilds first itself, then the cities. Armies, newly trained, cover greater distances. Crop yields increase through standardized agricultural magic, at the cost of a greater dependency on University oversight. The period also gives us Grandmaster Ushnisha, who, made incautious by the new possibilities, convinces the Imperial University that the solution to urban overcrowding in Ruhunapura is verticality, and proceeds to levitate an entire district into the sky. Unfortunately, even the wise cannot see all ends; Ushnisha has not accounted for plumbing and sewers, which, as Your Grace knows, is essential to the functioning of any settlement. Thus for days, the streets below received what the historical record has preserved as the Brown Rain of 660. As punishment, Ushnisha was demoted to Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of Sanitation. Nobody much minded the floating district, Your Grace. What people remember is what fell on them.

55.title: The Age of Makaraasoka, Also Called the Dragon Years
55.content: Year 730. The Empire again produces a ruler in the likeness of the great lords of old: Makaraasoka, often called the Dragon. He is said to have been a man of unusual height and temper, with yellow eyes that struck fear into all save the palace cats. As his first act he sends to each city the Rock of Responsibility, a monumental inscription detailing the duties of the imperial office and the principles of the social contract. As his second he begins rebuilding the state. Certain functions are forcibly wrested back from the guilds or duplicated under state patronage. Levies are raised; a portion of the accumulated fortunes of noble houses are melted into public infrastructure - courts, libraries, roads, schools - and consecrated in the names of those houses. The people get better towns out of it. The new nobility, whose private fortunes had grown to an inconvenient size during the years of chaos, get poorer, and are paid for it in public respect. Thus, roads are built and re-built. Tanks are constructed. Blighted croplands are restored. The ports of Basnapura are repaired at great expense and begin welcoming trade once more. Makaraasoka incorporates the Paladins into his armies; he raises and reorganizes new forces, and leads expeditions to quell local warlords. These victories stir the people. At his last, he turns his gaze to the North. The Hooniyang Pass is reopened; Makaraasoka defeats the Pendragon armies to seize Wattle. He bonds the arrangement with economic pressure using the Singhapura Merchants Guild, thus repaying them for the indignities suffered at his hands; he builds Churches, thus extending the reach of the Haugris Church while forcing it to do the work of auditing and modernizing the administration of these new provinces; he forces strategic marriages between the nobilities of Udanuwara and Wattle, to create blood ties as a brake against rebellion. In some accounts this age is termed the Time of Heroes, though the Time of Sponsored Heroes would be more accurate. Great knights screamed the names of commercial patrons while slaying beasts. The Lions of the South were technically the property of a consortium of garment manufacturers. Galahitiya the Crisp - one of the few unaffiliated knights in the empire’s history - served as champion of the Royal Biscuit and Confectionery Company and was bound by contract to shout either Sweet, Sweet Death! or Here’s a Savory Ending! at the moment of every killing blow. These are still the subject of many a comedy play for children in Singhapura.

56.title: The Grasshopper Dynasty
56.content: Years 770 to 800. The long investment in infrastructure pays its returns. The empire enters a period of peace and commercial prosperity under Kaaryasundara, the Grasshopper Adhiraj - so called for his slight build and contemplative disposition, both of which were mocked endlessly in his own time. Nevertheless, none of his critics can claim to have presided over an era of such stability and expansion. He reduces the military, opens trade missions, builds a merchant navy; and with the proceeds, initiates the Great Roads project, improving flows between the center of the empire and its periphery. He also establishes the Lesser Theoretical University of Daub, which Your Grace will find of more immediate relevance than the remainder of this paragraph. Wattle undergoes a violent revolution - the so-called Violet Wars; Kaaryasundara dispatches troops to protect Singhapura interests, but with strict instructions not to intervene in the politics. The bureaucracy, which by now has become bloated - many were recruited in Makaraasoka’s time - finds other applications for its capacities. The Ministry of Astrology, Prophecy and Prediction, having forecast a lunar eclipse for the Emperor’s fiftieth birthday garden party, finds that the moon had not been apprised of the occasion; it brings legal action against the moon for loitering with intent to shine, and wins the case by default, the moon declining to appear during court hours. This case is cited, with varying degrees of seriousness, in certain legal traditions. A decade-long dispute within the Taprobane Faculty of Evocation over the correct temperature of tea in the staff room erupts into a brief battle of magicians. Kaaryasundara spends the latter years of his life slowly reforming the bureaucracy and reducing its capacity for foibles, and dies peacefully in his sleep.

57.title: The Second Appearance
57.content: Years 811 to 860. The Adhiraj Kusumadevi, returning to her library, finds, waiting for her, a many-legged, many-eyed, many-tentacled entity that introduces itself as Nihilus, the Gray and Indifferent King. It is, by every account that survives, extraordinarily courteous. It commends Taprobane on the System of Magic, noting that it is an encouraging start and has the potential to become something interesting. It offers Kusumadevi its congratulations on Singhapura’s studious avoidance of the daemon realm - in its own words, since that little misunderstanding up North. It then inquires whether Kusumadevi might be willing to attend to certain conditions developing at the empire’s borders before, as it expresses it, things really heat up. For more than a century, every act of magic performed in the empire’s service has accumulated a cost. The Temple of Eighteen’s foundational sutras had addressed this directly, as Your Grace will recall from the section on magical systems. The magicians of Taprobane had discovered, over years of long study, the costs and effects of magic, and yet they had neglected the study of greater repercussions. For works performed systematically, across an empire, over the course of a century and more, the debt had travelled outward along the roads and settled at the borders, and there it began to show itself. In Katuwagoda, expeditions found patches of forest where the trees had teeth; where things resembling persons stood at roadsides, delivering threatening philosophical commentary upon the necessity of returning to nature. Near Meethota, ornithologists and explorers shared tales of dragon sightings. From the mud flats beyond Ruhunapura would come eyeless creatures possessed of strange claws and mouths. In Vel-Eliya, near Basnapura, Great Serpents were seen in the sea; fishermen’s nets, on occasion, would contain things that bore only the shape of fish, but had neither eyes nor innards. In Nagenapura, phantoms began to haunt from old battle-sites. Praying to Raavan will not aid you, Nihilus is reported to have said; it may be the office of the divine to inspire, but it is the office of the daemonic to contain. If you fail in this duty, it falls to us. It observed, again, with great courtesy, that the business up north should have furnished a sufficiently clear illustration of what daemonic intervention would look like, and that it would prefer not to repeat the experience. The Sin-Eater Legion was deployed that same year. Since then the Empire has demanded of its periphery such materials as it needs to furnish its legions: steel, leather, and any magical artefacts that may be of use.

58.title: The Prince of Deep Waters
58.content: This brings us to the present day, your Grace, and to the Adhiraj Anthardhana. His origins are curiously shrouded; some say that as a child he was trained in the Taprobane University, and rose to the rank of Master; some say that in his youth he was sent abroad, to study the workings of Rosantic politics and the counting-houses of Lusia; that as a young man he fought in the Sin-Eater Legion, and distinguished himself in battle under a false name. In court he was called Prince of Deep Waters, because while he was said to have great Authority, it was also said to be impossible to know what thoughts ebbed and flowed behind his countenance. Upon ascension he took a curious name, breaking with tradition: Anthardhana, The One Who Vanishes, reorganizes the military orders, and institutes the office of the Emperor’s Bitterness - that is Mohandas Siege, your Grace. The Adhiraj has ruled for decades, Your Grace. He keeps his own counsel, and as far as I know the only people he listens to are the few he uses as his instruments. If anyone tells you they know what he is thinking, they are lying.

59.title: Of Magic, and Its Uses in Governance
59.content: This is about magic and how to make use of it. I heard Your Grace’s critique on my last attempt - specifically I don’t care about the bloody theory, just tell me what use it is! . Firstly. There are two errors that the rich and the powerful (ie: yourself) make when dealing with magic. The first error is ignoring it entirely and leaving it entirely up to the specialists. This tends to end badly when the specialists realize they can kill thousands with a thought (given enough setup) and don’t really have to do what you want. Like what happened with Catherine’s Gate. And the dungeons at Harrow’s End in Wattle. Or even recent incidents, which we shall not speak of . The second error is treating magic like an infinite factory of wishes. When people commit to magical solutions without understanding what those solutions cost - well, the Waste is a great reminder of what can go wrong. This means yes, Your Grace, you will have to do some reading. And dare I say that the most useful ideas for for how to deploy magic often comes from outside universities and the like. For example, if I invent a Ritual that gives me infinite lumber, that would be very nice - a curiosity, something to research, maybe an excellent reputation bump with the faculty. But to a carpenter? That’s an infinite resource. To a king? Cheap housing, walls, shields, weapon shafts. To your Treasurer? A giant headache, because the price of wood is now effectively zero. Your Grace rules Daub. Daub sits at the intersection of several magical traditions. Admittedly, none of them are as developed as in Wattle, let alone Singhapura, but this just means that the problems are simply in the future. Avoiding magic is not a position that is available to you. So, on my second attempt at this quest, here is what I have for you: . One, the general theory of the workings of magic and types of practitioners involved, keeping largely to results and staying away from most of the technical. Where possible I have tried to give examples of who uses these different types and how. Two, a sampling from the Singhapura system of magics, which is also what the Lesser Thereotical University of Daub uses. There are thousands of potential Patterns and hundreds of Rituals, many of which are minor variations upon each other. Rather than fill a library, I have hand-picked a version of what we call the common corpus - well-known workings that most competent Masters are familiar with. I have arranged them in as practical an order as I can think of. This also lets me give Your Grace a warning. Not all magic can be done solo. Some require groups. Some require gifted Masters who can be quite expensive, and not the sort you keep on retainer. Ssome are possible in theory, but are functionally suicide. Some need resources. Workings of large magnitudes often need materials. These include enormous compilers and spell-plates, which means metal, metalworking, many days to inscribe, much effort to transport . sometimes it is much cheaper to hire men to watch your fields than to comission a magical scarecrow; sometimes it is easier send an ordinary army instead of a cabal of Masters. This is why I implore Your Grace, once again, to read, especially the magics I have listed. Examined together they should give Your Grace a basic understanding of what magic can accomplish, and what it cannot. There are some technicalities still. Most of these Rituals come from Taprobane or with the Lesser Theoretical University of Daub. The compiler differs between the two institutions: Taprobane Rituals require the Universal Ritual Interpreter, while LTU Rituals assume a Rossum’s Universal Translator. Your Grace does not need to know how these things work, but you do need to understand how to spot people who do. Most practitioners available to Your Grace should have discs or plates of tempered steel or bronze with both compilers etched on them, and should be able to draw the weaker but more portable Turing’s Array from memory. This is the most basic test of competence I can think of. Anyone who cannot can be safely diregarded as an amateur. If Your Grace wants to hire someone, at least let them prove they know what they’re doing. Confidence is more common than skill. For serious study I recommend the abridged Ustaad, Volumes One to Sixteen from Taprobane University Press, originally written by Paragon Bolgoda and translated by myself. If Your Grace wants just the principles and simpler workings, my own Art of Magic will serve, though I have to say that the target audience for that book was children under twelve.

61.title: Of the Various Provinces That Concern Us
61.content: The chapters that follow concern every place with a bearing upon Your Grace’s position, whether directly, as neighbours and trading partners, or indirectly, as powers whose arrangements decide Daub’s fortunes from a distance. A demarcation first. To the Singhapura mind, the North means Wattle, Daub, the Great Northern Waste, and even Ealdorfold beyond: the frontier, the periphery, the place that is always in the process of being managed. To a northern mind, the South means Singhapura entire: the empire, its dominions, its long shadow. Your Grace is in the unenviable position of inhabiting both at once, answering to Wattle while presiding over a city that the Empire treats as a piece upon a board it controls. It is my hope that by describing these lands and their affairs a little more closely, this work may be of some use in the matter. I had intended to include a great deal more on geography and historical development. Upon review I have discarded most of it. The arrangement of streams and hills is pertinent, but it does not much describe the present, nor can it be relied upon to augur the future. I have instead endeavoured to furnish Your Grace with an account of political realities: how each place is governed, where its pressures lie, and what its present course means for Daub. Singhapura is the largest fact in Your Grace’s world, and I have treated it accordingly. It is the condition against which everything else is measured. Yet I have not treated the western powers as remote. Lusian money is already inside Daub’s commercial life, as it is inside every significant economy in the known world. Rosantic free companies walk Daub’s streets. Both powers offer Your Grace something the Empire cannot easily replace: alternatives, and roundabout ways of getting things done. I have endeavoured to set down the strengths and weaknesses of both. Ealdorfold is further off and less immediately pressing, but I have included it because it is culturally foundational to the North. Culture is an odd force. It will flee before an army and then, given enough years, bring down the king who sent it; and I would ask Your Grace not to pass over that chapter. Tangowan I have included as a warning rather than a partner, and Your Grace should read it with Daub in mind throughout. The Dvorak Elves maintain the most comprehensive geographical and political record available. I have recommended obtaining a copy of the Annales Historici, and I do so again here. For those who prefer a living source to a written one, the Lesser Theoretical University and the Daub Merchants Guild can, between them, produce an expert on almost any subject covered in what follows. Ask both, if possible, and compare notes, since men of great wisdom in one subject are often great fools in others.

63.title: Other Records of Note
63.content: Of everything in this treatise, this is the part I have most enjoyed writing, because it concerns books. There are two histories Your Grace must have in hand before the rest of this treatise will be of much use. The first is Samarskand and the ancient world, which is where the present Empire comes from, and also where it draws most of its romantic ideas about itself. The second is the history of Singhapura, its growth and its blunders. I have written up both here, drawn from the Seven Great Classics, with such commentary as seems useful. I urge Your Grace to find time for the Classics themselves. I do not recommend them for their prose. Among Singhapura’s nobility, familiarity with the Classics is taken as a mark of breeding, and unfamiliarity as a mark of the opposite. Students and noble families hold contests of quotation and call-and-reply, and the same passages are cited in the law courts and in serious political argument. The people who hold power in Singhapura speak to one another in these books. A ruler who cannot follow the conversation is at the mercy of those who can. I have added the Modern Classics for two reasons. They tell the truth of their worlds more plainly than the official record does, and several of their authors were suppressed or exiled for it. They are also a great deal more enjoyable than the older works, and a reader drawn on by interest remembers more than one who reads from duty. If Your Grace begins with these and finds her way from them to the Seven Great Classics, they will have done their work. Last, there is a short section on books banned in Singhapura. People everywhere tend to celebrate the same things, but what a people fears is its own, and far more revealing. I would advise Your Grace to see whether copies can be had.

64.title: The World and the Ducchess Within It

65.title: Being an Account of the Powers, Places, and Politics of Singhapura and Its Domains
65.content: To Her Grace, the Duchess of Daub: . I thought about how to write this text for a long time. Your Grace has a copy my previous work, The Basics of Magic and Practical Applications for Governance. I know you had complaints. I specifically recall Your Grace asking Metric to read the book for you, and then you said summarize into ten pages or less or I’ll have you cleaning the toilets for a month. This book is its successor in spirit. Your Grace asked me to tell you about the places and powers that concern your operations; thus this work is broader, and I’ve tried to cover everything from the provinces to the politics in broad detail. But I want Your Grace to actually read my words, not just get some lackey to regurgitate them for you. So I thought about writing instead. If I was still in Singhapura I would have to open with the fanciest words I know and delight you with layers and layers of hidden poetry and tricks and messages under the surface. You know, like Kavyasekara writing to plunder, butcher, steal, these things they misname empire; and where they make a desert, they call it peace; the text is supposedly about the barbarians at the gates, but it’s actually an indictment of Singhapura’s own history and makes the barbarians sound like reasonable people. Then I read this Lusian fellow who wrote much simpler: .ideas dressed in fine sentences are often ideas that cannot stand in plain clothes. It it is my desire that this work should either pass wholly unhonoured, or that the truth of its matter and the importance of its subject should alone recommend it. I tried writing in that style, but then I read this strange book of meditation exercises from the Obsidian Empire that just opened with Let go, or be dragged. So let me write as me. This book is what I know about our world. I won’t say that it’s perfect. The work is small, and the subject is vast. In searching for usefulness, I’ve whittled away a great number of details - because the many millions of small details always change, even when the larger movements of the world go relatively undisturbed. You already have a great many advisors, courtiers, spymasters, soldiers and so on. These people have their own sources of information and their own ways of understanding the world, which are useful. Among them there are always going to be those who believe I have no businesses addressing you on the governance of a mud hut, much less Daub and the world. I’m going to paraphrase from that Lusian fellow for my defense: to understand the mountains, one must first stand in the valley and look up at them, and that to understand the valley, one must have climbed high enough to see its full extent. You who stand at a considerable height sees certain things. I have spent my life on both sides - looking down from above and looking up from the smallest possible vantage. And so I see other things with a clarity you may not. My hope is that what I have seen from below will prove of some use to one who commands from above. Read this work carefully, Maud. In it is the full measure of my hopes for your success. You have talent and fortune on your side. You are not the kind of person who lets go; you are the kind of person who drags. And most of all, many of us are now stuck with you, for better or worse. I’ve have enough of the worse, and I hope this helps make things better. Your devoted servant, . 72.title: On Those Who Work Magic, and What Each Sort Costs a Ruler
72.content: All magic, Your Grace, is based on the concept of Authority. There is an old word from Samarskand, and it captures the meaning better: Ustaadi, or your ability to affect the world. This means both willpower and hard-earned skill and knowledge but also every strength available: one’s magic, one’s material power, legal or instutitional abilities, every way of making the world do as you will. We now use the word Authority, but I remind you of the old meaning for a reason. A Master of the Lesser Theoretical University may have magic that can grow crops, from their Authority; but a farmer who has cultivated the land for forty years may have just as much, or even more. Your Grace has Authority, as well. It stems from your power that is legal; it stems from the loyalty your people have to you; from your competence; from respect; even from enmity. Keep this in mind. Magic is a way of harnessing Authority and stamping it more forcefully on specific things or deeds. This is the simplest reduction I can think of. Now, scholars have long attempted to impose order on the variety of magical practice. The simplest division I can offer Your Grace is one of method: those who work by intuition, and those who work by system. But this method is no longer regarded as useful, so I will try to summarize here how Singhapura classifies and sorts its practitioners.

73.title: Of the Seven Dependent Originations of Being
73.content: I. Primals . Primals are the purest expression of inherent personal power. They impose themselves upon the world, and the world yields, depending on the strength and will of the one imposing. Many great heroes of history fall into this category; so do a number of tyrants, kings, legends .it is not known whether all Emperors of Singhapura have been Primals, but the present Adhiraj almost certainly is. Ultimately, Primals, Your Grace, are grown, not made. You can teach a man to do the right thing, but there is no discipline or instruction book that can make one a hero. A way of spotting early Primals in your ranks is to look for those who have a skill and vigor and presence that exceeds what a rational man might expect. It is often said that those hermits who take to the wild and to the high fastnesses of the world become Primals through their own exertions. A Primal in Your Grace’s service is therefore a considerable asset, but a Primal in opposition is a problem. It is difficult to discover their strengths and difficult to decipher their true weaknesses. Johan the Grim, who is said to have founded Daub, was said to be impossible to slay within its borders, resurrecting to such an extent that he nearly became a religious figure; his assasination at the hands of Singhapura proved that his actual power was to create doubles of himself who could share their thoughts between them, and having one safely squirrelled away at all times. Likewise, the Bandit Prince of the Gontreach, for example, is a force that Wattle’s armies have been completely unable to capture; it may be because he is as fleet of foot as the stories say . or he may be capable of disguising himself, or a hundred other things to the same effect. Their weakness is sophistication. Your Grace will find Primals useful for the application of certain types of personal force, but not a great range of deeds. II. Binders . In this category we place those who use their power to understand and manipulate hidden Sympathy, or connections between things and people, thus binding them. The most common is the local witch or Vedic, however they term themselves - people who use the kingdom of plants, consumables, and the powers of place and local sympathies. The more famous are the Galdorcraeft traditions and the Hasselbad bards of the North, who use knotwork and stones and song. The alchemists of Lusia, working with rare metals and esoteric substances, can be said to be Binders of a sort. Binder magic is extraordinarily difficult to systematize and nearly impossible to predict with precision. It depends a great deal on the magician, on their understandings and intuitions, and on circumstances. For example, we know from the bards that a person who does not believe himself to be a musician will never be one, however great his underlying power. The entire enterprise relies on a certain relationship between the magician and his own self-conception, or self-delusion, elevated to an art. I will say from my observations that the Vedics are probably the lowest order, closer to folk wisdom than true magic, perhaps. Wards, simple healing, growth of crops, perhaps some rain or sunshine - these are village magics, often passed down through apprentices or invented off the cuff, and almost never compatible between practioners. Nevertheless, they are everywhere, and perhaps there is some use to them, but I will leave that to Your Grace to decide. The Bards are profoundly irritating but there is many a story from Ealdorfold where a Bard, being struck by inspiration, sang of a great victory, and turned doomed men into powerful heroes. Galdors are forbidden to set foot outside Ealdorfold, and thus rare. The Singhapura consensus is that they are the most powerful of this class, but heavily limited by connections to hearth and home and their runestones. The few travelling Galdors we have acquired are strong in their native lands but profoundly weak outside their domains. Your Grace should probably beware of any runestones appearing in Wattle or Daub. III. Invokers . Those who draw their power from an external source we call Invokers. This is the path of faith, in its broadest sense: the practitioner shapes himself to the requirements of a higher power and becomes, for a while, a vessel for something greater than his own Authority. What the Invoker gains in power he surrenders in autonomy. He is constrained, always, by the nature and requirements of what he channels. The major Invoker traditions Your Grace will encounter in Daub and in the Empire are: . Firstly, the Haugris Church. The Church claims to draw from the Divine Corpus of the Great Raavan, philosopher-king-god of the ancient Samarskand. Their approach is semi-systematic, codified in the Paramanu Thesis, which gives them more predictability than most Invoker traditions. Church practitioners are bound by whatever tenets of the Church they specialize in. A healer can heal, an Arbiter can fight, but rarely do these abilities coincide. Secondly, the Temple of Eighteen, which focuses on practitioners meditating and doing certain deeds with the goal of Inheriting the Virtues of their Litanies - the practitioner becomes, temporarily, an avatar of a specific divine principle. Or, as the Church says, they workship Yakshas and become their avatars. Official Singhapura policy is currently not to antagonize the Temple needlessly, even though the Church is aggressive in its expansions. Your Grace already knows of the issues between the Temple and the Church, especially those that spiral into the realms of governance. Though I grew up in Singhapura, I would suggest that the wise approach is to favor neither, but to make both work to maintain their footholds. The Church, for example, comes with healing and access to reliable messenger services - at the cost of Singhapura and the Church hierarchy knowing everything that passes through them. The Temple may be quieter, but as a wise man once said, it is a reed that bends in the wind. Its organization has survived many purges and wars, and has learned a great deal about doing much with very little. that Much of modern-day magic derives from precepts and sutras first expounded by the Temple. The Paladins operate on a simpler principle: live by the code, and the Light provides. Elsewhere, Lusian sorcerers work through contracted entities rather than deities; the power is external, but the relationship is negotiated rather than devotional. Many Lusian Archmages are said to have at least one contracted Yaksha (or, as they say, a Summon) that would, in the very least, match the Paragons of Singhapura. This is a powerful deterrant; nobody will risk war when the end result, regardless of victory, is total devastation for both sides involved. We suspect that Rosantic spellcasters, with their Grimoires (and sometimes decks of cards, as I’m told is now fashion), may also themselves be Invokers, drawing from the power of their Ascended, though there are arguments for placing them in other traditions. Most of our evidence comes from early studies of mercernary Orders, and that information may no longer be as accurate as we would like. The danger of an Invoker is not the Invoker himself but whatever stands behind him. When Your Grace considers the loyalty of an Invoker in her service, she must ask not only whether the man is loyal, but whether the power he channels has interests aligned with your own. The Temple Invoker serves Your Grace until his Litany requires otherwise. The Haugris Invoker carries the Church’s interests into every room he enters. They may be of great power, but Your Grace is well advised to regard them as vessels of foreign agents rather than those strictly under your command. There is a further observation worth making. It is rare for an Invoker to be a person of low personal Authority, because some degree of inherent power is always required to establish and maintain the connection to an external source. However, it is not unknown for foolish Invokers to be corrupted, puppeted or outright destroyed by the powers they seek. They therefore represent a double threat. The Haugris Church, out of its own self-interest, can be relied on to keep a careful eye on potential Invokers. The Litanies of the Temple and Raavan and the Light are not the only things out there. IV. Ritualists . We come now to the Taprobane System, and to the Lesser Theoretical University, which we name as working in the Ritualist tradition. Ritualists work through language and logical structure. The Pattern is the simplest unit. If Your Grace thinks of an essay, then Patterns are the words, and the Ritual is the complete thing: a composition of Patterns complex enough to sustain itself. Many Patterns are standardized; many Rituals are standardized; the result is the ability to break down problems into smaller ones, architect solutions, assemble them, and share them across the Empire. This is a type of power that no intuitive tradition can match. One may hand a trained practitioner a Ritual and he can execute it without understanding how it was built, in the way that a soldier may pick up and use a sword without having to forge it from scratch. I am not exagerrating when I say that Ritualism is to magic what the written word is to literature. Much as an architect hands her plans to a foreman, who can go on to build a hundred houses from one plan, a single new Ritual can spread the length of the Empire and allow thousands to do new works. This is Singhapura’s greatest strength: this is how the empire builds its formidable roads and towers and armies and keeps its people fed. The costs are the costs of all systems: the more complex they are, the more there is expense, specialization of knowledge, gatekeeping and the competition of peers . and dare I say a certain brittleness? . There are minor differences between the workings of Taprobane and Daub’s LTU. In Ritualist magic there must be a device for converting language to effect. We call this the compiler. Taprobane employs a device known as the Universal Ritual Interpreter. The LTU uses a device known as Rossum’s Universal Translator, which designed deliberately to omit support for certain complex Patterns, so as to be cheaper to manufacture. Both universities have together made significant strides in the theory and application of magic; the relationship between the two institutions is one of near-equivalence and some degree of competition and mutual territorialism. Your Grace benefits from this situation in the same way that you benefit from the tension between the Church and the Temple: two rivals who exhaust their ambitions on each other have less room to maneouver around you. At the far extension of the Ritualist tradition stands the Iron Pagoda, founded by the Paragon Sangamitta, formerly of Singhapura. The Iron Pagoda treats all existence as mathematical ideals and deviations from them; to the best of my knowledge, their work is about describing the relationships between concepts in a formalism that other systems cannot approach. It plays in a space of high energy and extreme specialization; it is not the kind of magic useful to most people, but it is the kind of magic that could end the world if something were to go wrong inside it. Your Grace is unlikely to require the Iron Pagoda’s services. But you should, however, know that it exists, in the same the way that a prudent shipmaster knows where the powder magazine is located. V. Consumers . Consumers are an oddity that no existing system has satisfactorily explained. The original name for them was Peretha Aathma, or souls of greed, but . we have since adopted less hostile language. Consumers are able to eat, or drink, or otherwise take into their bodies certain things that give them abilities related to those substances. A famous case is the Glass Witch, who reportedly ate glass and impale people with glass spears and even bend light; unfortunately for her, she was also extremely fragile, and it turned out nothing could protect her from being flattened by a boulder swung by an irate Taprobane Master. Or the Ash Beast that roams the Waste, who is said to be a man driven mad, consuming the fire of the sun to constantly burn and immolate everthing around him; he is said to be peaceful, and even helpful sometimes, but only at night, and only if he cannot be seen. Not everyone can consume anything. We have heard of Druids in Ealdorfold who can eat fruits and bark and leaves to become poisonous, or regrow limbs, and so on. There is one general in Singhapura who is said to eat iron before battle to turn his body to the hardest steel. But underneath this there seems to be some idea of Sympathy; certain people are drawn to certain things, but as to why, and how, we do not yet know to hazard a quess. The counsel I can offer is limited. In the instance of a Consumer in Daub, the best I can suggest is to reason with them, or to hold them off until you can reach out to Singhapura. VI. The Daemonic . The earliest classifications did not differentiate between the daemonic and Primals. We knew that the beings we call daemons, who occasionally interfere with our world, were kin to the Yakshas, who they call the world-walkers; we knew the Yakshas, in turn, obeyed the Great Old Ones of the daemons. It may even be (although it is often heretical to say) that Yakshas, gods, dieties, spirits, mythical beasts . it may be that all of these things are different names for the same type of being. As our understanding has developed, it has become clear that the daemon world has its own formal architecture of magic; it boasts its own universities and traditions, and much of it appears to be an attempt to reverse-engineer what they call the Word of God. For what purpose, we do not yet understand, but there is some indication that our Ritualist tradition and theirs are similar in intent, if not in ability. Much of what Taprobane systematized was influenced, at a remove of several generations of theorists, by daemonic universities. As for practicalities, daemons concern Daub in one of three ways. Firstly, some can and do cross over to our world. They tend to be extremely intelligent (as Your Grace no doubt knows) and seek host bodies; a rare few tend to be extraordinarily capable and powerful enough to create their own. I would strongly caution Your Grace to attempt reason rather permit the, shall we say, more zealous approaches of the Church. Secondly, the Yakshas - the so-called world-crawlers - are potent, if secondary figures in Haugris mythology, and are occasionally very real, especially in areas of great magical disturbance, like the Waste. There is a force of Yakshas specifically known as the NAAGA division that considers it their duty to punish particularly outrageous and powerful magic, especially those that might lead to mass annihilation (such as with Himakatupura) or damage the causality of the world in some way. The Church considers these to be enforcers of the Will of Raavan. The most appropriate approach to a Yaksha is to retreat and pray in silence. We do not know by which means they operate. At best they might be curious. At world they approached like some sort of natural disaster. The third are the Hollows. These are the gaps in reality that manifest in the Waste. I believe you call them Portal Worlds here. They are the main sources of the Relics on which Daub and Wattle depend. Our best knowledge is that these are deliberately made in some way by daemons, possibly to help their younger and weaker kind grow in what they consider to be safe, contained spaces. A significant portion of Daub’s commercial and military advantage rests on the equivalent of training facilities built by beings that look on us like adults do at a particularly precocious and annoying toddler. VII. The Diefic . The Empire worships the inheritance of a death and a legend: Great Raavan, who learned and codified all magic, and passed it down to all humans as his legacy. There is power there, but whether it stems from an active will is beyond me to say. The Litanies of the Temple of Eighteen exist. From time to time, a Litany has been known to appear, often in the face of great injustice or suffering. The Light of the Paladins is the one most faiths regard with jealousy, for its powers seemed to be freely given; however, it appears to be much weaker. Great Yama, said to be on of Raavan’s enforcers, and a daemon in the NAAGA division, is worshipped in Nagenapura in the East as a protector. Many households in the provinces will have a small shrine with a clay lamp; an offering to Ginisundara Devi, a minor goddess of hearth and home. Mahasona, said to be an ancient general under Raavan, is a dread figure whose name translates to mass grave; graveyard-keepers and soldiers smear ash on their hands in his name, and mothers use old stories of him to terrify unruly children. The iconography of Ratnamaris, said to be a god of the sea and of money, is often worn by merchants and sailors of Basnapura. The Rosantic have their Ascended. In Tangowan, they worship the Monsoon Sister and Ina Rasa and dieites said to live in hearths and trees. Are the gods merely powerful daemons? Are they Primals that have gone far along their path? Consumers? different categories of beings altogether? Your Grace need not resolve the theology. The only advice I can offer is that even when the beings themselves are rare, faith is still very real in the hearts and minds of people. Those devotions are a force just like any other, and must sometimes also be tended.

74.title: In Conclusion
74.content: By now Your Grace must have realized that you govern a territory in which this whole spectrum lives or has some effect. Even if Your Grace does not directly dabble in magic, you must understand and make use of the kinds of people who use them, and the relationship between the Lesser Theoretical University and those magicians who work by older, less systematized means - especially the Haugris Church and the Temple of Eighteen. If Singhapura has shown the North one thing, it is that institutions are far more powerful, and far more long-lived, than individuals. The North is full of memories and the tales of heroes and cunning trickters, but institutions with unique capacities inevitably develop political power and confidence to match. Your Grace must keep a weather eye at all times on these things.

77.title: Of Lusia, Its Cities, and its Relationships to the Empire
77.content: Lusia is easily reached from Singhapura or from the Rosantic League. It is a family of city-states rather than a single dominion. It lies west and south of the narrow strip we call the Taprobane Desert, in a country of rivers and fertile valleys, and in those valleys sit seventeen city-states, bound together by language, custom and a shared taste for fighting one another, and by no single government. Lusia invented modern banking, double-entry accounting and lawyers. Its money therefore reaches further than even its formidable mercenaries.
