Lusian banks have underwritten the ambitions of Pendragons, provincial lords and city-states across the known world; during the Mirrored States they held a controlling interest in the Sunset Empire itself, and ended that war when they judged that peace served the investment better. The Adhiraj has forbidden the Singhapura Treasury, the Haugris Church and the inner ring of the nobility from Lusian dealings, and treats the matter as one of state security. The prohibition does not extend to everyone else, and many a Singhapura noble has, at one time or another, looked at the terms. Four of the seventeen cities are of a size with Singhapura itself, which is more than can be said for the whole of the North put together. Let us begin with them.

78.title: Of the Four Great Republics and the Nature of Their Power
78.content: Each of the great republics is nominally governed by a Principe, a First Citizen whose post rotates every three years. The title misleads. The Principe’s function is chiefly ceremonial, and while he may sign in a city’s name, he does not always decide what he signs. It is around the various councils that the great noble houses orbit, each with its own private army and its own commercial enterprises. The joke is that every possible war between the Septimura and Altomente houses has already been declared, and only the scheduling remains. Picture Daub with nobody at the top to knock heads together, and you have something close to Lusia. Septimura is the first and oldest of the republics. Like Singhapura, it claims descent from Samarskand, and there may be something in the claim; it may well have been the seat of some far-flung vassal kingdom. It lies south of the Taprobane desert among seven hills, linked to the other cities by an extensive network of rivers. It is large, orderly and rich, and makes fine wool, silk and silverware. Above all it is home to the great banking families, the Orenzo among them. Your Grace may recognize the name; it was an Orenzo who built Adhiraj House. Septimura’s reputation rests upon law, and upon enforcing it. Its Senate convenes rarely, but when it does it enforces contracts regardless of political consequence. Its bankers have been known to purchase the other debts of a man who has wronged them, and to drive him to ruin and beyond. The general Septimus, said to have founded the city, has this upon his grave: No friend has ever served me whom I did not treat with gold; no enemy has ever wronged me whom I did not repay with ashes. Thus all accounts are settled. Behind the bankers stands the Order of the Sound of One Hand Clapping. Plainly said, Your Grace, the Order is dangerous. What it does is a direct counter to the kind of structured magic that underlies much of the Singhapura Empire. Its members are mercenary by nature (Mohandas Siege, the Emperor’s own Bitterness, comes from this cabal), but Lusia has made itself the Order’s chief patron, and Septimura’s families are close to it. When a contract with Septimura is broken, it is often the Order that is sent. This is the foundation of Septimura’s most useful function to the Empire: parties who do not trust Singhapura to keep its word call upon Septimura to witness their arrangements with us. The Adhiraj keeps Septimura publicly at arm’s length and privately close. Singhapura funds the Temple of Eighteen in Septimura generously, and many a Septimura noble travels to Singhapura for business or pleasure. Marezzia is a naval republic. Its wealth comes from controlling the sea routes between Singhapura and the other republics, and from glasswork of extraordinary quality. Its merchant fleet is said to be larger and faster than Singhapura’s, though more dispersed, and when one speaks of Lusian merchants at sea, one means Marezzians. Marezzians wear masks in public. Each style is recorded in a central ledger, and a mask is removed only among family and in negotiations of established trust. Vassal families wear cruder copies of the masks of the noble houses they serve, to display their loyalty. The Council of Ten, which governs the city, is drawn from the wealthiest and most powerful. Its members must be unmasked to one another and to nobody else. It is said that the post of First Citizen is offered to the youngest member first, as an education in the requirements of ruling. The business of masks is often dismissed as affectation. I would caution Your Grace against that. It is fundamental to the Marezzian and to Marezzian dealings. Everything is hidden, and everything is recorded; honesty and vulnerability are privileges extended selectively, and only after great deliberation. Altomente is the capital of the arts, and not of Lusia alone; I do not believe there is its equal anywhere in the known world. Long ago, it seems, its houses concluded that there was more profit in owning the region’s imagination than in matching their neighbours in arms. Altomente’s taste now sets the standard for music, theatre and the novel, at home and abroad, and its banking families collect both the profits and the gratitude of every artist they have raised up. Your Grace will recognize in this the echo of Ealdorfold, and I have said elsewhere how much weight culture can carry. Ferrocinto is the northernmost republic. Its mercenaries have fought in every conflict worth naming; its siegecraft and cavalry are without peer; and its border with the Rosantic League ensures that it never lacks for practice. It grows its own food, produces armour of great quality, and is said to employ a great many alchemists in peace and war alike. Nobody can starve it, disarm it or outbid it for soldiers, which makes it very difficult to coerce. It is commonly assumed that everyone from Ferrocinto is of a martial character. Those I have met were mostly reserved, and much given to the poetry and plays of other lands. In the shadow of the city sits the town of Petona, whose name means “little soldier”. Angry young men from all over Lusia go there to make their fortunes in Ferrocinto. Few come back, and the ones who do are no longer angry, having spent it.

79.title: Of the Condottieri and the Lusian Theory of War
79.content: I have said that the Lusian cities fight among themselves. War comes to them about as seasonally as the monsoon comes to Singhapura. Yet Lusia does not collapse into general civil war, and the reason is the Condottieri, the mercenary companies. When a feud grows beyond what the noble houses, or even a single city, can manage, the mercenary captains are engaged. These armies are professionals. They avoid fighting in cities, they avoid harassing the townsfolk, and they prefer to settle matters across open plains and vineyards and mountain passes. In this fashion they preserve their clients for future hire, and win honour for themselves and their patrons alike. This has produced a curious code. It is no great shame to lose a battle. It is deeply shameful to kill an innocent, or to fail to present a very large invoice afterward. Your Grace may find this amusing. In practice it makes soldiering a lucrative profession, and so Lusia can summon vast mercenary armies, led by some of the finest commanders of our time, at private expense, while the great body of ordinary citizens remains in relative safety. The endless squabbling keeps the Condottieri in practice. It also means that a great republic in the wrong may find itself facing a coalition hired by the smaller cities, and unable to proceed. This is why every proposed invasion of Lusia has been abandoned. The carrots are difficult to harvest, as they say, and the sticks are many.

80.title: Of the Temple of Eighteen in Lusia
80.content: There is a serious claim that the Temple of Eighteen originated in Lusia, and that what Singhapura received was an export. There are equally serious counterclaims. I would advise Your Grace against raising the question at dinner with Singhapura scholars present, as the record suggests this ends badly for the crockery. Any comparison between the Rosantic Ascended and the Lusian Litanies is similarly fraught. In Singhapura and its dominions the Temple was suppressed, and suppression held it together. The Temple in Daub still belongs to the same organization as the Temple in Ruhunupura, for instance. In Lusia, left to develop freely, it fragmented. There is no single Lusian Temple to negotiate with. At best there are individual temples, some of negligible influence, and some seated on the highest councils of the major cities. Each of the Eighteen Litanies has its noble house affiliations, its city patrons, its competing interpretations and its sects. There is significant traffic between these temples and the Temple that calls the North home. Before formal banks were established on those shores, Lusian commerce and finance often flowed through the Temple, and something of that habit remains.

81.title: Of Lusian Magic
81.content: Lusia may be said to have magic of two kinds. Lusian sorcerers fall broadly within the Invoker tradition, as do the Temple and the Haugris Church. Their particular method is the making of bargains with higher powers: gods, daemons and entities of uncertain classification. Where a Temple adherent approaches his Litany with devotion, a Lusian sorcerer approaches his with a proposal of exchange. Their books of magic are less grimoires than annotated contract portfolios, jealously guarded. A few are on display in the Taprobane museum in Singhapura, and are said to be woefully out of date. Lusian sorcerers are held to be of great power, and especially proficient in curses, protections and war. Taprobane has a long history with them, and Lusian Archmages have made significant contributions to magical theory, so it is wise to suppose their arts considerable. A sorcerer born to a family is cause for celebration, and may even raise the family, if it is vassal to a noble house. Those of uncertain heritage, it is said, are often adopted and given the finest education money can buy. It is not known whether the Lusian sorcerer developed from the worship of the Litanies, or whether the Litanies were themselves powers bound by the Temple and afterward cast into a religion. It is unwise to discuss the matter publicly. At present the sorcerer and the Temple devotee are two very different creatures, bound by different interests. The second kind is the alchemist, much as in the Rosantic League. In Lusia, however, there are no universities, and the alchemist is subordinate to the noble house or the mercenary company: a servant of rare skill, called upon to draft and design and solve problems for his employers, and rarely able to command great power in his own right. Lusian nobles do not dabble in alchemy as Rosantic nobles do, nor do Lusian alchemists hang their names in the street. It is thought of as a poor man’s sorcery. Yet a keen-minded alchemist may rise high within his master’s house, and some are poached by rivals at great expense and risk. In Singhapura we say that ability rises from any mud, like the lotus. I have often wondered how much higher it would rise if the pond helped rather than hindered.

82.title: Of What This Means for Daub
82.content: Lusia and Singhapura are deeply intertwined, through finance and through the Temple, and so is Daub. These threads cannot be cleanly cut. The question for Your Grace is how to keep the Lusian presence in Daub’s commercial life a resource and not a liability, and I offer three answers in order. First, I would advise Your Grace to operate on the assumption that unexplained money, in any political context, has some Lusian component until demonstrated otherwise. Learn which of Daub’s houses and merchants hold Lusian paper, and from which city. Second, I urge Your Grace to keep an eye upon the Temple. Its Lusian branches move money as well as prayer, and what passes between them and the Temple in Daub will not appear in any ledger the Merchants Guild can show you. Third, and to be blunt: should any creditor of Daub’s ever call upon the Order of the Sound of One Hand Clapping, Your Grace must know of it before the Order arrives, and not after. Nothing the LTU can raise will stop them. The only defence is to ensure that no contract with Septimura is ever broken by anyone Your Grace cannot afford to lose.

83.title: Further Reading
83.content: The Notebooks of Benjamin Colzi exist in seventeen partial copies, no two of which agree on the order of the entries; the original, if it survives, has yet to be found. Colzi, an alchemist of great talent, spent forty years in the employ of three noble houses and two mercenary companies, sometimes on opposing sides. His work was the foundation of the Ritual we call Benjamin’s Lightning Gourd. His theories on load-bearing alloys, on the extraction of useful compounds from common minerals, and even on the geometry of foundations were adopted wholesale by Lusian industry. Colzi died in ignominy, drawing caricatures in the street to feed his daughter. The Invoices of Battle, attributed to one Castruccio of Ferrocinto, is the nearest thing the Condottieri have produced to a written doctrine. It is short. Castruccio writes as a man advising his successor: how to read terrain without committing to it, how to arrange a surrender efficiently and with dignity, how to select clients, and what wages and provisions armies require in various circumstances. The chapter on the ethics of changing sides mid-campaign is the longest. The chapter on fighting in cities is a single sentence: Do not. The Count of Marezzia is a novel of revenge and financial conspiracy. Its storytelling is unmatched, but I commend it to Your Grace for its accounts of Marezzian banking and of contract enforcement across the Lusian city-states, including the harsh penalties imposed. Anyone who means to do business in the region, or who believes herself exposed to legal action within it, will find it instructive. Masks and Manoeuvres is another novel, concerning the great banking families of Altomente and their dealings with the Temple of Eighteen. It has been banned in Altomente. When those in power prohibit a mere story, it is seldom because the book is false. The ban has made it widely circulated, and it is now customary in Singhapura to discuss it. On the theological question of the Temple of Eighteen and its relation to the Rosantic Ascended, the Reflections of the Moon in Still Water is commonly recommended. I would advise Your Grace not to waste her time. The link is a single chapter and a pile of commentaries upon it, and there is less knowledge in it than in a tavern ballad. The novels will serve you better.

85.title: Maps
85.content: I’m not a professional mapmaker, so these maps are drawn using Wonderdraft and GIMP. Much of the detail, like cities and trees, are from brushes by KM Alexander, who extracts details from old maps and turns them into reusable assets under the Creative Commons CC0 license. pecifically, most of the trees, cities, and mountain symbols are from the Popple set (based on Henry Popple’s 1746 map of the British Empire in the Americas). Some mountains are from the Walser set (a reconstruction of iconography from a 1763 map created by Gabriel Walser). The compass rose at the bottom is an amalgam of the Sandakapahana of the Ridi Viharaya in Kurunegala, Sri Lanka, which is relatively close to where I live and this compass rose I found while trawling Wikimedia Commons. As for inspiration, I was mostly looking at the Carta Marina, created by Swedish ecclesiastic Olaus Magnus and initially published in 1539, which was made with a process somewhat like I imagine Singhapura mapmakers might follow - drawing from older maps, like Ptolemy’s work, and mixing in contemporary sources and sailors’ descriptions as well as their own observations. We can safely assume that no Singhapura mapmaker has made it past Catherine’s Gate yet . I’ve also spent a bit too much time poring over ESA Sentinel-2 data over at Watchdog, so I suppose at some point the structure of waterways and farmland just got stuck in my head and wouldn’t really leave.

86.title: The Known World
86.content: Click the map to view it at full resolution → . A map of the known world, with Singhapura at the center (of course). You can see that the map loses detail the further out from Singhapura and its more sophisticated trading partners - almost nothing is known about the Obsidian Empire, for instance.

87.title: The North
87.content: Click the map to view it at full resolution → . The region that Singhapura thinks of as “The North” (although you’ll find plenty of people who say that Ealdorfold is the true North). Readers who’ve come across Diana Wynne Jones’ a Tough Guide to Fantasyland might recognize quite a few things here . the biggest powers here - nominally - are the Kingdom of Wattle, currently run by King Allant, the Duchy of Daub, currently defined as “the city and whatever else Maud can hang on to”, and the various tendrils of Singhapura, especially the Haugris Church. A large chunk of it is the Great Northern Waste.

88.title: Ealdorfold
88.content: Click the map to view it at full resolution → . A very old kingdom whose previous civilization ended by the Tungolsweorc, when the sky itself is said to have fallen on it. What’s left is ruled by the Leohtgield, a council that elects a monarch - currently Ursule, Queen Under Heaven. Inspired to some degree by a strange mishmash of 19th century novels (especially the Brontë sisters), Anglo-Saxon mythology (especially the Arthurian corpus), Scandanavian runestone lore, Irish filids, and The Golden Bough: A Study in Magic and Religion by James George Frazier.

89.title: Singhapura
89.content: Click the map to view it at full resolution → . The Empire proper - the largest continuous economic and military power in the known world, run at the top by the Adhiraj, the Haugris Church, the Taprobane University, and the Guilds. Its heart-city, also called Singhapura, sits at the foot of the Raavanskandha mountains. Inspired by Sri Lankan history and mythology (especially the hydraulic civilizations of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa era) and by Kautilya’s Arthashastra, which I highly recommend if you ever set out to run something like the Maurya Empire - it’s got everything from fort-building to taxation to surveys to court systems to markets and trade setup.

90.title: The Rosantic League
90.content: Click the map to view it at full resolution → . Forty-three polities bound by charter, and one of the pre-eminent conglomerate powers of the world, backed up by powerful magic. Loosely inspired by the Holy Roman Empire at its peak - especially the constitutional patchwork and the French-German mishmash (Alsace, Lorraine, and so on).

91.title: Lusia
91.content: Click the map to view it at full resolution → . Seventeen city-states held together by language and old rivalry, inspired broadly by the Renaissance Italy of Machiavelli’s time - especially Florence, Rome, Venice, Sforza-run Milan, and the banking houses.

92.title: The Military of Singhapura
92.content: “All government is based on the legal monopoly of violence.” So wrote Pramudya Tata Praja in The Civil Service and the State. When the laws and the arguments and the coins have all failed, the steel comes out. These, then, are the Military Orders of the Singha Adhiraj. Like most things in Singhapura, the present arrangement descends from Samarskand. The ancient texts describe the Panchayudhaya, the Five Weapons: the Mace, the Sword, the Bow, the Discus and the Conch. The Conch was the messengers and the signallers. Early Singhapura kept to those five faithfully, until actual wars forced a change. A campaign cannot be fought out of a book of ancient sayings. The Chapter system replaced the Five Weapons and has been refined since about the year 500 of Singhapura’s reckoning. It has room for ordinary troops and specialists alike; commanders may combine Chapters to suit a campaign; and every faction with an interest in the army holds a large enough share of it that none can take the whole. Each Chapter is commanded by a Chaptermaster, the second-highest rank in Singhapura’s army. Above them stand the four generals, whom the Emperor appoints as he needs them. Some of those appointments have been brilliant and some have been disasters, and so over the last century an unwritten rule has grown up: nobody receives a general’s post unless he can defeat the sitting Chaptermasters in a series of war games. Everyone knows that Singhapura’s armies win. Raskeshwara holds that this has less to do with clever generals than with what he calls the Flowing Chain: the Empire’s capacity to move men and supplies wherever it likes, to keep them fed once they arrive, and to keep them fighting longer than anyone else can. The quartermasters and clerks of Singhapura win it as many battles as its soldiers do. Your Grace will recall from the histories that the Temple’s crusade in the First Ebbing failed for want of a calendar, not for want of courage. The Empire has never forgotten it.

93.title: The Main Chapters: One Through Eight
93.content: Chapter One, the Standing Line, is the largest force Singhapura has and the spine of the army: archers, line infantry and reservists, carrying spears, bows and shields. When other Chapters run short, the Line hauls their supplies as well. Every soldier serves at least five years, and a recruit from outside the Empire becomes a citizen at the end of it. Longer service brings land and a pension. For a great many people this is the only road upward, and the only road into Singhapura. The Line makes imperial citizens out of provincial farm boys faster than any law could. Chapter Two, Hammerfall, is the heavy infantry, placed in the path of cavalry. Hammerfall recruits only from the Standing Line, receives far better equipment and training, and is full of men who intend to die in uniform one way or another. Chapter Three, the Black Lightning, is the shock cavalry, drawn from the noble families. For a young noble who has made no name in scholarship or elsewhere, a term in the Lightning is the least he can do to be thought respectable. Three is an auspicious number in Singhapura. They scout and fight on horseback in units of twenty-five called Lances, and many riders furnish their own horses and equipment. The Empire finds this very convenient. It takes hot-blooded young nobles, gives them enough chances at glory to keep them content, and teaches them to follow orders before they learn enough politics to do real damage. Your Grace will have seen much the same among the knights of the North. Chapter Four, the Boiling Rock, does artillery, sieges, fortifications and heavy engineering, and many of its people are Taprobane mages. Between wars they oversee the great public works and see that imperial roads and walls are built to imperial standards. Its people move back and forth with the Stonemasons, so the men who bring down a city wall and the men who raise one are very often the same men. Chapter Five, the Left Hand of the Law, is the army’s own Watch. They keep discipline and investigate anyone suspected of disloyalty. Their authority runs across every Chapter, and they may question and detain an officer of any rank. The rest of the army fears them and resents them for it. The Adhiraj’s household guard are almost always drawn from Chapter Five (this is the so-called Hand of Silk and Steel, although it has no designated name). Chapter Six, the Iron Chain, manages supply, logistics and transport for the whole army. Most of its people come from the guilds, or are young men learning the trade in uniform before returning to commerce. Raskeshwara’s Flowing Chain rests upon this Chapter and upon the roads the Boiling Rock builds. In his words, without the Iron Chain the rest of the army is a great deal of expensive equipment sitting in one place. Chapter Seven, the Water Bearers, is Singhapura’s navy. It began as a merchant fleet and turned military by degrees, and it is now the second largest Chapter. Ealdorfold has more ships spread over more water, and Lusia is better on the deep sea; the Water Bearers are still learning. Their River Ghosts, who specialize in water and mist magic and in landing troops from the water, are a great deal better than the rest of the Chapter’s reputation. Chapter Eight, the Sin-Eaters, is the Chapter that frightens people most. Their only task is the destruction of magical threats to the Empire, and they are chosen from the bravest, the most violent, and those with the least wish to go on living. They are the only Chapter with no written code of honour, no anthem and no badges of rank. Their banner is plain black. They field heavily trained Taprobane battle mages and many Judges and Arbiters of the Haugris Church, and I am told there are Temple of Eighteen monks among them who have set aside their robes for the fight. The first Sin-Eater Legion marched the year the Gray King came to Kusumadevi’s library, and the Empire has been demanding steel, leather and artefacts from its provinces to equip them ever since. Some of that steel passes through Daub.

94.title: The Specialist Chapters: Nine Through Thirteen
94.content: The specialist Chapters are smaller and cost more, and the Empire is far more careful about when it sends them out. Chapter Nine, the Cobras, scout and sabotage beyond the borders. They recruit chiefly from frontier peoples, so that they may look and behave like the natives of places Singhapura does not yet formally rule. Daub is upon a frontier. Assume the Cobras know it well. Within the Cobras sits a sub-Chapter called the Crows, who specialize in counter-spying and “longterm operations” - ie: becoming permanent parts of a foreign order, rather than being spies. Many sources do not list them at all. They recruit chiefly orphans and nobles who have lost their lands, and a good number pass through the University and emerge with magic for concealment and for finding things out. The Crows have outgrown their parent in everything but name, and I expect them to be a Chapter in their own right within a generation. The Merchants will have to find a new joke about being the Fourteenth. Your Grace will deal with a Crow sooner or later, although you will very probably never know it. Chapter Ten, the Stone Lions, are the last line of defence for the places the Empire cannot afford to lose: elite heavy infantry in the heaviest armour there is, trained to hold their ground whatever it costs them. They now receive a good deal of magical training as well, and they are said to be unbreakable. That may be an exaggeration, but there are records of a handful of Stone Lions holding off hundreds while those they guarded escaped. Chapter Eleven, the Paladins, began as an independent mercenary order, and Makaraasoka took them into the Empire because they were so effective. As the Haugris Church grew stronger they fell out of favour, and the Empire is now allowing them to dwindle and handing their duties to others. Your Grace knows the recent events better than this treatise needs to record. The loss of the Paladins pushed the Empire to try magical specialist units in their place. First it gave the Stone Lions magical training. Then it took note of what the River Ghosts had accomplished in the navy. Finally it created the two newest Chapters. Chapter Twelve, the Thunderclouds, are mages recruited from Taprobane directly after graduation, most of them specialists in lightning and fire. Their armour stores the rapid magical charges their work requires, and it glows while they fight. On several occasions the glow alone has ended an engagement before it began. They are intended to replace the Paladins. Chapter Thirteen, the Special Affairs Division, is called the Heathens by everyone who must work near them. They are sent where soldiering will not serve and the Empire needs to be able to deny its part. They take special talents: practitioners of unorthodox magic, and people whose abilities are strange or outright forbidden. Talents the Sin-Eaters will not accept are said to end up here, especially powers the Church calls heresy. Almost nothing about them is public.

95.title: Other Forces
95.content: There are three further forces, Your Grace, of which you should know. The Charter Knights are a mixed body. When a soldier’s term is done, or he has spent too long at the front, or he is judged too old or otherwise unfit, he is sent to the Charter Knights. The Empire puts him through a University course in law and ethics and sends him home as a warden of the city, to guard it and keep its peace. Charter Knights answer to the local Governors and Justices of the Peace. The idea came from watching the North. Veterans there have always had to be paid off with land. While the North had plenty of land to go around, Singhapura foresaw natural limits and problems to this approach - a lord with more old soldiers than farms ends up with bandits, as Your Grace knows. Singhapura wanted something that would scale, and that would get some use out of the men besides. Hence the Charter Knights: a police and first-response force, paid from the public purse and put to work. Every major city has its own division, with local insignia added to the standard uniform and some freedom to do things its own way. This makes it hard to say anything about them in general. Singhapura’s own Charter Knights have enough battle mages to stop almost anyone. The Charter Knights of Giridhora, when I last saw them, were of no worthy character. Then there are the private guards of the guilds. The Merchants Guild keeps the largest, and it is nearer an expeditionary army than a body of watchmen. Inside the Empire these guards are bound by imperial law. Outside it they are treated as free agents, much like Lusian or Rosantic mercenaries. Last, there is the Emperor’s Bitterness. The post is comparatively new. The Bitterness holds authority above every Chapter and every military rule. He investigates, prosecutes, judges and executes, all in his own person. He requires no warrant and no council, and he is held to be the Emperor’s own hand. To obstruct him is to obstruct the Emperor, and to raise a hand against him is to raise a hand against all of Singhapura. The post is held at present by Mohandas Siege, formerly of the Order of the Sound of One Hand Clapping. I have seen him, with my own eyes, walk through the finest wards of the University as though they were cobwebs. The less I write of him in a book whose circulation I cannot control, the better.

96.title: Of What This Means for Daub
96.content: Daub keeps Charter Knights of its own, and the Paladins, and whatever mercenaries happen to be in town, and none of these would trouble a single Chapter of Singhapura for an afternoon. I do not say this to alarm Your Grace. Daub was never meant to hold against the Empire, and no sensible ruler of Daub would try. I have written in the chapter on Daub what I would do with the Charter Knights, and I will only add that the Paladins’ decline in Singhapura is a matter of Church politics and not of their worth. Your Grace may raise them where the Empire has let them fall, and the Empire will not object, since it has had their replacements in hand for some years. One last thing, and I say it as plainly as I can: keep Mohandas Siege out of Daub’s affairs. He is answerable to one man and to nobody else. He is not sent to solve a problem. He is sent so that the Empire’s will on that matter is never questioned again.

97.title: The Modern Classics
97.content: There is a second shelf of books that every person of consequence is expected to know. The Great Classics earned their place by age and by the institutions behind them. These novels earned theirs by getting their worlds right, and people love them for it. They are also a pleasure to read; and since Your Grace is not fond of the page, they may hold you a little longer. Masks and Manoeuvres is set in Altomente. Alba Vetturi comes from a respectable family of modest means, known for enchanted miniature portraits. This is enough to admit them to the great masked balls, and not enough to give them any say once inside. At one such ball she meets Lord Kassian d’Orenzo, heir to the most powerful banking house in Lusia, and dislikes him at once, since he makes no effort to hide what he thinks of her family. Over the rest of the book, through guild quarrels and her own sharp instincts, she discovers that each had judged the other wrongly, and that someone is forging magical contracts to bring the city down. Its account of masked negotiation and Lusian contract law is so exact that Altomente banned it, and it remains officially unavailable in Ferrocinto. Angenga concerns Vikram Aaloka, a magician of great ability who is admitted to the Taprobane Magisterium and expelled almost at once for forbidden experiments. The Concordant College, which in those days was all ambition and very few rules, gives him a place to work. There he makes a living creature out of Tungolstaana ore smuggled from Ealdorfold and the raw energies of the Waste. It is immensely strong, and it slowly and strangely becomes aware of itself, and Vikram flees from it in terror. From then on the book belongs as much to the Angenga as to Vikram, as the creature pursues its maker across the Waste, half mad with loneliness. Tangowan Straits follows Isara, a young storyteller learning to navigate, who signs aboard the Serpent’s Tooth. Her captain is a grim man with one leg who wants nothing in the world except to kill the great Azure Dragon that sank his last ship. The voyage carries them through treacherous island chains and at last into storms the dragon itself seems to raise. Your Grace can guess how the captain’s obsession ends for his crew. What nobody else has managed is the portrait of Tangowan and its gods as they must once have been. Read it, and consider what Daub would have to do to avoid becoming somebody’s novel. Emmeline concerns a healer’s wife in the country borough of Aeppelthorp. Everything she knows of the world comes from the magical story-scrolls sent out from the Leohtgield, full of great enchantments and grand passions, and her small life cannot hold her. She abandons it to pursue that world through secret affairs and costly magic, all paid for by a shadowy moneylender whose contracts are enforced by equally shadowy means, and it destroys her in the manner such stories require. It is also a detailed social history of the upheaval during the Leohtgield’s consolidation, and far better than the official histories. Staanbyrig is set in a hard Ealdorfold mining city. Raedwulf Sceaduweard, a penniless former student, has persuaded himself that great men need not obey the law. He murders an old galdor and her apprentice, is hunted, is offered redemption, and learns over the remainder of the novel that he is not one of the great men after all. It is a bleak book, and it may be the only account we have of how Ealdorfold justice works from within. The plot also turns upon a forged contract pushed through Valdermach, which brings in a long and accurate account of a Diet session. Whoever wrote it knew the courts of two countries from the highest bench to the lowest cell, which I find almost suspicious. The Lion Emperor’s Courtesan follows Lady Anjalee Devi, a celebrated and gifted noblewoman held in a political marriage. She scandalizes Singhapura society by falling for Count Weerasena, a war hero. Singhapura’s customs being what they are, the affair is ended, and the whole is a tragedy from first page to last. Alongside it runs the story of Devan, a Singhapura landowner who removes to a new estate in Wattle and must learn to live among neighbours who resent him, and slowly takes on their ways. I have mentioned this book elsewhere for its Rosantic court masque, which Rosantic diplomats have cited in their correspondence. It is also a good book on what Singhapura’s society does to people, and on how those who escape it learn to live with themselves and with people unlike them. Blooma Daeg follows three people through a single day in Aethelburh. Leofwine Blooma, a man of mixed blood, sells small enchanted trinkets through the city’s maze of markets. His wife Mereweef sings songs said to move men further than songs ought. Staelwyrhta Daedal, a brilliant young galdorcraeftiga, crosses the same city on business of his own, in search of the lost prophecies of the last Aethelgarth oracle. Their paths cross and part throughout the day, and nothing is settled at the end. It is the best portrait I know of how ordinary people in Ealdorfold live, and what they hope for. The Count of Marezzia follows Edmondo Alighieri, a promising young ship’s captain from a small trading family. Rivals betray him on the eve of his wedding, and he is condemned to a prison from which nobody escapes. There he befriends an aged Singhapura magician, a fellow prisoner, who reveals the location of a vast forgotten treasure and teaches him everything he knows before dying. Alighieri escapes, grows immensely rich, names himself the Count of Marezzia, and takes his time destroying every one of his betrayers across Altomente, Septimura and Ferrocinto. It shows Lusian high society at its most treacherous, with its feuds between cities and its corrupt great families, and it shows precisely how frightening Lusian debt and contract law can be. If Your Grace has made enemies in Lusia, read it soon.

98.title: On the Nature of Magic, and the Laws by Which It Operates
98.content: Now, Your Grace, we must read some theory. I know full well that you do not see much point in it. My last book, after all, you used as a doorstopper. Let me try again, because it is important that you understand this: . In the same way that there are limits to what a man can do by himself . in the same way that footsoldiers and pikemen alone cannot stop a charge of knight . in the same way that you must balance the natures and egos and abilities of many people around you to make Daub work, so, too, does magic have its own difficulties and limitations. If Your Grace is to govern magicians, you must understand the constraints under which we operate. This not just to improve your understanding of theory, but so that you know what you can get out of someone and what you cannot. There are reasons why a single magician cannot wave his hand and have a castle constructed overnight. There are reasons we cannot stop death, or explode an army with our minds alone, and why we hunt necromancers. All magic is subject to certain rules. These were first set down in the Sutras of the Temple of Eighteen, presumably by the first generation of their Litanies. After centuries of experimentation, almost all institutions - with the possible exception of madmen like the Iron Pagoda and the Order of the Sound of One Hand Clapping - have agreed that these fundamentals hold true: .

99.title: Principles that are Well Understood
99.content: 1) The Principle of Equivalent Exchange, or the Fire Sutra . Every working has a cost. This cost cannot be eliminated, only changed from one form to another. Vedics, for example, make wards with herbs and materials; these rot and wither rapidly, and thus their wards have to be maintained by constantly sacrificing groceries. For many magicians, the cost comes from themselves. Many low-grade Primals, for example, eat more than what a normal man would - this is probably why your kings and knights are so fond of feasts. This is also why young magicians might be full of fire and frenzy, but they grow old before their time, wnd why even very powerful Paragons walk slowly and hesitate to throw magic as one would arrows. Many of those who sit at the heights of power tend to acquire a certain instability of body and temperament - one of my Professors at Taprobane, arguably the greatest frost magician in the world, was little more than a brain in a vat. Those who carry heavy burdens walk unevenly, as they used to remind us. Much of the Patternwork of a Singhapura-style Ritual goes into handling these costs. It may be that to heat something up, something else might have to become cold (this is used in the baths that nobles favor so much). It may be that the spell-plates themselves corrode rapidly and must be replaced. Our ability to measure these costs and shunt them around has improved greatly. Even so, the Burden, or the Price, as some call it, must be borne and paid. Thus there are certain things you cannot demand for love or money; there are certain acts that, though it may seem trivial to you, would be a death sentence. Consider who you command and what they pay. 2) The Principle of Least Resistance, or the Water Sutra . Magic moves by the path of least resistance. A magician who has not thought carefully through her workings will find that even when they function, they will do so by unpredictable paths, often at great injury to others. This is similar to a leader ordering a general to capture a town or city, without thinking through the consequences. This is why us Ritualists have some dislike of Vedics and Bards and the like; there is a certain sloppiness to their approach, and a lack of understanding of cause-and-effect, that makes them unreliable even when allied. Your Grace should take care that the magicians she employs are wise, above all else. Bold moves might look like the key to greatness, but in this business surges of brilliance and power often leave behind devastating consequences. The Great Northern Waste is always a good reminder. 3) The Principle of Differential Permeability, or the Iron Sutra . For reasons as yet unknown to us, magic has three odd affinities. One, very few types of magic can directly interfere with a living being’s body. This is why you do not see magicians immolating one another with a thought. Where you hear such tales, it is always an effect of magic; perhaps wind splattering a poison on skin, or superheated air rushing to someone’s face. Unfortunately, Galdors and Bards seem to bypass this limitation, as do many entities both divine and daemonic. Two, magic is repelled by certain subtances. Salt is well-known; but most metals are far less permeable, as we say. Lead is by far the least permeable metal; this is why many of Singhapura’s anti-magician units bear shields with thin sheets of lead between the layers. Certain alloys of steel, in particular, are also exceptionally durable magical deadeners. This is why a heavily armored knight, whatever his other limitations, remains an effective figure against the many sorts of magical practitioners. However, as the North discovered in its clashes with Singhapura forces, the same is not always true for the ground under said knight’s feet, or the air he breathes, and so on . your Grace’s Charter Knights should bear this in mind when they are deployed. This is also useful. For example, spell-plates are commonly cast and chiseled out of bronze or thin steel, because once made, it is far more durable than the equivalent carved on wood or leather. The armor of Haugris Arbiters is nearly impenetrable by anything short of seige weapons. However, such feats take both extraordinary effort and control, so much so that it is much cheaper and more effective to send adventurers into the Waste to hunt down Relics; this limitation is directly a boon and a weakness to the economies of both Daub and Wattle. No-one has yet managed to make lead work with magic, but there are many techniques of inlay, plating, casting, and so on . there is a reason that foundries and metalworkers hold as much power as they do in both Singhapura and Ealdorfold. Third, much of our magic weakens significantly over running water, deserts and volcanoes. Some say that this is because such places lack the necessary energy, but the more modern intepretation is that large volumes of fluids (and fine sand can act very much like running water) diffuse workings. This area is being actively explored at both Taprobane and the Iron Pagoda. 4) THe Principle of Traceability, or the Graveyard Sutra . Magic leaves traces. Even simple magics leave behind traces of their intent, like a smell in the air that lingers. The most powerful workings can take decades or centuries to fully disspite, even after the working has been terminated. Generally, the more structured the magic is, the more “bones” remain - powerful investigators of the Compliance Division can even reconstruct partials, or fragments of workings, for later analysis. These traces are often corrupted by other magic, so areas where large, powerful workings have repeatedly been flung around - ie: battlefields - have a tendency to condense into a miasma (“the graveyard”), a sort of ephemereal hell. Graveyards, if left unchecked, become blights very similar to the Great Northern Waste - this last part was proven relatively recent in Singhapura history. Unfortunately, the only known way to disperse a fully fledged graveyard is to have people actively moving through and settling in it (and presumably surviving long enough to do so). Research into this has also led to the observation that people - or at least, anything posessed of self-awareness - slowly breathes in trace amounts of magic and returns it to the world, cleaned somewhat of terrible effects; certain magicians can work Rituals that enhance this process, at the cost of great trauma to whoever has to endure the process. This is why the Sin-Eater Legions exist. Sin-Eaters are honored as heroes in Singhapura - the penalty for striking one is death, even to nobles - but each soldier is given a ceremonial burial before they march out, because very few ever return alive and sane.

100.title: Principles that are held to be True but are Difficult to Prove by Observation and Evidence
100.content: 5) The Narrative Resonance Hypothesis, or the Heart Sutra . This is the idea that magic responds to a compelling story, and that the power to move hearts might itself be a form of magic. Or, as my colleagues used to say, bullshit plot armor. No serious modern practioner takes this seriously. The mechanisms of how this happens are very widely disputed, even by those who hold it to be true. After all, what a story is can differ so widely according to the time, the place, the culture, and even other circumstances. For example, take the tradition of gremling death poems. To them it may be a moment of great clarity, and a powerful story being written at the moment of someone’s death; to us it might be complete nonsense. This hypothesis remains unprovable, because there are simply too many variables to test a story coming true. The Hasselbad School of Rhyme is the most obsessed with this; one of their more far-fetched ideas is that the entire world is some kind of cosmic stage, and that many of the great and the powerful are simply roles played endlessly; Your Grace will understand immediately how ridiculous this is. 6) The Observer Effect, or the Mirror Sutra . This states that what a magician believes and understands shapes what his magic can accomplish. Let me try for a practical example: a man raised in forests who has spent his life attending to plants will do better with that kind of working than a novice reading about plants in a library. This is . perhaps bordering on common sense, so much so that a lot of us regard it less like a principle of magic and more like a fundamental observation of every sphere of effort. 7) The Principle of Causality, also known as the Wheel Sutra . This states that the universe has a natural tendency of motion (or, as my Professor used to say, the arrow of time goes in one direction). This applies to all phenomena. Reversing this motion is said to be exponentially costlier than aiding it. We have some evidence for this Principle. For example, making a fire burn hotter is easier than making it colder. Thus, cold blue flames are considered a classic way of warning someone that you are a powerful magician with exceptional control. Living things resist death; healing is much easier than killing directly with magic. Dead things resist return; necromany consumes so much energy and is so inefficient that catastrophe is almost inevitable. However, we cannot conclusively prove this theory. Not only because it would involve many heretical exercises, but also because we do know of certain workings that function within very predictable parameters despite this Principle suggesting otherwise. The lesson for Your Grace is this: those rulers who accomplish great things through the deployment of magic tend to be the ones who understand the nature of the world and ask for changes that are broadly in accord, rather than against it - not too different from the task of politics and administration.

101.title: In Conclusion
101.content: These six principles or sutras are the walls of the room within which all magic operates. Most practitioners cannot overcome them at all. The few who can are generally beyond the human; either gods, daemons, or beings of another order. For the purposes of governing Daub, Your Grace can dismiss such exceptions - the response to such things is far beyond what policy can handle. For decades, the Taprobane Imperial University has worked diligently on a grand unified theory that ties these principles together. However for now, it still is very much a work-in-progress, the realm of old professors and foolish young students and heated arguments among faculty. In the practical world, it is safer to use the tried and tested.

103.title: Of Oaths, Obligations, and the Enchantment of Objects
103.content: Singhapura has a great many tools in their arsenal. But of everything, perhaps the most important for the running of a kingdom is dealing with people: empowering them, binding people to their word, assuring consequences. Not everyone agrees about how these things should be done, but every tribe that grows beyond its village boundaries agrees that things should be done. Every sophisticated civilization, to the best of our knowledge, has magic that supports these things. Your Grace, let me show you the tools at our disposal.

104.title: Of Contracts, Bonds, and Obligations
104.content: The Taprobane Five Elements Oath . One of the most widely used Rituals throughout the Empire. The Five ELements Oath enforces contracts using the collective Authority of all participants. The costs require five distinct elemental correspondences to manage - hence the term. The idea is that anyone who violates the Oath has their own Authority turn against them. The Ritual is cast in two stages: the first stage makes active Oaths - at least the intent behind them - visible to the caster. The second stage will not trigger until everyone involved is there of their own volition. There is a degree of unpredictability - it seems that several Sutras play on the idea of oathbreaking, and generally the degree of damage differs widely based on the number of potential causal effects at large. People have been known to survive oathbreaking, but at best they are reduced to a fragment of what they were, and forever afterward register as an anathema to anyone with magical senses. This may be one of the most useful tools in Your Grace’s arsenal. Sapumal Keppitipola, the Paragon who led the design team, worked briefly as a banker in Lusia before devising this, and the mechanism perhaps reflects his experience. Sapumal’s Sundering . The Sundering was originally a testing mechanism for iterating over the design of the Oath. The current version of the Sundering is a very simple and minmal Ritual that cuts magic and dissolves bindings. It requires a violent burst of effort; the older and more established the binding, and the larger the Authority behind it, the harder it is to cut. Backlash from both success and failure is considerable, often destroying the materials on which the Sundering is engraved - this is why we do not produce mass-produce magical swords with it. Gajaba’s Thread . A Ritual devised by an LTU Paragon studying the Sympathy of Galdors and Vedics. It creates a connection between separated parts of the same entity, allowing effects on one part to propagate to the whole. Even the simple versions of this Ritual allow for enormous utility - such as coded long-distance communications, remote detonation on alchemical charges, and so on. The more sophisticated versions come with much higher costs but even allow simple Patterns to flow across, thus allowing workings linked over long distances. Skilled magicians work in deliberate asymmetries - the science delays, filters, or conversions is a whole Department. Manike’s Gate . Yet another lesson from the Galdors of Ealdorfold. This Ritual binds an abstract principle to a physical location, creating a space where that principle is magically enforced - held in or kept out according to the caster’s design. The Heart Sutra and the Iron Sutra play hard on this working: for example, a truth-binding takes more easily in an ancient temple of justice and fails entirely on a suit of new steel armor. It is common that courtrooms in Singhapura carry Gates of Truth and Justice to guard against deception. The consent factor is satisfied by someone taking the choice to step through the Gate. The Gate requires many casters, and often creates a great deal of magical residue, and Gate effects (even on people only temporarily exposed) are easily identifiable by magicians. Gananth’s Benevolence . This Ritual is derived from the study of Primals and the Diefic; it temporarily transfers an aspect of the caster’s Authority to another person. This turns the recipient into something resembling a temporary Invoker. Imagine a magical version of Your Grace temporarily lending a page your seal and authority. However, the impact to the caster is greatly unpredictable, and most people naturally do not want to give away their talents. Bbecause of this the Benevolence is not used lightly. I’ve heard it said that the Haugris Church makes heavy use of it by having elders - especially old Arbiters who cannot fight anymore - bestow their powers to younger generations as a last and final gift. Rehobaum’s Dark Binding . This Ritual cleverly exploits the Heart Sutra’s recognition of a near-universal cultural motif: across every tradition we have examined, the shadow is closely linked to the idea of the person, and often their soul. The Dark Binding temporarily redirects wounds make to the flesh to the shadow. However, the Wheel Sutra is its enemy; it will spend eternity undoing the result, and there are enough horrific stories of magicians haunted by their own vengeful shadows, their bodies and powers broken. The Ritual is banned across most jurisdictions and carries a kill order except in serious medical emergencies or in self-defense. Marambe’s Amplification . Searches the area for living plants and drains them of energy before providing said energy to a given target, be it person or Ritual. This is commonly used to defray the costs of a Ritual, and its overuse is blamed on the graveyard mismas that the Sin-Eater Legions now deal with. Living plants are among the finest conductors available - they have passed through the seasons of the world, seen growth and decay, and thus participated in the cycle of life. Now it is permitted for non-warfare reasons only with permission from the Taprobane University. Kumara’s Purifying Flame . Burns away traces of magic from a location. This is critical in purifying the miasma of magical Graveyards before they reach critical levels. Unfortunately, it can only be powered by the caster’s own life force. The Temple of Eighteen was the origin of this Ritual; this is the Taprobane formalisation. Accompanying the Sin-Eater Legions of Singhapura are magicians and Temple of Eighteen adepts known as the Pyre Wardens who specialize in cleansing with this Ritual. A Pyre Warden does not live very long. Becoming one requires being either exceptionally heroic or exceptionally foolish - magicians convicted of crimes are often offered this role as an alternative sentence. The families of Sin-Eaters are generally well compensated by the Empire, but even among them a Pyre Warden is considered special, and the names of every fallen Warden are engraved by the Emperor himself on the steles in his garden. Yamuna’s Heart . Enhances an object’s natural properties, at the cost of destroying it completely once the Ritual ends. It may also be used to replace certain properties for a brief period with those imagined by the caster. The Iron Sutra actively resists this Ritual; the Heart Sutra partially offsets this, but only for objects that already carry sufficient narrative weight. On a famous sword, a named ship, an heirloom passed through generations, it may be viable; on a brick of no history, the cost would kill the caster instantly. Tailor’s Power of Two . This exploits the superposition observations of the Paragon Sangamitta. For an infinitesimal period of time, this Ritual produces a double of the target. The double inherits physical properties, but not life, magic, Authority, or such. The cost is that the Ritual any thing it is attached to is almost immediately wiped from the universe. For this reason, a heavily minimized version isn used to amplify brief effects such as explosions; as the energy created in the explosion can fuel the spell briefly, allowing it to activate before vanishing. Stories about the use of it on uncountable nouns or living subjects are considered a fantastic way to teach overeager students caution. For example, the Great Flood of Taprobane is considered a classic case of hubris and poor calibration.

105.title: In Conclusion
105.content: Of course I cannot describe to Your Grace every possible variety of enchantment, but I have tried here to illustrate tools that Singhapura considers most useful. As Daub grows, these tools will most likely become increasingly useful. I am not entirely sure if these Rituals are commonly taught at the LTU, because much of this relies on Patterns that their RUT does not have. They can be emulated, but emulation of sophisticated effects on simple hardware greatly increased costs and makes the magic run much slower than it should. Perhaps this is a good reason to promote some cross-cultural learning, or even to lean on your Singhapura-affilaited acquaintances. Your Grace will surely see the benefits of these magics for many of Daub’s day-to-day operations.

107.title: Of Foreign Peoples and Distant Dominions
107.content: It remains to speak of those peoples who lie beyond the borders of the Known World. My knowledge here is imperfect, and I offer these observations as a foundation for further inquiry rather than as a settled account. In the Waste dwell the Gremlings. They are a warlike people of great stature and acute senses, possessed of an elaborate honour. Their arms and armour are magnificent; indeed the ashwakadu we use today descends from their great horse-cutter swords. They occupy themselves also with poetry, painting and pilgrimage through the Waste, and are known to assist travellers in need despite their terrifying countenances. Their city has never been seen, and they claim to originate from another world entirely. A people that has learned to cultivate both war and philosophy is among the most dangerous there is. It is wise neither to antagonize such a people nor to bind Daub to them until their nature is better understood. The Dvorak Elves are more elusive, and in certain respects easier to understand. They believe themselves to be the discarded drafts of their Creator’s work, a theology which, whatever its truth, has produced in them a people of remarkable industry and ingenuity. Their manufactures are of surpassing quality, and many Artifacts recovered from the Waste prove upon examination to be their work. More significant is their ability to move through the world by means we do not yet comprehend. They use this faculty for commerce and for settling disputes with their clients. Your Grace should not neglect the value of a people who move unhindered by borders. Many a Singhapura noble, secure behind his walls, has been surprised by a Dvorak wanderwagen trundling nonchalantly up the castle road. Their conduct in commerce is consistent. There are many accounts of professional, if expensive, dealing, and they have on occasion served as mercenary overseers and as architects of great feats of engineering. To the south, across the sea, lies Northern Abydos. The name raises questions, chief among them whether further Abydoi exist. The Singhapura Merchants Guild has begun expeditions, but the land, we are told, is desert and nearly inhospitable. Beyond it, known only from maps, are the Sathsunid and the Sahel, empires reportedly as old as our own, from whom we have no writings and no works. To the Far East lies what we call the Obsidian Empire. We do not know its extent. Of its peoples we have seen little beyond curiosities: bows of horn and ivory, unknown instruments of extraordinary sharpness, coins bearing unfamiliar characters. The Samarskand Commentaries speak of “the empire of black glass and the rising sun,” which may well refer to the Obsidian; though I must confess that the Commentaries run to six thousand pages and are notoriously unreliable. Of all lands, Your Grace and Daub are best positioned to explore this avenue further. Civilized people, wherever they may be, almost always have wares to trade. Barbarica, as the Lusians named it, lies in the Far West. It has since been acknowledged as a border state, but we have as yet no dealings with it. I set these down not to discourage inquiry but to direct Your Grace toward finer sources. The Annales Historici, maintained by the Dvorak Elves, covers trade routes, languages, economies and customs from the western sea to the verified borders of the Obsidian Empire. Merchants pay heavily for good editions. I would advise Your Grace to keep one at hand.

109.title: Of the Rosantic League and Its Constituent Powers
109.content: The Rosantic League and Lusia, its southern neighbour, lie only a few days’ sail from the westernmost shores of Wattle, across the Dwimmer Channel. I begin, therefore, with the observation that Daub can reach the Rosantic League, and that the Rosantic League can reach Daub. The League is neither a kingdom nor an empire. It is a coalition born of a charter signed in Valdermach in the previous century, binding forty-three polities together, and they are a curious assortment: seven “free cities”, eleven hereditary margravates, nine prince-bishoprics, various duchies and countships, and one river abbey which, despite lying within Valdermach, keeps an independent vote on account of having been the venue of the signing. Everything in the League depends upon the river Valder. The name carries at once the meanings of power, of rule and of forest-dwelling. It runs from the eastern highlands to the western sea, and every significant city in the League sits upon it or within a day’s ride. Whoever holds the Valder’s chokepoints has a great say in how goods move and who sides with whom. Taken together, the League approaches Singhapura in size, and Valdermach alone is a city to match the capital. Its states share a language, a broad culture, and common traditions in law, heraldry and religion. Unlike in Lusia, the letter of the law is the same across the whole body. But where Lusia sets great store by the writing, arguing and enforcement of contracts, the Rosantics prefer simpler oaths, and hold lawyers in general distrust.

110.title: Of the Ascended, and Their Involvements
110.content: We must begin with faith. Faith, Your Grace, is the dominant feature of the Rosantic League and its politics, and its central expression is the Communion of the Ascended. The Ascended were real people who, through great or terrible deeds in life, crossed at death a threshold that most cannot, and became something akin to minor gods. They are not equal. At the summit sit perhaps a dozen figures of League-wide significance, invoked for famine, for war, for the outcome of Diet sessions and for the birth of heirs. Centuries of dealings have fixed their personalities, and their miracles are extensively documented. Below them is a substantial middle tier of regional and civic saints, each commonly with a city, a guild, a trade or a category of person under protection. Below that is an almost limitless tail of local and specialized figures. Noble houses claim descent from the Ascended, usually from the patron of whatever territory they govern. This is taken seriously. It bears directly upon land rights, military obligations, inheritance disputes and heraldic law, and the heraldic colleges of Valdermach and Brenmark keep the records. The Ascended, and thus the nobility derived from them, have long and complicated histories with one another. Some were allies in life and are invoked together by tradition. Some are never named in the same prayer. A city whose patron saint has a documented enmity with the patron of a prospective trading partner has a very real diplomatic problem, however absurd it may seem to us, and the League’s history is full of such cases. The Diet maintains a subcommittee whose sole business is trouble between saints. Your Grace has difficulty enough keeping the Haugris Church and the Temple of Eighteen from one another’s throats within a single city, and may imagine the scale of it. The Litanies of the Temple of Eighteen are the nearest analogy, but it falls short. The Litanies have documented effects; there is a great deal of faith around them; and now and then one truly manifests. Yet by and large politics carries on without their daily intervention. It is not so with the Rosantic Ascended, who manifest far more often than most deities. One of the earliest Singhapura expeditions to those lands encountered what appeared to be an old woman offering wine to tired sailors. The sailors partook and fell into a deep sleep, and woke to find every ship sunk and every weapon corroded; when at last they returned home, their families had given them up for dead years before. Even a minor Ascended may have living devotees who claim to have been healed in person, or set upon their path, by a personal manifestation of their god. There is even some scholarly suggestion that the Light of the Paladins is a Rosantic Ascended, though the documentation on that particular name is scant.

111.title: Of the Cities That Matter to Daub
111.content: 1) Valdermach is the League’s commercial throat. Its noble merchant families rival Lusia and Singhapura for involvement in trade, and much of Singhapura’s tea, clothing, spices and processed materials is exported to the League through it. The trade in holy relics, being critical to League faith and politics, runs through Valdermach as well, together with the finer business of authentication and brokerage. It is a hold upon a great many powerful people, and one rarely visible in the open. 2) Brenmark is where things are made. It is at once a customer of the guilds of Singhapura and their rival. There are guilds here also, and they have teeth, to use the common term. The Goldsmiths’ Hall, for instance, keeps its own court, its own jail and its own ambassadors abroad. Brenmark is also a great pilgrimage centre, because many of its guild patrons are among the oldest Ascended. Pilgrims, merchants and spies all travel the same roads, and a whole economy of inns and way-stations lives upon them. 3) Orvaine is the centre of printing and grimoire production, and home to the Orvaine College of Natural Philosophy. The College is some four hundred years old, founded originally to educate the highest nobility, and its credentials are taken seriously even in Singhapura. It has produced twelve magicians of Paragon rank, contributed a great deal to Taprobane, and printed and reprinted much of the literature we commonly discuss. Its greatest feat was the Reformers Convocation, now a major power in the League; the Reformers’ founding theological argument was written by an Orvaine faculty member and first printed on an Orvaine press. It is often said that the other polities of the League hide behind the skirts of these three. Not so; a great many scholars and Free Companies come to our shores from all across it. But it is these three which, having filled their own borders, look most eagerly at ours. I will add one more for Your Grace’s amusement: the duchy of Halsmoor, beside Brenmark, which consists of one small castle and a bit of village, and has become the most artistic place in the League on account of the cheaper rent.

112.title: Of the Diet
112.content: It is a curious feature of the League that the number of noble titles is fixed. In the margravates and similar states, titles pass down in families and are held chiefly by force of arms, land and wealth, as they commonly are in kingdoms. In the free cities, the citizens vote every ten years on which families shall hold the titles, so that a title passes from one to another much as a role passes between players in a theatre. Twice a year, at the summer and winter solstices, these nobles convene as the Diet for six weeks, each representing their own polity. The Diet may pass resolutions, levy funds for common defence, arbitrate disputes between members and censure violations of the charter. The host city is decided four years in advance, giving it time to expand its inns and profit from the occasion. Valdermach hosts by default when no alternative can be agreed, and so accounts for roughly half of all sessions. The voting blocs are best described in the negative. The cities vote together on river tolls and divide on everything else. The prince-bishops form a coherent bloc on ecclesiastical questions and are largely ineffective on trade and war. The hereditary nobles distrust one another and the councilmembers of merchant origin. Certain margravates have feuded long enough that their representatives sit on opposite sides of the hall by tradition. Since the invention of the Rosantic printing press, the Diet’s proceedings have been published and distributed to every city. They are written to conceal the most sensitive matters, but they will still serve Your Grace as an account of how the League works.

113.title: Of the Convocation Schism and How It Pertains to Political Reality
113.content: The League originally had a single Convocation, established by the Diet. It may be likened to the Haugris Church: one institution of immense political weight, formerly in command of all theological matters. It has since split over the canonization of the Ascended. The Old Rites Convocation maintains the established process. The Reformers hold that the process is corrupt and open to political manipulation. The schism is five decades old, and its consequences continue to make work for the Diet. Neither Convocation holds a seat in the Diet, but each controls a voting bloc. Formal canonization under the Old Rites is slow, expensive, and runs through hierarchies that have made saints of the powerful. Popular acclamation under the Reformers ratifies what the pilgrims have already decided: a figure dies, miracles occur at the grave, shrines accumulate, and the Convocation confirms. The military orders hold a third position, that soldiers dying in sufficient extremity of faith and deed Ascend without waiting for tribunals, and that the orders may conduct their own verification. When either Convocation protests, the usual reply is that the Convocations are welcome to visit the sites of battle and bloody their own hands for once. This produces recurring situations in which one faction will not recognize another’s Ascended, to be resolved either by a sufficiently unambiguous miracle or, more commonly, by political manoeuvre. Much of the League’s near future is populated with crises that are theological in name and, in substance, concern inheritance, the ownership of land and military authority.

114.title: Of Rosantic Magic
114.content: Rosantic magic is not a system in the sense of the Taprobane tradition. It is a collection of practices resting upon broadly similar principles, whose methods vary greatly. The grimoire tradition sits at the top of the social register. Grimoires are potent books of magic, and sometimes decks of cards, a fashion that began with mercenaries and became popular in the streets. The workings of magic in the grimoires are often attributed to the Ascended. Supposedly each working functions as a contract that pulls for as aspect of an Ascended power; for this reason the most powerful spells, books and cards are jealously hunted and gathered. Their effects follow established patterns closely enough that we can account for what they do, if not always how. Their practitioners are called magisters, or mages, and the most powerful are Archmages, roughly akin to our Grandmasters. The League has adopted the Singhapura term Paragon for magicians of supreme power, though it is often applied to those expected to be canonized in due course. Alchemy, imported from Lusia, enjoys far greater prominence here than at home. Serious practitioners keep workshops that are at once laboratory, library and chapel. The noted alchemists of the day are overwhelmingly of noble houses, since the equipment is not cheap, but their potions, unguents and balms are so effective that remedies for flesh wounds are common fare in the cities. The term magister applies here too; there have been at least seven Grand Alchemists of note. Many talented Lusians of little national devotion migrate to the League, where their skills are better appreciated. The most consequential development is the printing press, a machine by which many words and letters are stamped upon rolls of paper. The Rosantic presses have made grimoires so widely available that the nobility carries them as a matter of fashion, and the richest change from one to another according to the day of the week and their fancy. The result is a well-fed population with significant magical capability and comparatively little training. Guild transmission is the least visible form. Knowledge passes from master to apprentice across generations, and with the knowledge passes a relationship with the guild’s patron Ascended, without which the guild’s secret capabilities appear not to function fully. Brenmark’s blades hold an edge beyond what their steel warrants and have resisted every attempt to copy them; Singhapura’s answer has been to approximate the edge with Ealdorfold steel. Orvaine’s bookbinders produce manuscripts that cannot be burned or soaked, and Valdermach’s coin stamps cannot be forged. The last tradition is what they call Carnival. For three days the Rosantics believe the barrier between the living and the Ascended grows thin. Treaties reached during Carnival are held sacred, and an agreement made then outranks any other vow.

115.title: Of the League’s Military Capacity, and of Other Matters
115.content: The League has no standing army. It has the Roses Levy, activated by the Diet, and it has the Free Companies. The Levy has every problem associated with conscripting citizens: unwillingness, poor training and poor equipment, save among the nobles and their retainers. The Free Companies are standing troops. They have much in common with the Lusian Condottieri: they are expensive, reliable within their contracted terms, and famous throughout the known world for extravagance in taste and dress. Each company bears a relationship to a patron Ascended, and inscribes its heraldry upon banners and uniforms. This is observed with complete seriousness in the field. Many of the men are second sons of nobles, or nobles fallen from favour, with the occasional young zealot on pilgrimage among them, and they will fight over an insult to their saint. The siege engineering of the Free Companies is without peer in the known world. It sits at the meeting of alchemy, magic and soldiering, and the border wars with Lusia have given it fertile ground. Lusia has tried for decades to produce engineers of equal quality without success, and Singhapura prefers to dominate by strength of magic. On the larger question of how the full Rosantic force would fare against Singhapura, I will say only that Singhapura’s armies are larger and would likely prevail in a direct engagement, but that many Rosantic capabilities remain hidden in ways that make this a dangerous calculation. The Free Companies and their descendants, the Paladins among them, first entered the Empire during the Second Ebbing, and it was their example that spurred Singhapura to raise its own specialist Chapters. More practically, the League alternates between feuds and alliances with Lusia and Ealdorfold, so that an invasion of any of the three risks a war the Empire cannot afford. The present policy is trade, and selective hiring as circumstances require. I close with an observation about the court masque. The Rosantics practise a highly allusive form of theatre that conveys political meaning through allegory. A performance may unfold its meaning over months, and full understanding is difficult without intimate familiarity with Rosantic high culture. There is a Singhapura novel depicting one such masque that carried a different meaning for each of the nobles who saw it, goading three to anger and one to outright war, exactly as its commissioner intended; the meanings, and the motives behind them, were fully deciphered only upon the participants’ deathbeds. Rosantic diplomats have been known to cite this work in actual correspondence. Either Singhapura’s novelists are very good, or Rosantic diplomacy is very strange.

116.title: Of What This Means for Daub
116.content: The League offers Your Grace two things the Empire cannot easily replace, and brings two dangers with them. I set them out in that order. 1) Soldiers. If Your Grace requires additional military capacity, Singhapura is not the only source, and the Free Companies allow a degree of independent action. I would advise Your Grace to hire them only for defined tasks with defined ends, since they come bearing their own faiths and quarrels and are not easily dissuaded from either. 2) Magic. The same presses that make grimoires a fashion in Valdermach make them easy to acquire and study in Daub. I urge Your Grace to support the LTU in reverse-engineering Rosantic magic. It is the one magical tradition within reach of Daub that Taprobane does not already own. Now the dangers. Your Grace must keep the Rosantic calendar and know when Carnival falls, because at least two mercenary orders now operating in Daub have named Carnival provisions that compel them to disregard certain oaths and orders. An agreement Your Grace makes with a Rosantic during those three days will outrank every other promise he has made, including to you. And I would invest, before the next Diet cycle, in a reliable translator of court masques. A performance staged in Valdermach may be an insult to Daub, or an offer, and Your Grace should not learn which from the consequences.

117.title: Further Reading
117.content: The Annales Historici, compiled by the Dvorak Elves, is the most comprehensive external source on the League. The Orvaine editions are far easier to obtain than the real thing, but those who have compared them say that whole passages have been quietly excised. Seek the unexpurgated editions. Halverson’s Trades and Their Shadows treats the guild secrets and their commercial implications with more precision than any other source I know.
