The Brenmark Goldsmiths’ Hall purchased the entire print run upon publication. The Taprobane Library holds copies; I know of none in the North. Mountefort’s Flower of Battle is a treatise on the provisioning and conduct of armies. Mountefort had to persuade everyone from commander to sergeant, so he wrote for a wide audience, and the result is an easily digested list of commonsense situations that apply to a great variety of armies. Its name and its central thesis both come from his conviction that disease and bad supplies kill far more soldiers than the enemy does. The Canonization of Irmgard is a legal drama, fictionally framed but closely based upon a disputed canonization of some three decades ago. A washerwoman’s reported miracles became the occasion for a proxy war between three noble houses, which drew in the Convocations, which in turn drew in the Diet. The author disguised the names with less effort than she perhaps intended. It shows how a dispute, however minor, may send ripples far beyond the control of any participant. The Carnival Concordat is, strictly speaking, a legal document, and the original is held in the Diet archive at Valdermach. It is a body of cases in which Carnival agreements, having superseded other oaths, led to League-wide affairs, and the commentary upon it now runs to several volumes. Read it before relying upon a Rosantic oath. Seven Seasons at Orvaine is anonymous, and has been attributed variously to a disgraced noble and to several faculty members. It covers seven years of court masques at Orvaine, explaining each in retrospect, with the full context of what each faction understood itself to be watching. Some editions claim it was composed as a reply to The Lion Emperor’s Courtesan, to explain the tropes and mechanics of the masque, perhaps in some discomfort that the leading account of the form had been written by outsiders. Staanbyrig is set in Ealdorfold, but its plot turns upon a forged contract processed through Valdermach. It contains an intricate account of a Diet session, especially revealing when set beside the official record of that session and the events that followed. The Lion Emperor’s Courtesan is set in Singhapura, but it contains the Rosantic court masque of which I wrote above, in which one performance carries four distinct meanings for four distinct factions, and the misunderstandings lead to a great many funerals. It is said to be an accurate account of Rosantic political communication, so much so that Rosantic diplomatic correspondence has referred to the scene.

119.title: Samarskand and the Ancient World
119.content: Singhapura makes no sense without Samarskand, Your Grace, so we have to go back a long way. I warn you now that the ancient world will leave you with more questions than answers. On the question of origins: the traditions disagree, and they do it with great variety and enthusiasm. Some hold that the world hatched from a cosmic egg. Others that a divine cow, afflicted with some celestial disorder of the stomach, heaved out the sun, the moon, the stars, the land, the oceans, the animals, and presumably other cows as well, which raises questions about the recursive possibilities inherent to cows. There is a tradition involving a one-eyed giant who lacked the depth perception to navigate a cosmic staircase, and from whose shattered bones and teeth we are mostly descended, though there are numerous competing theories about the pelvis. There is a drunken goddess of pottery who produced too many prototypes. The modern position is that nobody knows. Your Grace need not resolve this question, and would be ill-advised to try; the factions that have staked their authority on their favourite answer barely tolerate each other as it is, and I doubt they would welcome Daub’s opinion on divine cows. The Haugris Church calls such questions obstruments - tools, thoughts, or tasks that actively subtract value from a situation.

120.title: Of the Yakshas and the Naagas
120.content: The stories agree on a time before the age of human kingdoms, when the world was ordered by the Yakshas and the Naagas. To the Yakshas were given the high places - the mountains, the tops of great forests, the skies. To the Naagas were given the rivers, the lakes and seas, the jungles, the deep places of the world. This is the subject of much of the Samarskand Commentaries. We must think of Yakshas and Naagas as persons, though not necessarily in human form. Consider, as my old professor was fond of saying, a god of a small river. What shape would it want to take? What would it want? . Indeed, these beings may still exist. In the modern day, there is a category of daemon known as the Yaksha, able to leave their domain and traverse our world at will. There is the NAAGA division of the daemon realm, whose job is punishing the most egregious violations of magical principles. It is said Yakshas were ruled, in that time, by Raavan.

121.title: Of Raavan and the Origins of Magic
121.content: The official account is preserved in both the Samarskand Commentaries and The Assembly of Gold and Saffron. It holds that Raavan was a Yaksha philosopher-king of immense power, ten-headed, capable of splitting reality itself and summoning the fire of the sun onto his enemies. The Naagas are said to have been his equals in power if not in ambition. Some sources hold that they maintained the balance of the world, sharing wisdom and withdrawing it as they deemed necessary. Then there were the beasts, from which we are descended - it is said that Raavan took two monkeys and made of them men and women, and sent them forth to multiply and civilize the world. Upon his death, he gave to the world his essence - the Will of Raavan - and thus humans gained some small measure of his power as a reward. One may debate whether civilization was an improvement. After all, the monkey pays no taxes and answers to no law. Nevertheless. The Book of Lost Kingdoms puts forth a different origin: it states plainly that Raavan was not a yaksha but a human being, the first and greatest of magicians, part god and part man. To temper his arrogance, certain gods created Umesh, a wild man who became Raavan’s beloved companion. Together they slew the Yakshas, banished the Naagas, founded cities, and defied the gods, whereupon the gods, having arranged the situation to their satisfaction, killed Umesh. Broken by grief and terrified of his own mortality, Raavan traveled to the ends of the earth in search of eternal life. He failed to find it, but in the searching, he systematized the study of magic, which he passed in its entirety to his citizens before his death. The Reflections of the Moon in Still Water claims that from Raavan’s bones came the dragons and from his tears we rose, though it is widely agreed that the writer was far too fond of analogy. My own view is that both accounts have some truth in them, but the Raavan of the Lost Kingdoms seems to me more plausible than Raavan as a daemon king. The underlying observation - that Raavan’s death distributed magic - is the same in all three texts, so I shall take that as my starting point and try a more modern reading. Perhaps some great magician died; perhaps that magic uplifted what already existed: from the apes and the monkeys rose the humans; from the lizards rose the dragons; the beasts of the wild grew stronger and wiser, or were turned into exceptional curries.

122.title: Of Samarskand Itself
122.content: From this point we return to the Commentaries. Humans progressed rapidly after Raavan’s death; fledgling city-states flourished, though I hasten to add that we would hardly recognize them as towns today. Something drove people to band together, most likely rampaging Yakshas with nobody left to keep them in line. The Mahason Chronicle tells the tale of the Yaksha Mahasona - the name translates broadly as mass grave - and his rise to power over the leaderless yakshas; it is presented as pure fantasy, but it fills the gaps so neatly that I have my doubts. That is how Samarskand began. Other kingdoms - Kishar, Magan, Samis-A-laa - appear in references, but we know of them only because people in Samarskand wrote about them. Samarskand was founded with three relics of Raavan: a tooth, an eye, the index finger of the left hand. The Haugris Church claims those same relics as the Divine Corpus from which it draws authority; Raavan’s remains, it seems, keep very well. These relics are said to have given the early queens of Samarskand some portion of Raavan’s abilities, or at least magnified their existing power, such that they could seal away the Yakshas and Naagas and restore peace to the world. Having saved everyone, Samarskand spread from a city-state into a proud kingdom extending the full length of the Diamond River. The Commentaries record many monuments and the willing surrender of many awed peoples, spreading south to north, east to west. Two things Samarskand left behind are still with us, and they matter far more than its relics or monuments. The first is the formalization of magic. Until Samarskand, magicians, as far as we can tell, were born with their power, and there were very few of them. It was the mages of Samarskand who attempted a formal description of possible magics: a thesaurus, first, of what could be done, and then a proper symbology in which the description itself became the magic it described. This is what the Taprobane System descends from; this is what allowed Samarskand to field extraordinary numbers of magicians and to imbue its armies and infrastructure with dread magics. Ancient Lusian generals wrote of fighting Samarskand as a folly comparable to fighting Raavan himself. The second is law. Until Samarskand, most places functioned according to the will of whoever held power. There were kings and queens and princes and tyrants and councils, but it was Samarskand that sat down and wrote a code that would bind everyone from the highest to the lowest. That code is how Singhapura swallows its neighbours. It is also why an idle noble cannot simply help himself to Your Grace’s lands, and why we can trade across great distances and expect someone to put things right when they go wrong. The Book of Lost Kingdoms is relevant here too. Raavan as human magician-king - who built a library, systematized knowledge, and spent his final years in the service of his people - looks very much like the father of both. He could not save his friend, so he saved everything he knew; he could not live forever, so he made certain his work would. Singhapura does not tell that story about itself. I think its schools and its courts would recognize it anyway. The Samarskand system of writing remains in use for administration, poetry, and magic; the Samarskand system of laws, much revised and made complex over the years, governs all affairs the Empire touches; the Samarskand inheritance of Raavan’s power is formally accepted each time the Haugris Church bells toll for the Singha Adiraj. That is how Singhapura claims the right to rule, and it repeats the claim every time the bells ring.

123.title: Of Samarskand’s End
123.content: Samarskand did not last. It stood in the shadow of a mountain - Samar’s Kand, Samar’s Mountain - of which no trace remains today. Accounts from Lusia and Tangowan record a great flood that shattered the mountain, destroyed the city, and swept everything away, and with it the allied state of Taprobane. The mouth of the Diamond River is most likely the exact site; centuries of excavation have recovered what could only have been the ruins of that great empire. The damage was so great that the rebuilding fell to Samarskand’s outer provinces, and that project drained them over generations until the world entered a dark age of infighting and petty warlords. The grass grew over their graves, as we say. Much of what survives can be found at the Taprobane Magisterium museum and the Hall of Ancient Arts. Go and see it if Your Grace is ever in the city. Most of what the Empire is started there.

124.title: The Seven Great Classics
124.content: There are books that every person of consequence claims to have read, and very few have. The Seven Great Classics are those books. Your Grace will be glad of them on the day she sits across a table from a Singhapura envoy. I do not pretend they are exciting. I do say that you are at a disadvantage without them. The Samarskand Commentaries were first carved in stone. They hold everything Singhapura wishes it still were: ancient Samarskand, with its universal law, its justice and its terrible magic. Every family of standing wants a copy, and not, for the most part, out of love for ancient history. The Commentaries are also full of advice on how to live, for people of every rank, and they are treated as the final word. Book of X, Chapter Y, pronounced with sufficient gravity, will silence most rooms. More than one senior clerk or lord has been won over in exactly that way. The Singha Chronicle is propaganda paid for by the state, and everyone who uses it knows as much. It gives a carefully groomed account of Singhapura’s history, written to the satisfaction of the palace. It is also the official register of approved crests and sigils. In any dispute over lineage, precedent or the legitimacy of a claim, it is the Singha Chronicle that is fetched, and what it says settles the matter. I have written up the history in my own words, so that Your Grace need not wade through the fictions. You must, however, be able to recognize nobles, and know what they do and where they rank. The Himakatu Chronicle covers what the Singha Chronicle hurries past. It is a tragedy in the full sense, full of glory, pride and blood, and it shows the Empire at its worst. It may also explain the shame the Empire still feels when it looks upon the ruins of Wattle. Because it fills the gaps the Singha Chronicle smoothed over, playwrights and politicians quote it constantly, and mothers use it to frighten children. Read it to learn what Singhapura’s rulers fear. A people’s tragedies will tell you more of them than their virtues. The Assembly of Gold and Saffron is kept by the Haugris Church. Your Grace will not enjoy it, and need not. But to know it is to be able to converse with, and to persuade, the people who run one of the greatest powers within your own borders. In the same manner I recommend the Reflections of the Moon in Still Water, attributed to the Nameless Sage of the Temple of Eighteen. Produce a passage at the right moment and you will be taken for one of the Temple’s own, whether you are or not; and the Temple’s own will not hurry to correct the impression. The Ithihaasa Potha is a cycle of epic poems composed by seventeen philosopher-poets who had been exiled from Singhapura. It treats the past and then foretells Singhapura’s future, in extraordinarily complicated verse. It is the only work of prophecy known to have proven accurate every time, though always in the most indirect and perverse manner possible. I recommend it so that Your Grace may know what a great many people in Singhapura believe is coming. Even if they are wrong, it helps to know what your betters are dreaming of when you plan your own course. The Annales Historici, kept by the Dvorak Elves of Lusia, is a history and geography of the known world. It covers languages, peoples, economies, governments and trade from the western sea to the eastern limit of what can be verified. Merchants and princes pay well for fine editions. Of everything on this list, it is the one whose usefulness requires no explanation. Your Grace will have observed that most of these books matter less for what is in them than for what others believe is in them, or must pretend to believe. I do not set them down out of vanity. Learning carries great weight in Singhapura, and therefore in everything Singhapura rules, and the Empire does not call everyone beyond its borders a barbarian by accident. Know these seven, and nobody at that table will be able to call you one.

125.title: Of Singhapura, the Great Empire
125.content: The poet Additya Wickrama was a man of great gifts and greater debts, and he settled the debts by dying. He once wrote that there are two kinds of people: those who belong to Singhapura, and those who will. He owed me six hundred and thirty-eight Owls at the time, which colours my fondness for the line; but I have travelled widely since, and I have yet to find a reason to disagree with him. Singhapura is the greatest unbroken Empire in the known world, and the largest power of our age in politics, in money and in war. Nobody builds better roads, runs better schools, does more with magic or manufactures more goods. It stretches from the Diamond River Delta across the Balalpura Plains, one of the world’s great breadbaskets, to the Raavanskandha Mountains, said to be the bones of the dead god Raavan. From there it climbs into the mountain strongholds of Udanuwara and Giridhora, past the Hooniyang Pass, and from there it controls Wattle and Daub. To the south it holds the whole coastline, and the thousand islands of Tangowan are its vassal. Everything Your Grace does must take Singhapura into account. Fortunately I spent the greater part of my life there and know it well. Let me therefore guide you through it at some length.

126.title: Of the City, Which Is Also the Empire
126.content: To understand the Empire, one must first understand Singhapura the city, which is its heart. It was founded at the Diamond River delta and later moved, piece by piece, and rebuilt beneath the Raavanskandha mountains. All roads lead to Singhapura, or so it is said, and I have not found one that does not. Take any road from any corner of the Empire and follow the lion statues. Follow, too, the Diamond River, where the monsoon waters run so wide that one cannot see the far bank. At its end lie the Balalpura Plains: a sea of green, cut through with great moats that shine crimson, as if they had been watered with blood. This is the Rathmada Samudra, more than five thousand hectares of reservoirs, red with the algae that Taprobane cultivates to feed and water the land. Beyond it, at the foot of the Raavanskandha, stands the city itself, fronted by great bridges. From those bridges Your Grace will see crowds and houses and buildings long before the walls. The walls rise higher and higher toward the centre, until at the very apex stand the great towers. Singhapura holds more souls than Valdermach, and Valdermach is the largest city in the west. Inside the walls it is all glass and metal and spires, with the hum of the waterworks and the arcane machinery everywhere, and roads that cost more than diamonds. The city is arranged in rings that stand for the order of the heavens. At the centre is Adhiraj House, built by the Lusian architect Andretto d’Orenzo together with Taprobane’s finest mages. It holds the Adhiraj’s quarters and all the essential offices of government, and its towers are the ones visible from the bridges. Below it lie the Botanical Gardens, which hold a specimen of every plant from every place the Empire can reach, trade with or rule. The rings below hold the sprawling Taprobane Imperial University, the greatest university in the world, where magic was remade and is still being remade. The Red and White Councils of the Haugris Church have their offices there also, with all their attendants. At the very bottom, beside the great roads, the merchants unload their cargo onto vast rune-driven conveyors. They come from Tangowan, from Wattle, from Lusia, from the Rosantic League, and from lands further still. The waterworks alone are something most states could not conceive of building, let alone in mountain country. Should Your Grace see what appear to be great stone roots laid over the city like a hand, that is the Mahabag Subha. Its canals, some below ground and some above, join the public reservoirs across the whole city, and some run hundreds of miles to supply entire towns. The Sunken Church sits behind the city and above it, cut into the foothills of the Raavanskandha. The Haugris Church keeps the Divine Corpus there, which it holds to be the preserved body of Raavan himself. It is a holy place, and a steady grey stream of pilgrims climbs to it from the city. East of the city, out on the plain, are the Ruins of Vidyaakara, restored by the Temple of Eighteen. They are said to be among the oldest remains of ancient Samarskand: stupas, a university and monasteries, with sealed sections nobody has yet explored. The whole site is about as large as Daub. The Empire keeps a city of that size standing empty purely out of regard for the past. There are satellite cities also, as large as the capital if not as storied: Nagenapura to the east, Basnapura to the west and Ruhunapura to the south, the last of them built upon the Empire’s original site. Between them lie a thousand towns and lesser concerns, all the way up to Udanuwara and Giridhora, which guard the road north. Somewhere in the middle is Manikwila, the only natural lake in the Empire. Every other lake in Singhapura was dug by a king with nothing better to do. Your Grace will not deal with these cities directly. As Duchess of Daub you technically outrank most of the governors and provincial nobles you will meet on the road south, and I would urge caution there. Whatever you say to them will be met with smiles and hospitality and nothing more, and reported to Singhapura before you have left. Nor will anyone say anything of consequence unless the capital has told them they may.

127.title: Of How the Empire Is Actually Governed
127.content: Political theorists (Weerasingha and his student Molligoda among them, the latter of whom I shall spare Your Grace) have long tried to sort empires into kinds, as Taprobane sorts magicians. By their scheme one may call Singhapura a divine-right absolute unitary state and be correct. One may also call it an aristocratic legal feudal state with federal characteristics and be equally correct. This is what happens when theory meets a real country. From Daub, the Empire looks like a single solid block. That is the face it shows to everyone on its edges. Let us begin with the nobility, Your Grace, which works differently from anywhere else. Elsewhere a title generally comes with land and the people upon it. In Singhapura one may live in a mud hut or a city tenement and still be ennobled, for great scholarship, great art or some brave deed in the service of the state. Various Adhirajs have bestowed land, but these days an ennoblement usually comes with a yearly payment sized to the deed. Grandmasters and Paragons of the Taprobane Imperial University receive the privileges of nobility with their rank. Land now belongs to the state, and to the state alone. A badly run estate may be given to another, broken up, or taken for public works. This has been so since Makaraasoka melted the fortunes of the noble houses into roads and libraries and consecrated the results in their names; the houses have been poorer and more respectable ever since. There are fixed rules about crests and customs, about forms of address, and even about weapons. Unless the Adhiraj grants otherwise, a member of a noble family may carry only one kasthane, a curved blade worn as a sign of rank. It is often richly worked with lions and sometimes with gems, but the blade itself is kept short, so that it hangs no lower than the hem of a coat. Titles do pass down in families, but the Adhiraj, the Church or a noble’s own peers may strip them. A commoner from a distant province may win a crest with the right patrons and the right deeds to his name. The Adhiraj appoints the officials, and they answer to him: a Justice of the Peace, and Low and High Courts, in every territory. These officials are nobles, but their power comes from the appointment, not from their birth. Thus the nobles of Singhapura are not where the real power lies, however rich some of them may appear. It is best to think of them as merchants and officers with titles, families the Empire places wherever they are useful. The true summit of the Empire is four powers: the Singha Adhiraj, the Haugris Church, the Taprobane University and the Guilds. They bargain with one another without end. None can do without the others, and each restrains the others while seeking advantage over them. The Adhiraj is the Highest of the High: First Prophet of the Haugris Church, Judge and Arbiter Above All, and High Commander of every army. His word is law, and in theory he controls every aspect of the Empire. In practice others wield most of that authority day to day, while the Adhiraj makes the laws, directs the grandest strategy and public works, and reserves his full power for the moments that require it. The throne does not pass from father to son. The Adhiraj selects a successor from among the nobility and adopts him as heir. In theory anyone of sufficient skill may be chosen. In practice it is commonly one of the Ministers of the Interior, Trade or Justice, so the succession is never settled and always political. The Haugris Church manages the Empire’s messages and controls much of its money, its schools and its medicine. It is governed by a Red Council and a White Council. The White Council decides internal policy and the great judgments; the Red handles regional appointments and logistics. Beneath the Councils are three Sequences that do the Church’s work, and a fourth that is not discussed in polite company. The Sequence of Letters runs the post, and beneath that function it runs the most sophisticated intelligence service ever built. The Sequence of Discourse trains the officials who staff the Church’s offices. The Sequence of Acts is the face the public sees: priests, healers, diplomats and explorers. The fourth is the Samanera Corps, which the Church raised in its day as an answer to orders such as the Paladins, and which is a great deal more violent and more capable. In most of the outlying territories, Your Grace’s included, these four Sequences are what the Empire looks like. On paper the Taprobane University stands outside politics. In fact the people who devise and control the most powerful magic in the world are involved in every part of Singhapura’s growth, and the Taprobane system, which is modern Ritualism, gives the Empire its decisive advantage in everything it does. The University trains lawyers, judges and engineers as well as magicians, so its influence reaches from the architects of the wealthy to the smallest country court. Taprobane calls its rivalry with the Lesser Theoretical University of Daub a friendly one. To Taprobane it is a game against a smaller opponent on the same side. Last are the Guilds. It should surprise nobody that those who make the Empire’s goods have a great deal of say in it. I would not underestimate them; it is well said that the Military Orders are the Adhiraj’s sword and the Guilds are his arrows. The Guilds hold no legal authority over anyone but their own members, and in practice they have a hand in everything. The greatest by far is the Singhapura Merchants Guild, which is trading house and bank with private armies and fleets attached. The Empire’s ideals are the backbone of the whole operation: one law for all, the Taprobane system, free schooling, a single administration, open examination for almost every post, and heavy investment in new invention. What actually holds it together is simpler. All four powers have concluded that this arrangement suits them better than any alternative on offer, and that together they are stronger than any of them would be alone.

128.title: Of the Empire’s Tensions and Opportunities Therein
128.content: Nothing so large runs without strain, and I would be failing Your Grace if I listed Singhapura’s strengths and left out the cracks. The first is steel. The Empire needs good steel for building, for its armies and for nearly everything else. Centuries of mining have exhausted the easy ore of Udanuwara, and the Empire is pushing north again after it. This is why the trade through Wattle and Daub matters so much more now than it did a generation ago. Whoever controls the northern trade roads has a hold upon the Empire, and has also put a noose about his own neck. More than anything else, this is why Singhapura wants Wattle. The second is religion. The Haugris Church is on top, but the Temple of Eighteen remains strong in the eastern provinces, and the Iron Pagoda grows in the southwest. Taprobane chafes more and more at the Church’s say over how magic is regulated. I suspect the Singha Adhiraj holds all of these in careful balance so that none grows too strong. Daub has both the Church and the Temple within its walls, and what Your Grace manages as a local matter is a small piece of a much larger war between the faiths and the scholars. The third is the frontier. Wattle and Daub lie to the north, with the Waste beyond them. Tangowan lies to the south. Lusia and the Rosantic League lie to the west, and the border cities carry many Tears, left by magic used to excess. Any sensible empire watches its borders. Here that means the Military Orders, and they cost a fortune, and the cost climbs as metal grows scarce.

129.title: Of the Governance of Daub, and What It Means to Stand in the Shadow of the Empire
129.content: Which brings us to Daub. Your Grace rules a city and province too well placed for the Empire to ignore. Even so, if I may make so bold, the arrangement Daub enjoys (tribute, polite deference and the occasional imperial errand) is a far softer noose than I would expect, especially while Wattle is drawn so much tighter. The Adhiraj may be content to let Daub grow as a vassal. He may also be letting the fruit ripen before he picks it. My own belief is that the Empire, and its Guilds above all, want trade with the lands beyond, the Obsidian Empire for one, and that having watched Lusia they have seen what a free port in the north could do for them. Thus: what should Your Grace do about it? . First, I would advise Your Grace to know exactly what passes through Daub and what the Empire would pay for it elsewhere. The steel and ore of the North are the Empire’s present anxiety, and a ruler who knows the value of what she holds can name a price. One who does not will be told one. Second, I urge Your Grace to keep the Military Orders in mind whenever the Charter Knights, the Paladins or the mercenaries in Daub’s pay are discussed. Those Orders have trained for war against the North; that is their present orientation and capability. Nothing in Daub should look, from Singhapura, like preparation to meet them. Third, the Church and the Temple are in a quiet and tense dialogue across Daub’s wards and provinces, and the Merchants Guild will trade and intermingle whether or not it is invited. Your Grace must keep all three in the same balance the Adhiraj keeps, favouring none in public, because the Empire’s own arrangement rests upon that balance and it will not welcome a vassal who upsets it. I shall not advise Your Grace on how to deal with the Adhiraj directly. I will say only this: for all its polish and power, the Empire was built by human hands, is kept running by human institutions, and is moved by the same tides as any other large human enterprise. It shows one face to the people on its edges. Daub is close enough to see behind that face. What Your Grace takes from it for Daub is for Your Grace to decide.

130.title: Further Reading
130.content: Singhapura produces, in abundance, the means by which it prefers to be understood, and Your Grace will find the pattern familiar. Many states do this, but Singhapura is more thorough about it than most. Every major ward and province has its own censor, who inspects material before publication, down to plays and novels. The same Additya Wickrama I mentioned earlier was fond of saying that the most dangerous thing anyone can do is to believe the Empire’s account of itself. My own writing here is protected partly by censorial precedent (everything in it is already on some public record) and partly because that law does not reach Daub and the other outlying provinces. Even so, if this book is ever to be read in Singhapura, either Taprobane must grant it special accord and keep it for internal use, or it must be edited to suit the censors. With that stated, Your Grace, let me recommend that you read two works: . The Singha Chronicle is the official account of the founding and growth of the Singhapura Empire. Your Grace will learn a great deal from it about how the Empire wishes to be seen. It also holds the most complete register of approved crests and sigils, and for that reason alone it is indispensable in any dispute over lineage or the legitimacy of a claim. I have compressed the histories into a more readable account in another chapter. The Himakatu Chronicle covers the affairs of the North that the Singha Chronicle prefers to pass over quickly. It concerns the building of Himakatupura and the failures of Empress Kudakaali II that led to the daemon breakthrough, and in the end to the Great Northern Waste. It is a tragedy in every sense, full of glory, hubris and violence. It is the Empire at its worst, and it may explain the shame the Empire still sees lingering in the ruins of Wattle.

132.title: Of Tangowan
132.content: Tangowan lies far to the south, and its commerce reaches Daub only at several removes. I include it not because Your Grace will have much occasion to deal with it directly, but because it is the clearest demonstration available of what Singhapura may do to a place unchecked. Wattle and Daub are partial incorporations, where the Empire’s hand is shown rather than closed. Tangowan, with no armies and no great industry, is the fullest expression of the Empire’s power.

133.title: Of What Tangowan Is and Was
133.content: Tangowan is an archipelago, and a vast one: thousands of islands, dense jungle, volcanic mountains and monsoons, spread across a territory almost as large as the entire North. Its natural wealth is extraordinary. Daub must labour for its crops and Singhapura must engineer its water, but Tangowan simply produces: rarewoods, fisheries, spices, wild game. It is said that one may assemble a decent meal by strolling about in the morning. The sea yields to its fishermen and divers with a generosity that has no equal in the known world. The people of Tangowan named their lands the Sagarika Mandalam, which renders approximately as “the Realm of the Ocean”. We call them Tangowan, owing to a translation error made by the diplomat Vanarkali in the seventh century. The world knows them by the second name. Nobody in Singhapura has ever troubled to correct it. Before Singhapura, governance rested with a council of nineteen governors called the Paridarakas, selected by lot, each holding a major island or a cluster of smaller ones. Periodically, it is said, a Paridaraka would call for a Maha Sabha, a great gathering, to resolve some matter of consequence. Outside the Sabha, each administered his domain as an independent body with its own customs. Laws were not written down. Custom arose from need and circumstance, and disputes were resolved by the community, and especially by its elders. In this we see no great sophistication, Your Grace, but the mechanisms by which a family governs itself. The failure of such a system before Singhapura is most instructive. The Paridarakas held authority over small lots, but none had the capacity to set forth a common purpose, or to arm all of Tangowan under pressure. In times of peace and plenty ordinary people may pool and share what they have. War requires a grim purpose and an authority that cannot be swayed by the winds of opinion and fear. When Singhapura arrived there was no single throat to cut; there were nineteen fragments, each with its own interests. Even where a ruler opposed Singhapura, some great part of his community could be swayed, and the Paridarakas who resisted were in time cast aside by their own people. The economy compounded this. Tangowan is known for its kula, family clans of artisans whose techniques pass down the generations. Their craft is intricate and remarkable; even today Tangowan produces some of the finest carvings and most elaborate seaworthy vessels in the world. But the clans kept to themselves, and to one born outside the right families there was little to do. Talented young people with an aptitude for engineering or large-scale organization drifted toward Singhapura. From this, and from the flight of the alchemists of Lusia, one may draw a general lesson: talent in a poorly organized place always drifts toward wherever organization exists.

134.title: Of the Singhapura Merchants Guild And Its Acts
134.content: Here I ask for Your Grace’s particular attention, because this is where Tangowan’s incorporation bears most closely upon Daub. The lord who enters a territory with an army has announced his intentions and provoked resistance. The merchant who arrives with goods and services that the existing institutions cannot provide is greeted with benevolence, and even love, until the day he is indispensable. So it was with the Singhapura Merchants Guild. At first they came for crafts. Then, having persuaded others of the profits of such trade, the Guild moved by degrees into everything outside the protected traditional crafts. Singhapura metals and jewellery and silks became items of great value. Tangowan had no immediate need of grain, but the Merchants sold it cheaply regardless, together with such spices and tea as are ruinously expensive to grow except upon very large estates. These actions decimated what little farming Tangowan had. It was more profitable for a man to spend a few hours idly whittling, and trade a small carving for a sack of rice, than to spend days labouring over his crops. Having thus enticed the populace, the Merchants set about acquiring land. There are records of Tangowan governors handing over vast acreages for a pittance: a hundred swords here, the furnishings of a mansion there. Without an economy, or an authority that understood one, the value of land went wholly unrealized. Upon these lands the Guild planted tea, pepper, cloves, nutmeg, saffron, fruit, cotton and whatever else Singhapura required, and much of Tangowan embraced it with enthusiasm. There was nothing in place to resist. The kula had no means of operating at scale. The rulers had no banks and no organized trade beyond their individual arrangements. When the Guild arrived with credit, supply chains and the capacity to turn Tangowan’s natural wealth into reliable exportable income, it was seen as a great opportunity. Soon the Guild held dominion over large tracts of Tangowan. The rulers who accommodated it earliest did best in the short term; that this was also the mechanism of their demise became clear only afterward. It remained only for the Adhiraj to issue one command, and all of Tangowan, having already surrendered its livelihood, fell to its knees. This is not a novel pattern. The history of Singhapura is full of kingdoms new and old that fell in this manner: Ratnapura, Ridheepura, Balalpura, Udanuwara, Giridhora. The Singha Chronicle records these entries proudly, and takes great care to mention that they profited from the arrangement. But of Ratnapura and many others, Your Grace, only the names remain. There are no great histories of their works, save a few scattered legends and minor works of poetry and theatre. One day the name Sagarika Mandalam, too, will be a footnote of that kind, reserved for entertainments and little else.

135.title: Of the Church’s Intrusions
135.content: The Haugris Church is now building schools and hospitals across Tangowan. I wish to dwell upon this. Schools and hospitals are commonly received as instruments of benevolence, and they are a great deal more. Consider what a school does, Your Grace. It takes children at the age when the world is still being explained to them. The children of the Church schools will learn the Singhapura account of history, of legitimacy, of what constitutes proper governance and proper devotion. They will not remember the Maha Sabha as a living institution. They will know it, if at all, as a thing their grandparents clung to, some primitive and naive notion rightly dispelled by the civilization of the Empire. The memory of the old order need not be suppressed. It need only be made archaic, a matter for the history-books that bore children. Thus a new order is securely established, and a people so educated, even should they rise in rebellion, can only replicate the mechanisms the Empire has given them. Hospitals work similarly. A population that receives its care from the Church has reason to think well of the Church. The care is real, and those who give it believe fully in the virtue of what they do. But gratitude is a form of loyalty, and loyalty established at that level, upon visible bodies, is remarkably lasting, especially where nothing of the kind existed before. Any new order must then face the question of how to provide a service the public now firmly believes is its due.

136.title: Of Tangowan Religion and Spirits
136.content: It is a curious feature of Tangowan that it has not wholly embraced the Church and the worship of Great Raavan. It may be said to be the only form of rebellion left to it. Tangowan worship centres upon two classes of being. The Yami are powerful and unpredictable nature spirits, inhabiting ancient trees, rivers, volcanoes and the like, and requiring appeasement through offerings and ritual. The Uso are ancestral household spirits protecting family and hearth, honoured through daily domestic practice. Most Tangowan people worship as many Yami as their circumstances require, without the exclusive affiliations that mark Temple or Church devotion. Indeed, many have adopted Raavan as one more Yami to appease, and go about their lives unbothered. Some scholars propose that this is a hybrid of deity worship and something like the Rosantic Ascended. The scholarship matters less than the fact of this one resilience, which I attribute to culture rather than to any institution. It is not resistance, exactly. It is more in the manner of the old adage: the bamboo bends with the wind, but does not break. The Empire has so far had the wisdom not to attempt a direct reorganization of it. I note that it has become fashionable among Singhapura’s nobility to holiday in Tangowan for purposes of spiritual communion. The Yami, from what the accounts suggest, do not respond well to aristocratic tourism. Nevertheless the income appears to be raising the living standards of certain groups upon the coast, in the same manner that certain villages of Daub benefit from tourists. I leave the matter there.

137.title: Of Tangowan’s Errors, Stated Plainly for Daub’s Benefit
137.content: A Duchess who wishes to learn from another’s misfortune should be able to name the errors precisely. Your Grace will naturally see more than I do. Here is my list, and after it, what I would have Your Grace do about each. 1) The structure of the Maha Sabha, and its weakness when the time came to act collectively against an outside power. Your Grace’s own council arrangements should be examined with this in mind. The question is not whether they function under ordinary conditions, but whether they would function under extraordinary pressure. 2) The export of talent. A territory that exports its most capable people is, in a real sense, financing its own death. Tangowan’s best minds became artisans, engineers and administrators in Singhapura, and were of no service to their home, and with good reason. Your Grace has a partial answer in the Lesser Theoretical University, but the LTU alone cannot make up the deficit among those in the countryside who lack any gainful employment. 3) The absence of redundancy. Every essential function in Tangowan was performed by a single family, or by whoever the ruler appointed. A system with redundancy may be called bloated; a system without it has no resilience, and shatters when any single piece is removed. This principle I take from my studies and practice of magic and Ritual. In this regard the overlapping complexity of Daub’s institutions may be an asset, provided a careful hand shapes it into something more than mere factionalism. Competing institutions drain resources; they also guard against the weakness of a single load-bearing pillar. 4) The confusion of natural wealth with strength, which contains all the others. Tangowan was rich, but riches alone are not strength. Strength is the organized capacity to defend a state. Tangowan is thus a perfect example of what not to do. Should Your Grace ever doubt, it useful to always ask yourself whether you’re repeating these mistakes. If not, there may yet be some hope.

138.title: Further Reading
138.content: For the incorporation of Tangowan under Singhapura rule, the Singha Chronicle devotes one paragraph. The Annales Historici devotes forty pages, and the scholarship of the Dvorak Elves recommends itself to us once again. Tangowan Straits is a novel of a captain’s obsession, set in the archipelago. Its account of the spirit geography, the Yami, their invocations and their jurisdictions, is perhaps the only written account of those rites. That the most reliable source on the subject is a novel is a small tragedy. It seems the truth must sometimes be buried in fiction to survive.

140.title: Of Transit and Intelligence
140.content: These are workings related to the crossing of distances in some way. Many of the most useful workings have to do with communication. Given the scope of Your Grace’s operations, I think you shall immediately see how useful these can be. Timmet’s Threshold of the World, also known as Timmet’s First . Transports the caster’s astral body or soul (the distinction is still hotly debated) to a transitional realm for formal congress with daemons. This became possible with the consent of daemons after the success of the first Sin-Eater Legion. Entry and exit are tightly governed; the Ritual will not activate unless a counterpart on the other side consents to the intrusion. It is cheap, and a great Ritual for teaching new students how to shunt costs from themselves to materials - but for most practitioners it does nothing at all: as with politics, you must know people before you can get through the door. For the select few, Timmet’s First is of remarkable value. The daemon plane is a strange and mesmerizing city, and air and water are freely available. The daemons formally observe our activities, and in some cases take a more active hand, but they only seem happy to lead people to what they call “conference rooms” (of which we believe there are millions) and let us be. We cannot remove things from the daemon world (this has been tried, and all records sealed), nor can we trade objects, but we can communicate as normal. This allows, for example, spymasters from across the entire Empire to meet and exchange information regardless of distance. Some (very) high-level political scandals have even involved romances conducted this way. Obviously such a Ritual is controlled to some degree: at the Taprobane Imperial University, only faculty are ever introduced to daemons. I suppose similar rules exist at LTU. Nothing prevents daemons from introducing themselves and abducting people. The degree of information about the daemon world that can be shared varies widely depending on what the daemons call “visa permissions” - even I cannot write more than this, or name daemons of my acquaintance, without some kind of permission. Without this the words simply vanished from my mind. This is classified as a protective magic of a degree and sophistication that Taprobane’s Cognitohazard Department has spent over fifty years and vast sums trying to break it, with very little success. Timmet’s Hall of Ten Thousand Turnings, also known as Timmet’s Second . Transports the caster to a second transitional realm between planes. Unlike the first Ritual, this one leads a series of endless hallways and rooms, each leading off from the others, containing no air and no water. It is suspected to either be an abandoned realm; enquiries with knowledgeable daemons have resulted in signs that say SITE UNDER CONSTRUCTION on the doors. There are traces of older civilisations in the form of artefacts and partial structures of unknown origin. Survival requires continuous energy expenditure. Some believe that these are remnants of the Graveyard Sutra residue from extremely large, extremely old magic, possibly from Samarskand. Others believe that this is similar to the Waste, which generates Hollows or Dungeons seemingly ad infinitum. The cost of this Ritual is continuous and very high; there is a specialised research division at Taprobane University called the Halldivers that treats this as their professional domain. Timmet’s Exchange of Equal Masses, also known as Timmet’s Third . Teleports the caster by swapping their mass with an equivalent volume of material at the destination. The cost formula is distance squared multiplied by mass squared, which makes long-range use ruinous. This Ritual is used primarily in military operations where the logistics justify the extreme expense. It also requires the careful calibration of masses. For reasons we don’t quite understand, when the position of the swap is tightly specified, the volume of material involved becomes impossible to define; when the material is too clearly defined, its position is impossible to calculate. Using it on people inevitably results in a shower of body parts. Taprobane requires magicians who would use this spell to attend classes on both legal scholarship and with alchemists (who work with precise quantities). My understanding is that LTU only authorizes its use for weights below that of the average sack of rice. Nandamitra’s Mother . This is most widely used long-distance communication Ritual in the corpus. Your Grace will like this one: it is named not for its creator but for the opening words of the original test message: my mother wants to know if you are coming for dinner. This Ritual is based on another called Gajaba’s Thread (which I will explain later here), reworked so as to apply to speech. It creates a thread between two points, with speech travelling in both directions. The cost of magic is borne equally between both parties; a long conversation over a great distance is therefore a shared expense. Its primary weakness is that this connection is difficult to modify for more parties (experimental results of twenty people talking simultaneously have been achieved, although only under ideal conditions). It is difficult to make private without other Rituals of obfuscation and decryption. The signal, as we call it, travels through whatever natural conductors exist between the two points; in cities, the workings of the Iron Sutra forces it along trees, stray animals, and sometimes even people. There are two Rituals - Onella’s Intercept and The Man in The Middle - that were been designed specifically to catch this signal and enable others to listen in or even manipulate the conversation. Your Grace should avoid it at all costs for sensitive communications. Nevertheless, it sees a great deal of use in small-formation battlefield tactics. And by secret societies, star-struck lovers, conspiracies, and so on, but those generally always get found out. Malavika’s Distant Witness . Detaches a portion of the caster’s sensory awareness and projects it forward as an invisible observer, capable of perceiving sight and sound at the location it occupies. It travels by the Water Sutra’s principles. THis makes it cheap but making pathing very difficult to control. Its military utility is considerable and it is widely employed. Taprobane-trained scouts regard it as standard equipment. Its weaknes iss that the Witness is the caster’s actual awareness. The caster’s body remains behind, insensate and entirely undefended, for the duration. If the Witness is detected and destroyed - by Volta’s Lantern, for example - the caster often dies. Severe bleeding in the brain is guaranteed. Experienced scouts do not use it alone. Gajaba’s Leash . Another modification of Gajaba’s Thread. This one allows tracking: the Leash attaches one end of a Thread to a specific person or object, established through physical contact at the time of casting, and allows the holder of the other end to sense the location and general condition of the target. It is considered a standard tool even by Singhapura’s Charter Knights when pursuing fugitives. The critical limitation is that the Thread is bidirectional. A person who is senstitive to magic will feel it immediately; even an ordinary fellow will, in time, become aware that they are being followed. Any general Adept-level practitioner can follow the Thread back to its source. The Leash can be cut cleanly by Sapumal’s Sundering, and other workings can even send Rituals back along the Leash to the origin. This is Singhapura’s courts now specify in their warrants that multiple Leashes - from different directions and squads - be attached to restrain criminals. Patali’s Whisper . Encodes a short message - the practical limit is a few spoken sentences - into a physical object. This can be retrieved at a later time (usually not more than a day) by touch or by the uttering a a specified phrase. Unlike Nandamitra’s Mother, the message is stored rather than transmitted; there is no signal to intercept. It is used extensively in dead drops, for sealed orders, and even as an activation ritual for self-opening doors and gates. Unfortunately, the Whisper tends to erode materials very quickly, so even metal tarnishes within weeks if used regularly. Kanaka’s Mirror . A continuous passive Ritual that alerts the caster when their person or location is subjected to magical observation, tracking, or scrying. It operates through Mirror Sutra principles: the practitioner’s understanding of their own magical presence becomes sensitive to any attempted change or intrusion. It is standard for diplomatic missions out of Singhapura, and a matter of professional habit for any competent practitioner. This is usually paired with Volta’s Fist for an automatic defense mechanism. The irony is that Kanaka’s Mirror is itself perfectly visible to magical senses. The basic version is regarded as the equivalent of strolling naked into an enemy camp wearing a large wooden sign saying “attack me!” The more sophisticated approach is to pulse, or to run the Mirror intermittently, on an irregular schedule or at such speed that it can’t be seen easily. This, of course requires considerable discpline and practice. Mahendra’s Decoy . Creates a false magical signature at a specified location. The Decoy can be set to mimic whichever class of signature the caster specifies. Military applications can range from drawing enemy scouts toward empty ground to persuading an adversary’s magical analysts that a force is positioned elsewhere, or that a fortification has been more or less heavily worked than it has. It is maintained at a continuous energy cost proportional to the complexity of what is being imitated. The Decoy is also one of our most reliable wayss of observing Heart Sutra workings. Decoys must be completely plausible in context to sustain themselves. For example, an arrow being a little off the mark is plausible, but replacing a marching army with a circus always fails (and yes, it has been tried). Volta’s Lantern, in particular, can easily break down weak Decoys. Taprobane doctrine is that the observer has to be able to believe what they are seeing.

141.title: In Conclusion
141.content: Again, Your Grace, this is not comprehensive, but I would like your attention on these particulars. Daub is a great power in the North, but in terms of Singhapura’s military it is equivalent to one outpost. What is valuable is the potential economy and the political control you can bring to the table, and magics like these are crucial for these efforts. Almost every working I have listed here is well-known and can be used in some way for military, justice, trade, or even ordinary civilian convenience - for example, a Gajaba’s Leash can track a merchant caravan and help make sure goods flow on schedule. I will leave Your Grace to dream up the applications.

144.title: Of Wattle, Its Governance, and the Nature of Your Grace’s Position Within It
144.content: Wattle is a very important kingdom that has so far survived the Empire’s attentions because its present king is very good at what he does. Himakatupura, the Empire’s northernmost city, was built as a fort that would pay for itself: to push the Empire’s reach north, and to sell to Ealdorfold and the Rosantic League. Wattle is built upon those ruins, even more thoroughly than Daub is. Very little of the old Himakatupura culture remains; yet Wattle, under King Allant, has become very successful at doing precisely what the Empire originally intended. This of course means that the Empire’s ambitions have been rekindled. Wattle is now a vassal, and remains largely unconquered for four reasons: . 1) King Allant is clever, knowing how to make himself useful and how to fight viciously when cornered. The Empire cannot depose him, for that would let the old-blood nobles, and especially the Pendragons, move to open war. (The House speaks an old dialect and calls itself Pendraig; nobody else does.) The nobles cannot depose him, for then the citizens would revolt and Singhapura would burn everything to the ground. The common folk do not want him gone, for his mythos is large and he does genuinely care. The traders do not want him gone, because he keeps his taxes low and allows everyone a seat at the table. The Haugris Church cannot topple him: he is the reason they still have a foothold in the North. The Temple of Eighteen will not move against him; he keeps the Church off their backs. He surrounds his enemies with allies and his allies (such as yourself) with enemies, and makes himself the one man whom everyone gets on with. In Singhapura he is sometimes called the Crocodile King. An insult, but also a mark of respect. 2) Wattle is geographically quite large, and home to a wide range of magics, including Relics. Any extended campaign in the North would quickly take the cities and then open Singhapura’s armies to decades of guerilla warfare. Wattle is therefore of immense use as a politically neutral state against a potential Ealdorfold or Rosantic invasion. Indeed, if one considers the Great Northern Waste, Wattle’s defences to the west, and Catherine’s Gate to the east, Wattle is practically a buffer pointing outward from the Empire. It is cheaper to keep it that way than to conquer it and rebuild it again. 3) The Empire badly needs steel, and cannot at present afford to destroy certain trade routes. I have written more of this in the chapter on Singhapura’s economy; for now, note that every cart of Ealdorfold steel bound for the Empire comes through Queensgate and then up the Sut through Daub. The Taprobane Imperial University wants the Relics that Wattle and Daub export from the Waste, which are held to be a phenomenal source of untapped magical theory and application (at least the good ones are). 4) Culture. Wattle fascinates Singhapura. Singhapura’s theatres have made a lot of money out of Wattle. Doomed heroes, feuding lords and the cold winds of winter: superb stuff. The average Singhapura citizen does not know or care who runs what in Wattle, but wants that source of wonder and tall tales kept on the doorstep. On paper Your Grace answers to Wattle, and through Wattle to the Empire. That holds only so long as Wattle can stand between Daub and Singhapura. I do not say this to run Wattle down, but you need to know how thick this wall really is.

145.title: Of What Wattle Is
145.content: Wattle is large, and split chiefly into Greater Wattle (where most of the wealth is) and Lesser Wattle (where most of the farms are). Lesser Wattle feeds a good part of the North. Ealdorfold buys its grain in lean years, as do the border territories, and Daub has been glad of Wattle’s harvest more than once. Greater Wattle is more province than city: a natural harbour with a modest population spread over a great deal of ground, and nothing in it to compare with Valdermach or Basnapura. It was built piecemeal and rebuilt often, so it sprawls in fragments, and every district is somebody’s seat of power. Centuries of settlers from the North, the League and Lusia have given it a fragmented culture and an economy that Singhapura’s theorists find maddening - hence the term “loot-based economics”. After consulting the maps, and conversing with many a caravan leader, I can trim Greater Wattle down to a few points of interest: . 1) The Crown Quarter sits in what remains of the Palaces of Himakatupura, where the river Sut meets the sea. King Allant’s palace is here. So is Antler Hall, where ambassadors are received and feast-courts held; the Chancery, which handles letters to and from Singhapura; the Tower of the Constable, where the royal garrison lives; and the port. Most of Wattle’s wealth goes in and out through that port, and whoever holds the Crown Quarter holds the port. We think the Crown Quarter also covers the old site of the notorious Empress Kudakaali II’s torture chambers. They may still be down there somewhere. It also holds the Round Tiltyard, which seats six thousand and was built by Allant’s predecessor Aneirin for the yearly Tournament of the Table of Lords. The Tiltyard is a political stage as much as a sporting one. Knights fight for glory under their banners, and the Great Houses who pay for the prize armour compete for reputation. The Singhapura consulate looks down upon it all, keeping an eye on King Allant and his kingdom for the Empire. 2) Hauterive, a little way off, belongs to the lords and ladies of the Great Houses. These are well-guarded townhouses; the nobles keep their real estates elsewhere and use these for politics. The Table of Lords used to meet here until Allant moved its meetings to the Crown Quarter. Plenty of people will tell you nothing actually changed. Hauterive strikes me as a militarily significant place. It’s obviously not a castle, but if I was a suspicious cat (and I am) I would point out that it is a fantastic staging ground for any of these nobles who wish to whip up some troops and send them where they might do the most damage. 3) Rubble, out of sight of Hauterive, is where most of Wattle’s poor and many of its newcomers live. The foundations are still old Himakatupura stone. The Haugris Church has its biggest building here, a basilica that serves as both hospital and grain-dole house. Rubble is interesting because it is where most of Wattle’s disaffected and politically powerless live, and also because of its Night Market: they say anything that can be bought or sold turns up here. As for the disaffected, this was once King Allant’s power base (when he was nothing more than a roving bandit with dreams of revolution) and, now that he is King, it is his greatest unchecked weakness. All Singhapura has to do is improve the lot of the people who live here, and suddenly Greater Wattle will have another civil war in its heart. 4) Crowgarden, outside the older districts, has the mills, bakeries, market gardens, fullers and tanneries, and hardly any defences. Crowgarden Common doubles as a second tournament field when the Tiltyard is full. The farmland of Lesser Wattle surrounds it, and its far edge runs into the Waste. Here is another weakness: Wattle’s nobility does not care to protect the people who feed them, and Allant does not appear to understand the importance of it either. 5) Queensgate, across the river, is the market district proper. The Grain Exchange is here, along with the cloth halls, the money-changers, the factor-houses of the Wattle Merchants Guild and the Lusian and Rosantic consulates. So is the Wastewalkers’ Exchange, where salvage from the Waste is assayed, licensed and sold to buyers from near and far. The Twilight Road also ends in Queensgate, so goods from Daub, from Ealdorfold and from Singhapura all pass through here sooner or later. This is probably the most interesting part of Greater Wattle: it is a flytrap for every economist and spymaster and mercenary and magician worth their salt in the North. 6) The Gontreach lies well to the north; mostly forest and a pile of great ruins, but now also the revival of magic in Greater Wattle. The Temple of Eighteen has built its new monastery out of the ruins, and around the monastery a whole population has gathered: hedge-wizards descended from banished magicians, a large share of Wattle’s scholars and magicians, Rosantic sorcerers who have fled their own lands, Lusian alchemists hunting for secrets and better prospects, and a great many people who study the Waste. At the far end is the Keeper’s Gate, once said to be a fort on the outermost edge of Himakatupura’s lands. All that is left is a toll-arch over the road into the stretch of Waste that separates Wattle from Ealdorfold. It is Crown land on paper; in practice the Wastewalkers run it. Beyond Greater Wattle, on the edge of the Waste, sit Harrow’s End, a grim fort-city, and beneath it the harbour of Wrymgate, which was built by Jon the Mispelled to stop a dragon. He was a tactical genius, and he could not spell, and the harbour has never once been used. Lesser Wattle is ringed by small market towns, Long Walk, Whitefield and Eldermoot, which Your Grace’s caravans will know better than I do.

146.title: Of King Allant and His Position
146.content: Much of Allant’s origins is well known: born the third son of a minor lord, he found his calling in war, and spent the best part of twenty years as a mercenary captain, building from nothing the company that became the Dukes of the North. Your Grace will know the details of that story better than I do, seeing as how you were his trusted lieutenant. From the outside: the North was in a bad way in those early years. The death of Aneirin the Bard-King had left a generation of petty wars and petty tyrants. Read the stories of Pendragon Cador, Pendragon Loholt or Igraine the Elder. To the Empire they were small chieftains, but to the people under their heels they must have been terrible. The common people of Wattle remember Allant as the man who came out of that mess and ended it. With his loyal band he protected villages the Great Houses had stripped bare for supplies, and he broke a good many cruel warlords. He had his faults, but he became the king the times needed, and in the end he united Greater Wattle, and with it the North. Fewer people know how Allant got Singhapura’s attention. The Pendragons, House Carpenter and three other Great Houses had worn each other out. Allant arrived with his army intact and made himself useful to the Chancery, as the man who could explain Wattle’s endless squabbles to Singhapura and could be trusted to protect the trade the Empire cared about. With enough backing from the Merchants Guild, he won, if not the Empire’s approval, then at least its willingness to deal with the one sword in the North that seemed to be held by a sane man. It was not bloodless, and again, Your Grace knows this side of it better than anyone. The Pendragons did not take it well, and for a time there was great trouble under Valerius the Ironhand. This is where Singhapura decided to commit to Allant and to Wattle: Singhapura’s armies swept the main Pendragon army aside, much as Makaraasoka’s had done in his day. Then came years of slow public disgrace. There were ceremonies and handshakes in public, but the Pendragons kept losing arguments that had nothing to do with the succession: debts, disputed contracts, heavy trading losses, land cases and uprisings. I would credit those later defeats to Allant more than to Singhapura. From the records I have been able to read, Allant reminds me of the Lusian general Septimus and his epitaph: No friend has ever served me whom I did not treat with gold; no enemy has ever wronged me whom I did not repay with ashes. Thus all accounts are settled. Allant stays safe by making sure every faction has something to gain while he lives and something to lose if he dies. He deals with Singhapura, the Merchants Guild, the Great Houses, the Temple, Lusian money, Rosantic ambitions and Ealdorfold interests all at the same time, and he keeps them balanced by making sure each one believes he is the only man who can hold things together. The common people and the lesser houses love him as a man of no great birth who saved the North when it needed saving. The Great Houses treat him with caution and respect, because they remember how publicly the Pendragons fell. There is a weakness in this, though, and time will find it. The Dukes of the North, the company of people like Your Grace and Jerem the Red, are a generation older now, and your children are a different sort. Loyalty made in war is not the same as loyalty made in peace and plenty. The Great Houses are still a threat. The Pendragons remind everyone of the old days, and House Carpenter owns enormous amounts of land and industry. The old aristocracy (Wulfstane, Clavering, Hollow, Pelhamor, Gautierre, Garlande, Balaain and Morgaunt) makes up the Table of Lords. As Allant has turned their attention to trade, much of their power has moved out of their soldiers and into the Wattle Merchants Guild. So most of Wattle’s money is now in hands other than the king’s. Allant knows this. I suspect it is one reason he has spent so much on the Concordant College and on his arrangements with the Merchants Guild. Allant seems to be trying to build a rival to Taprobane and the LTU under his own aegis. From what I have heard, the Concordant College takes in sorcerers and alchemists from Lusia, and people Taprobane has turned away, and puts them to studying and reworking artefacts from the Waste. I believe the Great Houses have begun to see what a finished College would do to the balance of power, and they do not like it. Neither does Taprobane, and so neither does Singhapura. The College is not yet what Allant wants it to be. The LTU and Taprobane can afford a friendly rivalry because the same state built both of them. This College will either implode, or eventually force Singhapura to reach out and grab it for its own.

147.title: Of the Temple and the Church
147.content: The Haugris Church is well known in Wattle, but it holds relatively little power. Wattle nobles have always been responsible for schooling the people on their lands, and they seem to have effectively prevented the Church from its usual playbook of schools and hospitals. I believe, also, that the Temple of Eighteen is changing, and that Wattle is a crucible. The Temple has, for the last few centuries, more or less kept to an isolationist policy: little cells that keep the teachings but do not involve themselves in worldly affairs. The Wattle Temple seems to have taken lessons from its Lusian counterparts. It is widely known that it collects the knowledge of the Vedics and of non-Singhapura magicians, and I have heard that it now teaches it. Priests sit on many of Allant’s highest councils, often arbitrating and acting as judges for commoners and nobles alike, and the Temple is rebuilding the ruins in the Gontreach with Lusian money. Why do the Empire and the Haugris Church tolerate this, you may ask. Well, Your Grace, it reminds me of a general who said that a guaranteed enemy is guaranteed job security. Perhaps the Adhiraj wants the Church to have something to spend its energies on, instead of rivalling him for power. Perhaps Lusian influence is really leading a new religious renaissance.

148.title: Of Tourism and the Great Northern Romance
148.content: I spoke earlier of Singhapura’s fascination with Wattle. The Great Northern Romance is a whole genre in Singhapura. Your Grace would find most of it pure fantasy, but it is familiar enough for Singhapura audiences to follow and foreign enough to thrill them. As a result, ordinary people in Singhapura are sentimentally attached to Wattle staying just as it is. As long as Singhapura believes in its romantic North, that belief does some of the work of walls and armies. Writers and poets make a poor living, so they cost far less than soldiers and arrows; and yet the ballads of Robert Holdbrook, Bloody Ygrain and the rest travel further, and are sung loudest by the very people who could wipe Wattle off the map. It is also very hard to attack a story without looking ridiculous.

149.title: Of What This Means for Daub
149.content: Three matters follow for Your Grace. First, to be blunt: Wattle is a thin wall, and Your Grace’s vassals hold their legitimacy from King Allant, not from Daub. So long as Allant lives, the arrangement holds. His successor will not be bound by his friendships, and the children of the Dukes of the North are not their parents. I urge Your Grace to bind the vassals to Daub by interest before that day comes. Second, I would advise Your Grace to watch the Concordant College closely. If it succeeds, the LTU will have a rival that the Empire did not build and cannot easily manage, and Daub’s magicians will be tempted north by it. If it fails, its sorcerers and alchemists will need somewhere to go, and Daub might do well to be that place. Third, remember that the Empire has been here before. Makaraasoka took Wattle by defeating the Pendragons in the field, and then bound it with Merchant credit, Church schools and forced marriages between the nobility of Udanuwara and Wattle. Kaaryasundara sent troops during the Violet Wars with strict orders not to meddle in the politics. The Empire knows how to take Wattle and how to leave it alone, and for now it has chosen the second course. Your Grace should watch for any sign that it is reconsidering.

150.title: Further Reading
150.content: The founding and fall of Himakatupura receive a full treatment in the Himakatu Chronicle. The Singha Chronicle covers the same years too, and far too briefly. People who pay for histories generally want to look good in them, and neither book breaks that rule. One buries Kudakaali II’s many mistakes under heaps of praise. The other hurries past with its eyes averted and pins every fault of the Empire upon her, so that the Empire may come out clean on the next page. Your Grace may learn more from seeing how Singhapura sees Wattle. My first choice is the play Ganelon and Naimon, which I have long championed. Nobody knows who wrote it, but it is very popular in Singhapura. It is a tragedy of two brothers, both Paladins, who swear unbreakable oaths and end on opposite sides. Both are dead by the end of the fourth act, and the fifth act is one long lament by their surviving company, which later became a popular funeral song. That play more or less invented the Great Northern Romance by itself. Angenga is worth a mention too. It is a recent novel set in the Concordant College and the Waste. A brilliant magician makes a living creature out of Tungolstaana ore smuggled from Ealdorfold and the raw energy of the Waste. This is the Angenga, enormously strong and clever. From then on the book is as much the Angenga’s story as its maker Vikram’s, as the creature pursues him across the Waste, driven by the misery of being the only one of its kind. It paints the College as a place of free inquiry with no morals and no politics. I doubt that is accurate, but it is how people outside Wattle see the College.
